product_title: Outdoor Technology Wired Chips Universal Snow Helmet Audio
review_headline: Awesome system, fantastic value, don't hesitate!
review_body:
I purchased these for a recent ski trip and will start out by saying - if you're hesitating about purchasing these, go ahead and do it, you won't regret it!!

I am an intermediate skiier and have only recently gotten to the point of being comfortable with music on the slopes - last time I brought earbuds but they were too uncomfortable under helmet pads. These integrated seamlessly into my helmet (Smith Holt), though I had to switch the right and left headphone due to the zipper orientation on the earpad pouch. Installation was easy and the earphones fit well into the ear pads without making them too tight against my ears. Since they're not earbuds, they don't block out the sound around you, so I was still able to easily carry on conversations and hear the snow. The sound quality was pretty nice, lacking a little bass but not nearly as tinny as I was expecting for headphones in this price range. The highest volume is plenty loud and leaks some sound (others sitting on the lift could hear music) but I wouldn't expect to have it that loud other than for testing the limits of the speakers.

The button control interface is great - you just tap on the left ear once to play/pause, twice to fast forward, hold for voice, etc. Volume can only be controlled via the knob on the inline controller, but you shouldn't need to adjust that often and it's possible to do so with gloves still on. This made it easy and fun to interact with the music/voice even while traveling downhill at high speeds.

The killer feature of these is the ability to initiate voice control when plugged into a phone - I have a Samsung Galaxy S3 and was able to control it using google voice, meaning I could request songs ('play some artistName"), text friends ("text person message") and check the time ("what time is it") all through the headphones. I could do all these things without ever having to take off gloves (a big deal!) or pull out my phone, which was super convenient.

If you're debating between these and a bluetooth version, know that unlike the bluetooth ones, these do not require charging. The cord is coated in a braided coating and seems like it will be pretty resilient, plus it's smooth/wide enough not to easily get caught in a coat zipper. Also included are 2 stickers (red, square with a walking man logo) and a carrying bag. Very happy with this purchase.

EDIT: after a winter of sporadic skiing, the chips had started to occasionally lose sound in one ear, a problem which worsened until sounds only ever came from one ear. I emailed support and they had a new cable immediately mailed to me, which has fixed the problem. product_title: FiiO X3-II High Resolution Music Player (2nd Generation)
review_body:
Pros:
- This player has very rich sound, and excellent power. The bass is full, the mids are incredibly detailed, the highs are delicate and crisp.
- A choice of memory chip is a welcome feature.
- It is a good match for Bose earbuds.
- The dial shuttle takes some getting used to, but eventually I found I like it better than buttons.
- There are five or so tasteful themes.
- Battery life is acceptable.
- It comes with a soft plastic cover, and screen protectors. There is already a screen protector installed. Very nice touch!
- USB 3.0.
- Charges very quickly with a 2 Amp wall charger.
- 10-band graphic equalizer. Lots of equalizer presets.
- Supports many audio formats.
Cons:
- There is only one custom equalizer setting. Two would be perfect, one each for quiet and loud environments.
- The battery life is not as good as the Sony Walkman 2.
- It is bulkier and heavier than other popular players.
- The font size is very small and hard to read. I ended up picking the theme with the best contrast so I could read the menus. Still, with less than good eyesight I can barely read the display.

In summary:
Superb sound detail. Lots of great features. Very configurable. Solid player, with generous goodies. What's not to like? This is one of the best examples of "you get what you pay for". I had a Sony Walkman 2 for years, and was happy with it but I outgrew the memory. I find the FiiO X2 Gen 2 is a big step up from the Walkman 2, and worth the investment it in many ways. I would recommend this to anyone who is picky about sound quality, or has difficulty hearing the finer features of music. Everything else is gravy.

product_title: IBIS 2-port HDMI Switch, 1080p and 4K @ 30Hz, Bi-directional (1x2 or 2x1), HDCP 1.x and 2.2, Dolby-TrueHD/DTS-HD 7.1 Surround, 3D, by Sewell
review_headline: it is excellent; it is reliable
review_body:
The four stars I give the IBIS 3x1/1x3 HDMI switch arises for its ability to fulfill my needs; it does not detract from its excellence or reliability. As I recall, some other reviews here for this item touted its ability to substitute for the "V" part of a KVM switch when HDMI video connections are desired. That is, it would mean that you only need to push a second button when supplementing a KVM which doesn't support HDMI.

In that respect, it is excellent; it is reliable. But it really wasn't made for that purpose. It needs to re-establish the HDMI handshake when returning to the original PC. This still works great, if one only has a single monitor connected to the HDMI switch and therefore to the PC connected to the switch. However, if you also have a second monitor (such as my HDTV) connected DIRECTLY to the PC, the computer relocates the desktop to such a second monitor when switching the HDMI-connected monitor away from the PC. This by itself isn't much of a problem: the desktop re-establishes itself on the switched monitor when switching back to the original PC. But if you set up Windows Media Center to use the monitor/HDTV with the direct connection to the PC, Media Center itself relocates to the switched monitor. This is enough of a nuisance that I chose a different strategy, mentioned below.

It is still a feasible choice for the purpose I had in mind for it, but it is not ideal for my peculiar configuration. I bought the switch with the idea that it might fall short, coupled with the idea that I can redeploy it differently if it didn't meet my expectations. And I did that -- too. It is now part of my AVR/HDTV configuration. And I suspect that I can use it to switch between two PCs for that purpose, as opposed to using it for my desktop monitor. Turns out -- my BenQ gaming monitor fulfills the "V" part of my KVM needs as well as any HDMI-capable KVM might do, except for the inconvenience I suffer in havingto switch both the KVM and the monitor itself.

The only other drawback? HDMI itself, which only allows for a monitor/HDTV running a 60 Hz refresh-rate. For most people, that's not much of a shortcoming, and it is no shortcoming of the IBIS. I suspect that future revisions to the HDMI standard will allow for faster refresh rates, but even now 60 Hz is the limit for "Ultra-HD" or 4K monitors and TVs.

product_title: Sennheiser PX 100-II
review_headline: Obvious BASS BOOST improved with burn-in -- and then WOW!
review_body: Right out of the package -- quick first impression was positive. Good detail. Relative coherence. Nice bass warmth and "punch." But after a few musical samplings I became more and more disturbed by a consistent mid-bass boost on everything I played.  On early CD material, which routinely suffers from chronic "digititus" and is notoriously "thin" and harmonically truncated, the coloration adds a positive dose of "warmth." However, on more contemporary material (and/or quality re-masterings from original analog tape), the exaggerated mid-bass tends to can get thumpy -- and lumpy.  After some more listening in another session -- I was sorry for the purchase. My conclusion at the time was -- these headphones are (egads!) Bose wannbes (with all that artificial thick mid-bass nonsense).  Now, after listening primarily during heavy-duty cardio on my Airdyne (using the PX100s mated with Sansa Clip MP3 Player) and some off the sound card on my notebook -- the verdict is not quite as regretful.  No. I'm not 100% satisfied with the purchase. But the overall package -- fairly good retrieval of musical information, relative comfort (tho by no means luxurious) and "perceived value" have me right at the 6 out of 10 rating point.  Good musical performance. With obvious issue. Good value. But not outstanding due to the irrevocable EQ.  A bit of a caveat emptor product. But many will probably love it!  1-13-2015 Update: with extensive burn-in the bass region has improved -- tho still EQ'd a bit, the balance is notably better.  Updated rating = 7 out of 10 stars.  A solid "B" performance.  Update #2  These phone need extensive burn-in and after 100s of hours I have upgraded to 5 stars!  Put it this way, dollar per dollar, these have to be one of the preeminent values in the headphone universe!  I am now using with the excellent FiiO X1 with 100 uncompressed WAV files -- the results are stunning -- way beyond what one would expect for the$$$. I've tried a ton of in-ear buds at twice the price and these things embarrass most -- though of course you do NOT have the acoustic isolation of buds. review_headline: Good fully automatic charger for a wide range of batteries.
review_body: This was probably more bells and whistles than I needed, but some of the info, like cell voltage, is fairly useful.  Unfortunately, while there's a nice bar graph that shows what the charge state of the battery is, there's nothing that tells you what you really want to know - how much longer it will take to finish charging.    Lost one star because the maximum 500 mA charging current is pretty anemic.  Compared to my old Lexar charger, this one takes 3 times as long to charge my NiMh AA batteries.  If you need a faster charge for batteries with capacities in excess of 2000 mAh, or you need your batteries charged quickly in less than 4 hours, look for a different charger.  The only batteries that charged in less than 4 hours (from being completely discharged) were the 800 mAh 16340 cells and 900 mAh AAA cells.  2000 mAh AA NiMh batteries took over 6 hours.    Lost another star for what is best summarized as DON'T BUMP THE CHARGER, because the batteries are not held securely and are easily dislodged from the contacts.  The battery compartment's width is designed to accomodate C-size cells.  When you stick a smaller cell in, NOTHING keeps it from rolling off the contacts other than the spring tension.  Charging AAA cells in this charger is reminiscent of setting a mousetrap.  Get one battery in place and the other comes off the contacts.    Got one star back because the low charging rate turned into a blessing.  I can use this charger with my portable Goalzero solar panel.  The charger that came with it only charges four AA or AAA batteries and must charge all four at the same time.  The Lexar wouldn't charge even one cell because of the higher current requirements.  Like Baby Bear's porridge, the D2's power requirement is just right.

For the audiophiles out there, I'm running both 15 & 20 amp dedicated circuits. Both outlets are cryoed hospital grade. The 20 is ZeroSurge (no MOVs) panel protected; the 15 has the APC. End result is silence without limits :-) Most importantly, cleaned up protection from the AZ grid.
Thumbs up for APC...TrippLite, how about bringing back the rack mount unit?

product_title: Brainwavz Zirconia Headphone Stand - Suitable For All Headphone Sizes
review_body:
This is a nice, inexpensive headphone stand that's fine for lighter headphones.

A headphone stand is not a necessity but I grew to like them as a way of keeping organized. Instead of throwing your headphone on the desk or hanging on a nail or something like that, you put the stand someplace and hang the 'phones on the stand.

This one is nice enough looking, which is a definite requirement. What's the point of an ugly stand? It has a short round base and a thick vertical piece, notched at the top. You just put the middle of the headphone band in the notch. You can wrap the cord around the bottom if you like, or dangle it behind a bookcase.

Other stands, like the Peridot, are larger and allow you to wrap the headset fully around the stand. This provides much greater stability at the cost of, well --- cost, in addition to size and bulk. The Zirconia is compact and inexpensive. It won't tip with lightweight phones, but heavier phones present more of a challenge. The single point of support also will eventually make a dent in the cushion of the headband of heavier phones.

So it's your choice. I like the Peridot more, but if you have small headphones and want something compact that fits easily on the edge of a bookshelf, the Zirconia is fine. I give it four stars for economy and looks. One star off for limited utility with large headsets.

review_headline: Fantastic Speaker With Great Features, But One Drawback
review_body: Researched all similar options for a small bluetooth speaker and finally decided on this one. I couldn't find another one that had all the features this one does: volume control, track forward/back, micro SD card ability, microphone, auxiliary jack and cable, wall plug and USB cable for charging, appealing design. Speaker definitely has great full sound for its size. Impressive. The cables it comes with are shorter than I'd like, but I have much longer cables I can use instead (or you could easily buy another longer cable for very little money) so that's not a big deal to me. The biggest issue I ran into is that the speaker will not play when fully charged and still plugged in. It will play when plugged in while it's still charging, but once fully charged, nothing. I'm forced to unplug it at that point to be able to use it (hence I docked a star on the rating). Which stinks because ideally I just wanted to keep this little speaker always plugged in so I didn't have to think about when it needed to be charged. Maybe the one I got is defective in that regard, I don't know. I may try ordering another one and see if that one works the same way, but I suspect it will. I love this little speaker otherwise so that particular drawback is a bummer.

review_headline: Excellent wall mount for Sonos Play:1
review_body:
I wasn't sure if the ball mount could hold a play 1 speaker, especially with the longer angle arm. I needed the angle to use the speakers as surround with my couch against the wall.

I mounted the bracket to the wall with screw in type drywall anchors. The ball mount is even more versatile than I expected and you can angle the speakers in almost any direction. I have mine angled slightly forward and downwards. The mount is very stable and has no play once fully tightened. It hasn't drooped in over 2 weeks and shows no signs that it will.

The key is to fully tighten the ball mount the very first time. It has friction ridges, and if you do not tighten it very well the first time, those ridges can become dull when the speaker droops, and then no amount of tightening will help.

product_title: Silverback Speaker Wire by Sewell
review_body:
I was very pleased with the quality of the cables. I ordered 4 10' cables, and I had a similar experience to other reviewers with respect to some the banana plugs being randomly loose when I received them. Can't say I can figure out why this is, as it is simply a matter of just finishing screwing them tight with your hand. I did fully unscrew and remove the banana plug outer casing on several of the plugs to examine how the plug is attached to the cable, and to check out the raw cable itself. I was impressed to find that the banana plug itself is attached to the cable by two separate threaded screws on opposites sides and ends of the shaft, and held approximately 1/3 to 1/2 inch of the exposed cable wire. All of the banana plugs that I opened up were very well clamped down on the wire by these two screws despite some of the outer casings simply not being hand screwed all the way to not rattle, etc. Also, having handled a fair amount of wire and cable in my day, this wire does appear to indeed by 12 AWG as advertised (I've noted reviews of some other cables here were purchasers were skeptical that their product was really the advertised gauge, so figured I'd offer that observation that these seem to be).

As for working with the cables themselves, they were easy to get to lay pretty flat once uncoiled, and the banana plugs fit very securely in both my speaker posts (Fluance XL7F tower speakers and Fluance XLC7 center channel) as well as my receiver (Onkyo TX-NR3009). Sound quality was noticeably improved from some older Monster cable that I had been using previously. I highly recommend these cables for the value the represent--the quality is very good and this is overall a very worthwhile overall purchase!

product_title: Polk Audio Omni S2 Compact Wireless Wi-Fi Music Streaming Speaker with Play-Fi
review_body:
Forgive the long review. These speakers are a new product category for many people and the intent is to make this review as complete and comprehensive as possible.

Several well-known audio manufacturers (and some new-comers) are jumping in to a relatively new category of product, the internet speaker. I use the term \\"jumping in\\" quite literally because most of what's being sold ranges from ill-conceived to not-ready-for-prime-time. The idea sounds good on paper, in fact the idea sounds great. But the execution of delivering a viable consumer product is falling far short of what it could be.

An internet speaker is basically a table radio that tunes in stations that supply an audio feed over the internet. No internal tuner, you use your phone/tablet to link to those audio feeds. Some internet speakers only need to be told once what to connect to and they stay connected even if you turn your phone off or leave the house. One disadvantage of the Polk is that the phone must keep the app open (draining the batteries) and cannot be taken out of range of your WIFI signal.

DO YOU REALLY WANT AN INTERNET SPEAKER

The idea of an internet speaker sounds pretty high tech but the reality of what it is and what it does raises a big question of whether it's worth it. There are numerous ways to hook up an extension speaker (which is really all these are ... most need to be plugged in to work). An internet speaker simply permits you to play audio from online sources or in most cases from a playlist on your phone or tablet. If you have a device with Bluetooth there are hundreds of models of Bluetooth speakers that cost less, often far less, than an internet speaker, which is generally a basic portable speaker with the same capability you already have built into the speaker, and you still need your phone/tablet to control it. The lure of thousands of \\"free\\" stations fades quickly when you get your first internet speaker and learn that a huge percentage of those are \\"free samples\\" that interrupt your music every few minutes with commercials from \\"Progressive Flo\\" (voted the most hated commercial ever) making duck sounds at 10x the volume of the program content. If you want to kill Flo you have to subscribe, but if you like variety in your music you must subscribe to EACH content provider, usually at between $10 - $25 per month each. That would be like having to subscribe to each individual channel you watch on TV. The cost of having a wide range of music content to choose from could cost you several hundred dollars a month. Your other option is to pick ONE music service (like Pandora, Spotify, etc) and pay for it each month but you're still limited to what playlists are available from them. And unfortunately, Polk has a very limited choice of such subscription services available and missing are some of the most popular, including SiriusXM. So maybe what you really want is a nice table radio?

There is no easy direct comparison between the current brands of internet speakers like Sonos; Denon/HEOS; Pure/Jongo; etc, they are much too different in terms of design and how they operate. The most glaring issue with all of them is that there is no interchangeability or compatibility. If you have a Denon in one room and a Polk in another room you have to run them from two completely separate and incompatible apps, not all of which can access the same music service. It's like owning 2 TV's that each require service from a different, and incompatible, cable company.

If you stick with one brand (as I'm sure the manufacturer hopes you will do) you shouldn't run into many compatibility issues. However if you mix brands, as I do, there are some weird issues syncing the exact same channel between different internet speakers. For example, I can choose a particular music service and select a channel. I can do that with 3 internet speakers from 3 different companies so I \\"fill my house with music\\". Sounds simple, right? Guess what? Each speaker is out of sync, playing the SAME station. Sometimes by a little, sometimes by a lot (it varies). Sometimes a commercial starts on one speaker while the other is still playing music, then a DIFFERENT commercial starts on the second speaker. The result is chaos and definitely not what anyone would have in mind as a whole-house music system.

Internet speaker systems tend to be ultra-sensitive to even brief interruptions in the WIFI signal (most routers hiccup numerous times a day). Instead of a loss of sound for a second or two, however, the speaker can \\"forget\\" its connection, which requires re-pairing it with your phone again, starting from scratch. The Polk is far easier to pair and drops its signal FAR less than the Denon HEOS which has a reputation of NOT playing more often than it IS playing. The following observations from me, being an owner and user of each brand, might help:

SONOS

Sonos is pretty much the granddaddy of internet speakers. They are differentiated by being one of the companies with no legacy in audio or speaker manufacture but the one who forged new territory in this yet emerging technology. So you would expect them to get the technology end right, and hopefully deliver a good sounding speaker. You would be right. Using the Sonos app is easier and more intuitive than any of the others and it offers the widest range of music sources and connectivity. Their speakers are very contemporary looking and, while not the leaders in their category for kicking out the best sounding music, they are remarkably listenable for a company with no real history in speaker hardware design and manufacture. Sonos has thrown down the gauntlet in terms of product pricing and what this genre of product is expected to do, with the others left to try to outdo them, or at least match them in a game of \\"me too\\".

JONGO by Pure

This is a company who has some recognition in the European market but never caught on in the U.S. They have by far the most cumbersome and convoluted app design and like Sonos, are not an old-line pioneer in speaker design. Much if not most of what they do is non-standard. Their speakers are slightly cutting edge and have some truly unique technology such as the user-selectable sound surround field settings that virtually turn one speaker into several. To their credit they have a user-replaceable rechargeable system but to their discredit they have chosen to make the weird decision to not built Bluetooth into the device but rather utilize a plug-in dongle.

HEOS by Denon

This is a product you want to like but they just can't seem to get it to work. The #1 problem with HEOS is that it has a terrible memory problem; it constantly forgets that it's connected and has to be re-linked, sometimes several times a day. Their method of linking their wireless speakers to your wireless device is inexplicably a WIRE, making it very inconvenient if you prefer to locate the speaker in a hard-to-reach place. But even using a hard wire to connect them, often the speaker simply refuses to connect. The other side of the coin is that they win hands down for sound quality by a wide margin. They also have at this point the weakest repertoire of source options, notably lacking AirPlay and Sirus XM and they do not support BlueTooth. HEOS speakers are house-current powered only so they can't be run on battery power for things like backyard use. HEOS is also the winner for looks, they weren't afraid to break the mold and design speakers that are at the cutting edge of trend setting.

OMNI by Polk

Polk was just not ready yet to release this product category. They hit the market by acknowledging almost non-existent support for iOS (DUH!) and their Android app is clunky. They make an offer to iOS users to download a desktop app but it is worse than clunky. The most unfortunate thing about Polk is that, despite the fact that they are one of the most respected names in speakers, this series is toy-like in look, feel and sound quality. And horribly overpriced for what you get. The owner experience is that the speaker looks, feels and sounds like a $75 utility speaker but costs twice that. For what? Frankly, not much.

SUMMARY OF POLK OMNI:

1. They are two 2\\" speakers, they sound good but not spectacular, they are only 2\\" speakers
2. Doesn't feel expensive as it is
3. Easy setup, stayed connected better than competitive brands
4. App is poorly designed and difficult to navigate
5. App download warns you that the app is huge (77 MB) - and that's to your cell phone
6. According to Polk, their Apple app is not ready yet but yet they have released it
7. Contrary to the instructions, the indicator light on back doesn't do anything
8. Sounds like a medium-price table radio, in other words it sounds like you would expect it to
9. White grill cloth looks weird on black body
10. Must sign a contract before being permitted to use the required Polk app

So the bottom line is that these are not bad speakers. Nor are they great speakers. They are cursed with trying to exist in a product category that has been rushed to market and can be very frustrating for the average consumer. As is true with competing models you can't just press a switch and start listening to \\"the radio\\". Listening to some sound sources is difficult and listening to other sound sources is impossible. The most unfortunate thing about Polk is that, despite the fact that they are one of the most respected names in speakers, this series is toy-like in look, feel and sound quality. And horribly overpriced for what you get. The owner experience is that the speaker looks, feels and sounds like a $75 utility speaker but costs twice that. For what? Frankly, not much.

SUMMARY OF POLK OMNI:

1. They are two 2\\" speakers, they sound good but not spectacular, they are only 2\\" speakers
2. Doesn't feel expensive as it is
3. Easy setup, stayed connected better than competitive brands
4. App is poorly designed and difficult to navigate
5. App download warns you that the app is huge (77 MB) - and that's to your cell phone
6. According to Polk, their Apple app is not ready yet but yet they have released it
7. Contrary to the instructions, the indicator light on back doesn't do anything
8. Sounds like a medium-price table radio, in other words it sounds like you would expect it to
9. White grill cloth looks weird on black body
10. Must sign a contract before being permitted to use the required Polk app

So the bottom line is that these are not bad speakers. Nor are they great speakers. They are cursed with trying to exist in a product category that has been rushed to market and can be very frustrating for the average consumer. As is true with competing models you can't just press a switch and start listening to \\"the radio\\". Listening to some sound sources is difficult and listening to other sound sources is impossible. Rated on their own merit, the Polk Omni rates between 3-stars and 4-stars. They get bumped up to 4-stars primarily because they seem to be easier to use and more stable in operation than their competition.

Compared to my more expensive Sennheiser 580's the sound is a bit rougher but the tonal balance is actually a bit nicer, and there's fairly decent passive (no battery, no cancellation) isolation from outside sounds. Idk but I'd guess it's about 9-12db reduction in ambient noise. It wouldn't completely block noise on an airplane, but it would help and for less severe settings it's more than adequate.  I use these outside and it pretty well blocks the nearby traffic (school zone) while I'm working on the computer. The impedance works well w/ my older macbook (unlike the 580s), I don't own an mp3 player. product_title: Sony SRSX5 Portable NFC Bluetooth Wireless Speaker System
review_headline: I thought the JBL Charge 2 sounded much better, and I started to feel buyer's remorse
review_body:
I bought this speaker without ever having heard it in-person before, just solely on the reviews all over the internet. I did not buy it on a whim, I had researched both this speaker and the JBL Charge 2. Last week, before I received this speaker in the mail, I tested the sound on both this speaker and the JBL Charge 2 at my friend's house (a tech junkie), and at the time, I thought the JBL Charge 2 sounded much better, and I started to feel buyer's remorse.

This week, the SRS-X5 arrived at my house, and I decided I wanted to test the two speakers again, before I return it. So I borrowed my friend's JBL Charge 2, and tested both of them at my own house. Wow! The Sony SRS-X5 blew the Charge 2 out of the water! I'm really into bass, and the Charge 2 is really heavy on bass, so I thought it sounded good during the first test. But I realized when testing at home, in the quiet of my own house, that you could actually hear the singer's voice and background beats with the SRS-X5. You wouldn't even know that those background beats were there with the Charge 2 because the bass is too heavy and distorted.

product_title: Mount-It Wall Mount
review_headline: How to hang this with one person
review_body: Love this heavy duty mount.  Sturdy and well made.  If you have to put it up by yourself,  this worked well for me:  found the studs using a stud finder,  extend the arms of the mount all the way out,  put the mount over your shoulder with the wall plate in front of you, hold it up to the wall and put a small level on top of the wall plate (helps if it has a magnetic side to it), make sure it is level and mark your four drill spots (if you can only mark the top two, the bottom holes are 7 1/4 inches from the top holes, use a laser level to mark the bottom drill spots), once you have made the drill spots, get the 4 lag bolts and washers in your pocket, get a ratchet with the correct bit,  pick the mount up again the same way as stated above, start the lag bolts with your fingers--you will be able to twist it into the drywall far enough that it will stay up,  then start ratcheting in the lag bolts--put in the top two first and the mount will hang on its own,  secure all four lag bolts and you're done!

product_title: Sony Hi-Res Stereo Headphones
review_body:
These are peculiar headphones.
A quick listen can result in a "meh" or "wow". It takes a while to appreciate them and (yes I will say this, athough I never believed in it) it takes a while for them to break-in.
The first week I listened to them I felt they were a mixed bag: absolutely wonderful with some CDs and pretty disappointing with others.
They have this sadistic pleasure to alter the sound-balance and soundstage with different recordings in an extreme way.
I wasn't able (still not) to label them laid-back or upfront, because they can be both depending on the recording.
Yes my Denon D5000s and Audio Technica ATH-A900Xs both have enough clarity to show differences in recordings as well, but overall they have their own 'default' sonic character which is pretty consistent, and yes depending on the recording they can be both a bit more laid back or more upfront, but never as extreme as the Sony's.
The difference in loudness between recordings is another thing that bothered me a bit. The first week I constantly had to adjust the volume, sometimes in the same track. Their dynamic range is incredible, and I had a hard time figuring out at what volume level to listen to.

Now that I am used to them and they have 'broken-in' those differences in loudness and soundstage are no longer an issue and I can safely say that they are wonderful and that they are the best pair of headphones I've ever owned.

review_body:
[[VIDEOID:68b55820a0a99267c35f79431a51f47a]] Full Disclosure: I was given this product in exchange for a fair and honest review.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I was not really expecting too much from this headset but in fact I was pleasantly surprised by them.

The headset arrived nicely presented in an attractive windowed display box with the information on it largely in Chinese. Inside was the headset itself, a red USB to micro-USB charging cable, a white 3.5mm jack to 3.5mm jack audio cable, a warranty card (in Chinese) and a dual language User Guide which although poorly translated was large, easy to read and simple enough to make sense of. There was also, and this is not something I have encountered before in a Bluetooth headset in this price range, a user replaceable rechargeable battery.

The build quality seems pretty good throughout. The body of the unit is made from a tough plastic with what feel to be durable hinges where the earcups swivel and revolve, the mechanism to extend the arms seems positive and firm too. The rather small on-ear cups are reasonably well padded as it the headband, the earcups are marked as L or R, which is nice. The left earcup has an input for the jack cable which allows the device to be used when the battery is dead or with non Bluetooth audio devices. On the side of this earcup at the top there is groove you can get your nail into to gain access to the battery compartment where the replaceable reusable battery is housed. I mention this because the User Guide illustration is unclear which earcup the battery is housed in and I spent ages trying to open the wrong one! The battery compartment cover is secured by a magnet and once the trick is known can be easily removed. Another nice touch is the inclusion of a small ribbon to prevent the battery cover getting lost. The right earpiece has a micro-USB slot for charging the battery as well as the controls for the unit. There is a large and easy to feel central MUltifunction button with the volume and track controls housed along the four sides of the earpiece panel. The buttons are large and well positioned but are not easy easy as they could be to find touch alone. Perhaps it's just me but instinctively I went to press the top button for volume UP, the lower for volume Down and the front and rear for track controls. No, here it is the other way around. There is a single quite large blue/red status LED on the right earcup which flashes when the device is in use.

Setting the device up was quick and easy by holding the MF button to initiate pairing. It is a pity that there are no voice status prompts as only the old style bleeps are available with red/blue LEDs.

Sound quality is excellent and places this device amongst the best Bluetooth headsets I have used for music reproduction. There is plenty of bass, but not too much as the Dr Dre ones are. The mid tones and treble are good but good be a little punchier - but better that than being to sharp or abrasive. No, the sound here really is very good indeed.

Phone calls are easily made and received with the voice easy to make out both ends. Calls have to be initiated and responded to by pressing the headset MF button -there is no option to make or answer calls by voice alone.

This is an excellent set of Bluetooth headphones and has to be one of the best I have used, perhaps the best in this budget price range.

A great buy

The Good
Great price
Great sound quality
Replaceable battery
Easy to use controls

The Bad
No Carry case
Earphones do not fold for storage
No Voice status prompts
Can't make or answer calls by voice

product_title: SOL REPUBLIC Tracks Air Wireless On-Ear Headphones
review_body:
For reference, my daily drivers are Shure SE315 IEM's and Sennheiser HD280 Pro's. I've been in the market for a pair of high quality wireless headphones, but after trying a number of different models I never found one I was happy with. Everything else has either been uncomfortable, used some kind of proprietary cable or sounded like crap.

I was at Radio Shack and they had the Tracks Air on sale for half price. I'm a sucker for a 50% off sign, so I bought them. After putting away all my other headphones and using these exclusively for 48 hours, here are my impressions.

1. Comfort - the Tracks are comfortable for on-ear headphones. They don't compare to the Sennheiser HD280's but very few headphones do. That being said, on my larger than average head I had no problem wearing these for several hours. I also wear glasses and other on-ear headphones often squeeze so tight that it pinches my ears up against my glasses (Beats? I'm looking at you!). No complaints so far, although they might get a little hot in the summer.

2. Sound Isolation - the Tracks are only moderately successful at sound isolation. Again, I've been spoiled by the superlative Shure SE315's but even so, I wasn't blown away by the Tracks. I am very happy however that they didn't attempt to include any Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) as it frequently degrades the quality of the music. The Tracks are perfectly fine for commuting and wearing around the home/office, but I can't recommend them for air travel over a good pair of IEM's like the SE315's.

3. Sound Quality - this is where pretty much every Bluetooth headphone I've ever used has fallen short. The Tracks aren't perfect either, but they're worlds better than many others. The Tracks are light on highs and a little heavy on the lows, but tweaking the EQ on my phone got them to a good place. They don't lack for power or punch, and the bass is excellent but I with they were just a little brighter or at least more balanced. Overall, they are at least accurate and free of distortion.

4. Durability - I can't comment after just 48 hours of use, but I will say that they are solidly build and the headband feels damn near indestructible. Some have complained about the left earpiece going dead, and I can't speak to that. I will say that because of the modular design you can replace each of the earpieces and the headband separately, which is nice considering any other pair of headphones is trash if just one part goes bad.

TL;DR - heavy on the bass but overall great sound, comfortable, good battery life, so-so noise isolation, good looks, an excellent choice for home/office or commuting.

Assembly, while time consuming, wasn't difficult. I was able to do everything myself and really only struggled when putting the center support in like everyone else. I unclipped the screen on the top and bottom and was still struggling to get it into place. I ended up lubricating the aluminum and the back of the screen where they and support bar made contact, and it was much easier to slide into place. I made sure to be thorough in cleaning up the lubricant to make sure it didn't stain or drip in the future even though it is on the back.

Installation was a snap and it's been an amazing improvement. The screen is beautiful and the felt really eats up any bleed.

I almost purchased the 120" screen and I'm incredibly happy that I went down to the 100" option.

We had friends over to watch season 5 episode 9 of Game of Thrones and we were all in amazement how much the screen size increased the intensity of the show.

I cannot wait to spend more time watching movies and TV.

product_title: Bluedio Bluetooth Wireless Headphone (Bluedio U)
review_headline: An improvement over and already fantastic product.
review_body:
Full disclosure: I'm a happy purchaser of three pairs of R+ for various members of my family. Bluedio approached me with an offer of a free pair of ttheir new UFO series for a review. I am so happy they did, even though they have now spoiled me.

You see, I was an $80 headphone guy. The R+ was everything I could have wanted at the price range. They sound terrific, they are comfortable, they have wire or bluetooth, they connected to all my devices with no problems. How could they be better ?

Simple: They could be the UFO. It's hard to quantify, but the UFO's are even more comfortable. I work in an open office environment, and wear headphones several hours a day to block out sound. The R+ was acceptable. The UFO's are like they aren't even there. I've used headphones since the 70's, and I've never had a pair that I could forget I was wearing.

As a nice added touch, instead of just responding with beeps they speak out what mode they are in as you push buttons.There are other small improvements, like the hard case with a pouch for the cables.

The sound: I thought the R+ were fantastic, and there is nothing wrong with them. Until you hear the UFO's. They are clearer, I wish I could give some technical reason involving frequency response and signal/noise ratio -- but all I could do was switch back and forth over and over. They just sound crisper. I've played classic rock, 80s, metal, and classical through these. I used Bluetooth and cabled. In every test the sound was superior.

If your budget is around $100, you will be very happy with the R+. If you have $200 to spend on headphones, I can highly recommend the Bluedio UFO series.

product_title: Panasonic ErgoFit In-Ear Earbud Headphone
review_headline: Can't be beat for $6 or even $12, unless you can get the Sony MDR-EX100AP for less than $15.
review_body:
Just received these along with the Sony MDR-EX100AP from Amazon: http://www.amazon.com/Sony-MDR-EX100AP--Ear-Headset-Smartphone/dp/B00BN0N03U/ref=sr_1_1_m?s=aht&ie=UTF8&qid=1434157881&sr=1-1&keywords=mdr-ex100ap

This is a mixed review since I got both at the same time. Various music sources of various quality on the same computer with the same software and equalizer settings for all comparisons. I punch up the base, mids and the highs to +2.5-3.2 on an 10 bar setting eq and go about midway at +2db on the inbetweens. This is about as good as one can do with typical audio cards. The settings emphasize the overall range and punch in the bases with mids. This usually causes grief to slower responding headphones and clashes with high end distortions, especially when listening to scratchy vinyl recordings.

1st song, Dixie Chicks Travelin' Soldier - I love this song, great dynamic range, instrumentals and harmonies. You get a base punch that is either missed or overruns the instrumentals with lower priced headphones. The Panasonic's played this very cleanly as it did with ever song, base was good and the resolution on the instruments was clean. I liked the sound of the Panasonic. It played the instruments very well, banjo, steel guitar, drums, base - all were discernible. It lacked the hard punch I like out of my base. Base was good, not great. Mids and highs were as good as anything I've used. The Sony MDR's were all of this and better. With the Sony's the base punched out from both sides and hit you in the middle of the head in full concert sound. There was an amazing difference between the two headsets. The Panasonic's played very well, but they were more sterile, kind of like just setting the eq to the middle setting for all frequencies (bars) and expecting something spectacular. The Panasonic's delivered very good to excellent sound and resolution, but the Panasonic's would not compete with a more expensive very good set. I changed the cups and reseated the Panasonic's and there was no noticeable improvement. Played with the eq settings and ran through the list again, still no real punch. Good Base, no where near the Sonys.

This was the theme for the Panasonic's through Two Cello's - Smooth Criminal: Beethoven - Sonata 29 OPUS 106, B flat and Violin Concerto; and SuperTramp Crime of the Century. The opening of the Violin Concerto has a couple of kettle drums starting out very softly and the Panasonic's did not grab them until around the second measure. The Sony MDR's hit them from the get go and it just got better. I like all of these music pieces, know them very well and all of these pieces really pit Base and Treble against each other with the Middle frequencies messing things up. These music pieces break poor performing headphones and the Panasonic's held up very well though not great when compared to the $16 Sony MDR's.

That being said, they are spectacular for $6 (get the green for <$5) and play better than most other brands I've purchased for up to $21, just not the Sony MDR-EX100AP. The Sony's are unbelievable, the Panasonic's are very good and you really can't go wrong with them at this price point and playback quality. I'd give them a 3 if they were $12.

Both sets blocked sound fairly well. I played with the cup sizes and ear sealing. They worked the same and as expected were not truly noise cancelling. I was after noise cancelling (ok I'm cheap) and thought I'd try these sets. I did not expect to get true noise cancelling since not fully covering the ear, but I wanted something better than my travel set to use with the FiiO mini I ordered along with the earphones. Got about what I expected out of both sets.

product_title: Valley Enterprises Icom CT-17 USB FTDI Chipset CI-V Cat Control Programming Cable 3 Feet
review_headline: FTDI ADAPTER RESTORES ICOM IC-735 HAM RADIO
review_body:
I'm using the Valley Enterprises FTDI USB/Serial adapter cable to tune frequencies on my ICOM IC-735 Amateur HF Radio. The FTDI driver download was simple and the cable adapter works fine on my IC-735 in conjunction with the Ham Radio Deluxe Software Package and my old XP/SP2 Laptop. The FTDI device is running on port 5 at 1200 baud with an CI-V address of 04.

The IC-735 radio had become unusable due to the failure of an irreplaceable optical tuner which was used to set operating frequencies on the radio. The FTDI adapter is functioning as a "work-around" to that problem and has restored a really desirable radio back into full service.

The only actual problem I had using the FTDI cable was due to the 3/8th inch CI-V serial interface jack on the 1980's era radio. The jack had a bit of corrosion on the "tip conductor" which which blocked communication between the Computer/FTDI combo and the Radio. This was cured by a shot of De-Ox spray on the radio jack.

The cable works fine, was easy to implement and has restored my ICOM IC-735 HF Transceiver back to service.

product_title: Sabrent Wifi Audio Receiver (Supports DLNA and AirPlay) for Home Stereo, Portable Speakers (WF-RADU)
review_body:
Was quite curious to play around with this. I have been looking for a decent work around for my a car (a fiat 500e) where sadly the bluetooth works for everything but music. The bluetooth solution i had in place required a manual switch on/off everytime you wanted to use it so I was interested in trying this out as a nice compact alternative. Package itself is fairly small and can be tucked out of sigh depending on where your connections are located in the car.

Powered on, phone (Iphone 6+) saw the network soon enough and connected. Took a grand total of about 5 minutes to figure out and set up the whole thing. Confused me a bit initially on how to get data via my network while still connected to this. But instructions on the sabrent site are pretty clear on how to do this. Here are the instructions if you need it :https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=12HeopQ-w1M

Once that was done, both my wife's phone as well as mine were hooked up and ready to go. Worked flawlessly. While a lot of folks say the audio quality is much better, it wasn't particularly noticeable to me as opposed to bluetooth. But I did like that I it worked seamlessly now without having to switch on/off anything. BTW, I am on the latest firmware 2.0.7

The only con I can think of with this device is the boot up time. It takes almost a whole minute before a connections is established to getting an output. great device otherwise.

product_title: Nyne Aqua twister
review_headline: Great way to listen to music in pool.
review_body:
As pool and beach is upon us, many people will be using outdoor speakers to play music. Of course, there's always a concern that your device will get wet. This NYNE speaker attempts to solve that issue by being fully waterproof, as well as being able to float.

The device comes with its own cool-looking red charging cable. The blue light will turn off when it's done charging. It was very easy to pair with my iPhone 6. The sound quality is pretty good, but not as clear or powerful as a standard Bluetooth speaker in this price range. There is an option to change EQ presets, but unfortunately there is no way to determine which preset you are currently on. There are also volume and phone buttons on the speaker itself.

In terms of floating, it worked well when I did a float test in the bathtub. The speaker is on the heavy side, so it may not be light enough for frequent air travel (if you want to take it with you on a vacation). But you could certainly make it work.

Overall, this is a great purchase if your main goal is to have a waterproof speaker that floats. If you put a priority on sound quality, I would go with another brand that may not necessarily be waterproof.

product_title: Marantz SA-8005 Super Audio CD Player
review_body:
I did not purchase mine through Amazon because there is an authorized dealer near me and I was concerned about factory warranty in case I may need it in the future.
I have owned several players over the years, Pioneer Elite, Sony ES, Cambridge Audio, Oppo (several models and I currently own the 105D), I cannot fault any of them but my favorites has been the Pioneer Elite and the Sony ES and they had something in common, both were made in Japan. At the time I replaced them I thought that advances in playback would give me a better aural experience but for me there was something I miss but could not put my finger on it. My latest purchase was Oppo 105D which is a wonderful machine but even though with all the superlatives that accompany Oppo's reviews, to my ears, it still missed something, finally the SA8005 came with wonderful reviews but what made me try it was that the current batch was made in Japan, call it bias, placebo effect or whatever you want to call it but actually I enjoy more my CDs and SACDs with the 8005. I am selling my Oppo? no I need it for my video needs, Blu ray, DVD and my Blu-ray audio and DVD-audio discs, the difference might be subtle but is there for me. I lack the verbage that Hi Fi reviewers use but all I can say is that at least to my ears the Marantz has a small edge over the Oppo when it comes to Red book playback and SACD, which for me is good enough.
For those interested the associated equipment includes, Martin logan Clarity's, Emotiva mono's and Pre, Adcom Amps and pre, Monster cable, Emotiva cables, Oppo universal player and the latest top Pioneer Elite receiver (I don't want to mention especific models because I don't want to make this sound like an Ad).
I hope this small review, although very subjetive, help a bit those thinking about purchase.

product_title: Audio-Technica-USB Direct-Drive Professional Turntable in Silver
review_body:
I have been torn over which record player to buy for a long, long time. If you're like me, you want something pretty simple but good since you like to play vinyl quite often. You know what Crossley is, but you want better than that. However you don't want to spend $500+ for some technically-intense DJ type turntable. In the end, I settled on this unit. It was relatively easy to set up. As soon as I played the first record on it, I was thrilled. This thing is so awesome. It reminds me of the very first time I actually bought a car that wasn't a beat up piece of crap. I test drove 20 different cars, but settled on a Subaru because of many small, but important nuances about the car. The car has a solid, heavy feel to it and everything from the radio to the spedometer have a smooth fluidity to them. I felt that same sense in using this record player. I like that the cover is a heavy piece of plastic that feels like you're really closing the thing. I like when you stop a record, it halts instead of just cruising down to a stop. I don't know why these little nuances mean a lot. Maybe it relays to me that some dude at Audio-Technica actually sat around and said, "I'm going to make a mean- a$$ machine," and he did just that. I'm thrilled to own it. I'm even considering leaving my wife, because with me record player and my records what else do I need her for? Oh, yeah. That other thing.

update January 2016
I use this thing twice or more a day pretty consistently. Have not had one issue. Love everything about it.

product_title: Bose SoundTrue In-Ear Headphones
review_headline: These may not be for you if...
review_body:
These in-ear headphones may not be what you are looking for if: you don't like full bodied sound, true across the normal hearing spectrum: you don't think ear buds should stay in place all day and still be comfortable: you think all ear buds are alike and shouldn't cost more than $30.
HOWEVER, if you are looking for In-Ear Headphones that are head and shoulders above just about any other earphone in this price range, these are the ones for you! I have owned multiple of these earphones over several years and am continually blown away by their fidelity, comfort and ease of use, so much so that I purchased (actually got them as an award from work ;) ) some for my wife to use--she won't give them back. The three sizes available make for very easy fitment to just about any outter ear canal and are flexible and won't fall out easily. These are NOT noise cancelling, so don't even think about these if that is what you are after. They aren't made for that function, though Bose DOES make models to fit that need. Their stated use is to give you full sound that you can enjoy for multiple years and they do that extremely well. I've tried on multiple occasions to use lesser earphones, but none come close to the sound quality these provide; either the bass is totally gone or nearly so, or the mids and highs are tinny and uncomfortable to hear.

In conclusion, if you want great music quality, you are going to have to pay a bit more than the usual. If you do so and buy these, you won't be sorry.

product_title: Caseling Premium Hard EVA Case Travel Bag Pouch for Bose Soundlink Mini Bluetooth Speaker
review_headline: This case hits all the high points
review_body: I searched for a long time for a case that was somewhat larger than the Bose branded travel case because I wanted:-  1. better protection than that provided by the OEM Bose case 2. to store the charging base, charger and a short 3.5mm interconnect cord 3. to keep the BOSE bumper case on the speaker 4. to spend much less than the $45 Bose wanted for their case.  The Caseling hard case provides all of these benefits. The charger and audio cord fit comfortably in the mesh area in the lid while the charging base sits in the bottom of the main compartment with the speaker docked in it.  The case is actually a little TOO large in that the speaker moves from side to side - but only slightly. I placed a small piece of foam padding between the case and the left side of the speaker and that solved the issue perfectly (see photos I uploaded showing the piece of white foam and showing how the charger and cord fit into the mesh pocket in the lid).  All of this usability comes at the price of a somewhat larger form factor than the Bose original case but to me it's a small inconvenience for the additional functionality of the Caseling case.  It appears to be well made and I am confident it will provide excellent travel and storage protection for what is a fairly expensive portable speaker.  It also looks really good with a tight nylon mesh effect on the exterior and a softer felt-like interior lining that will not scratch the speaker.  In other words, it is of the quality you want for a higher end speaker like the Bose Soundlink Mini.  Note that although this case is described as 'hard' it is actually more what I would describe as 'firm'. It will deform under pressure but it springs right back out again. That way it won't break but will protect the speaker.  Highly recommended.

product_title: Creative Sound Blaster Roar: Portable NFC Bluetooth Wireless Speaker with aptX/AAC
review_headline: Great, feature rich solution for the price.
review_body: I purchased my unit about 8 months ago and personally I am quite satisfied.  Is it perfect? No, of course not, because nothing is.  However, for the price I believe it is worth it and it is a good balance of features, audio quality, and build quality.  I will say now that I would highly recommend based on price/quality, performance, & features.  If that has you interested read on.  Features: Proprietary and USB charging 8 Hour Battery Life 3.5mm/USB input 5 Drivers - 3 Active, 2 Passive Bluetooth, NFC Hands Free Calling/Answering Records Audio Micro SD Slot - Can be loaded with MP3/WAV/WMA Format files to play without a connected device - Shuffle or List Alarm ROAR - Substantially boosts volume and spaciousness of the sound Terabass - Increase bass output at lower volumes Bedtime Mode Dual Purpose Battery â€“ charge other devices Sound Blaster Control Panel  Before I start with my pros, cons and other statements/conclusion, please take a second to keep in mind that this is a portable speaker and it has limitations.  Don't compare it to 2.1 systems, larger units, or headphones.  The purpose and design is different.  Also, if you want one thing something else has to give.  You want strong sound you compromise battery life, weight, and size.  To get strong, not muddy bass you need bigger drivers (speakers).  You want more battery life it again needs to be bigger and heavier.  You want an indestructible brick it costs more.  Build: To start the speaker is well built with a steel grill that is mostly what the speaker is on the exterior.  The user panel is covered with a soft rubber with some LEDs for battery life, bluetooth connectivity, and ROAR; along with the main buttons like power.  Additional buttons/switches, the microSD slot, USB/microUSB port, and ac port are on the back of the unit.  Two rubber strips are on the bottom of the unit that act as nonslip "feet" for the unit, so it will not slide if placed on an angled surface.  The entire unit is a bit on the heavy side, and it is also a bit on the larger side at roughly 8" x 4.5" x 2.25".  The battery life is decent and is stated to last 8 hours (most if not all battery life estimates for speakers are for 50% volume with no extra features activated).  Overall the build quality is good and solid and user panel is easy to understand.  Sound: At this price point the sound quality is quite good coming from 2x 1.5" drivers on one channel and the 2.5" driver on another.  Vocals are clear and easy to understand.  The treble is clear, the mids are nice and warm, and the base is rich and strong.  If anything the bass and lower mids are slightly accentuated.  There is little to no distortion at max volume + ROAR and rarely, if at all, gets muddy compared to its baseline.  The bass scales well with the treble and keeps pace with the mids and highs even up to max volume.  If you want to pick at it maybe it falls just a little short, but itâ€™s enough to send lots of vibration through my desk and into the floor (yes I feel it in my feet when itâ€™s on my desk), and the bass driver isnâ€™t even pointed downward.  The speaker by no means omnidirectional, but that is an "issue" with almost all speakers.  The mid and upper frequencies are highly affected by orientation and the smaller drivers are situated on the side and the base driver is directed upwards.  For a more omnidirectional sound the upper range drivers need to be aimed up or down like the UE Boom, but that can result in muffled or tinny/airy sound with less lateral range.  Bass is not affected much by orientation except on whether or not you can hear it (thatâ€™s why subwoofers can sit on the floor by themselves off to the side.)  Personally I wouldn't change the orientation of the drivers.  Something you may notice is the speaker might have a little trouble fully powering all the drivers to max volume (+ROAR), and the bass will be exploding and then tone down once the melody and vocals come in.  However, if you plug in the can better cope with the power demand, much lessening or even eliminating the effect (may also depend on how the music was recorded).  Do take into account that max volume +ROAR is easily adequate to fill a small sized reception hall with sound, so at home or in your living room full volume + ROAR is overkill and might even give you a headache.  Features: Bluetooth - I haven't had any trouble with the bluetooth like some others may have.  In playing music and taking or starting calls I am heard and hear clearly with no dropping or blank patches, granted I stay in range of the speaker.  I personally have not used the NFC because I use only one device with it, so I defer to others for that.  MicroSD - I really like the ability to play music off a memory card in a list or shuffle.  I don't have to play from my connected device.  I haven't tried to record anything, but from what I've read it is mediocre at best, but that's not what we're buying the speaker for are we.  For recording I defer to others.  Alarm - The SBRoar can sound a loud siren when the alarm button is held down (hold down again to turn off).  The practical applications of this are kind of fuzzy, but I suppose that if you're in trouble you can turn it on.  Otherwise is a seemingly useless feature.  ROAR â€“ A feature unique to the SBRoar that significantly boost volume to all drivers when activated.  It does add a little bit of airiness and spaciousness to the upper frequencies, but on purpose.  Some people donâ€™t like that specifically, but it helps the speaker fill a room with sound better than just simply making it louder.  I personally believe it works considering the form factor here.  Terabass â€“ activated by pressing the â€œAlarmâ€ button once, which increases bass at lower volumes.  The effect is quite apparent as the bass does seem to disappear faster than the mids and highs at low volume.  This was implemented to combat this phenomenon, but it is left up to you.  It can be turned on and off (default off â€“ needs to be activated each time the unit is turned on).  For some the bass is fine at lower volumes.  The added bass is reduced as the volume is increased.  Bedtime Mode â€“ Something I still have never used because Iâ€™m not the kind of person who sleeps to music.  When you activate sleep mode the SBRoar will play music for a set period of time gradually decreasing volume until it is off.  If you like to be lulled to sleep with music feel free to try this feature.  Dual Purpose Battery â€“ If you happen to not be using your speaker at the moment and your phone is dying you can plug into the speaker via USB and use it as an external battery.  Sound Blaster Control Panel â€“ allows you to fine tune your speaker and change the sound signature to your liking.  I have not used this feature and I defer to others.  Other Thoughts/Conclusion: When the unit is in use, especially at high volume, it can get quite warm to touch (especially if plugged in and charging at the same time); not at all to dangerous temperatures, even for little kids, but something worth noting.  The power struggle at max power +ROAR is noticeable when not plugged in, but not really a negative as it is really loud at that point and I wouldn't say it takes away from the listening experience.  It can receive analog 3.5mm or digital USB input, which adds versatility.  The SB Roar comes with a proprietary charger, but can also be charged via USB and can charge other devices, which again adds versatility. Overall the Sound Blaster Roar is very solid product with high build quality, sound quality, and an ample amount of additional features.  Is it perfect?  No.  Is it the best?  That is subjective.  Is it worth it?  Certainly.  This is a product that I personally believe that youâ€™re actually getting a little more than you paid for when compared to other products within its price range.  That accounts for the product as a whole and not just the sound signature.  At the end of the day, personally the product is highly recommended and I donâ€™t believe it will disappoint.

product_title: Yamaha NS-IW280CWH 6.5" 3-Way In-Ceiling Speaker System (White, Pair)
review_body: I bought 3 pair of these from Amazon for the 5.1 home theatre setup in my living room (using one for my center speaker... So now I have one left over).  They installed very easy with the included cut-out templet.  I painted the speakers flat white to match my ceiling using a basic primer/spray paint in one, which was also easy with the included protectors (which are located inside the grills... I thought I got shorted when I didn't see them during unpacking). They seam very well made.  I didn't have ANY issues with the clips that hold the speakers in your ceiling as others have had.  Just make sure you use a hand screw driver, go slow and don't over tighten.  Also, place some roll insulation on top of the speakers to make them sound better and not allow the sound to bleed into the space above.  I tested both with and without and they definitely sound better with insulation.    As far as sound goes... They sound pretty dang good.  I guess the point is though... They are not $700 a pair speakers (hence the 4 star rating), but they are an AMAZING value for the money.  However, you might be a little disappointed if you aren't running a subwoofer with these... They don't have a lot of bass.  All in all though, I don't think you will regret buying these.  Here are a couple of pointers:    1. Use the included cut out template to create a hole in a box.  Place the essembled (grill and protector on) speaker in the box. Now you can paint the speaker without getting paint all over the bottom the speaker.  After the paint dries, you can carefully remove the grills with a paper clip before installation.    2.  Use a long Phillips head screwdriver to tighten clamps, slowly and carefully.  Don't over tighten and DON'T use a power driver... You will break the clips.  As you begin to tighten, the screw will seem loose at first. This is normal, as the clamp is moving in to the locked position.    Enjoy!

product_title: Mohu Leaf 50 TV Antenna Amplified 50 Mile Range MH-110584
review_headline: Who new going old school with an antenna would get you more channels?!?
review_body:
I didn't buy this product from Amazon because I had a gift card to another site, but I did use the reviews here to inform me on making my purchase. I would first like to say that I am blown away by how amazing this product is, for years I was just using the cable that came from the wall and plugging that into my HTPC. This would give me about 6 channels, I really only cared about the major networks so this was sufficient for my needs. I live in the middle of Hollywood, CA, and recently my service provider "Time Warner" started encrypting their free channels that I would get simply by plugging in the cable into my HTPC, after contacting them it turned out that I would have to rent a digital adapter from them on top of paying for a tv package through them which was going to cost me $30 extra a month on top of my internet bill, just to get 20 channels. I am a true cord cutter and have been for many years and really don't want to pay for television.

After doing some more research I stumbled across this amazing little product. I purchased it and set it up last night. According to tvfool.com I was expecting to get about 34 channels, but after finding the sweet spot in my apartment I am now getting 56 channels! All of the major networks look just as clear as if I was running the cable from the wall still. My apartment is located in sort of a weird place so finding the sweet spot to stick the Mohu took about 30 min. I live on the first floor of a 2 floor apartment building with my living room facing away from the direction of the towers. I found that if I stick this on my window that faced directly at the building next to mine that I was able to get a great signal for most stations, especially the major networks which I was mainly interested in, I'm guessing the signals must be bouncing off the building next to mine.

All in all this product truly lived up to my expectations and I am now receiving far more channels that I was before and I couldn't be happier. I am already trying to figure out how to run a cable from the roof and maybe get the Mohu Sky and really get every channel possible! If you are in the same boat that I was the Mohu Leaf 50 will not disappoint, just be patient when finding the right spot to stick because moving it just 5-6 inches really does make a big difference in signal quality.

product_title: Bose SoundTouch Series II Wi-Fi Music System
review_headline: Like Most Bose Products, Simple, Elegant, High Quality, and Very Functional.
review_body:
To Review a Bose you need to know a few things about sound technology and reproduction. When you go to a concert hall or a well-adapted theater for sound reproduction, the sound you hear hits you at various times based on how it's reflected. Some comes to you direct and some takes a longer path off the front, back and side walls of the hall and even the floor and ceiling. To get a good reproduction of a concert experience you need those time lags. Back in the 1970's Bose worked to reproduce this experience with a set of speakers that resembled the shape of a house. Instead of the typical large woofer mid-range and tweeter arrangement, Bose employed a series of 9 smaller speakers arranged to project sound in several directions. The goal: to try and reproduce the concert experience through reflection.

Next in the 80â€™s and 90â€™s and still today you had many variants of the â€œWaveâ€ technology radio a smaller self-contained unit that produces big sound with a relatively small size. This used wave guide technology, two 26 inch long baffles within the device that route the sound. Wave guides are used for fiber optics and other purposes, and the use is that you can direct the sound along a path while obtaining almost no energy (sound) loss. It also created a delay that again mimicked that concert hall like sound. More recently Bose introduced â€œacoustimassâ€œ a term for compressing and injecting sound out from a relatively small driver with the power of a larger speaker. I believe all three of these technologies are used in this unit.

Aside from that it is made for modern music listening from MP3â€™s and streaming web stations or music services. The quality varies. I would have liked to see a self-contained system on the unit to connect to my Wi-Fi, but since it did not have that, I had to use the USB cable to connect it to my computer during set-up. The Sound Touch application had a nicely designed interface, but I had a lot of trouble trying to work through MS Media center to get to MP3â€™s. This was probably more my own issue since I donâ€™t archive them in that system. The internet radio stations were easy to set up and I set presets for some of my favorites easily.
Sound the MP3â€™s I had on the machine were high quality and you could really tell it playing them in a very large 22â€™ X 25â€™ back bedroom. Nice base and good midrange and high reproduction. I tried several of the internet radio stations, and the sound was good but not great like the direct MP3â€™s I believe this is due to these have a lower grade of MP3 data files playing. I noticed some promised an HD sound if you subscribed, similar to the music services. Still the degraded sound was good enough for standard radio, and I could see how good it can be if I ever decide to subscribe.

Bose likes to be compact and elegant in their systems very few bells and whistles just for their own sake. Six presets and a key pad on top for those and duplicated on the small remote. Plenty of sound to fill a big room and you get that spatial quality only Bose can reliably deliver. This system is recommended if you can afford the typical Bose price. Bose tries to stay up with the times and this is a welcome addition to their line of quality systems. Itâ€™s a choice you can get a lot of conventional components for the same price or less, but you have to deal with a lot of wires, set-up, and loss of space. Bose often gives better sound without all the extra work, and saves your space for say those new 80â€ TVs!

product_title: JLab JBuds Hi-Fi Noise-Reducing Ear Buds (Purple)
review_body:
I received a pair of these headphones as a gift in a pack or razors many years ago. They fit my ears perfectly and the sound was as high a quality as you could expect from tiny headphones. Over the years, they became worn and I wanted a replacement. After many calls to Schick I discovered that JLab was the manufacturer. Sure enough, the JBuds are the exact same headphones with JLab written down the side of the buds.

If you've tried hard plastic or hard foam earbuds, you may know that they can hurt if worn for long lengths of time. The JBuds use a very soft material that doesn't hurt even if worn for hours at a time. The sound meets the requirements of MP3 files (which already clip off the high and low ends of the sound spectrum). The stem of the buds doesn't bother me and helped keep my old headphones working without broken wires for multiple years of daily use. I purchased another pair just in case JLab decides to kill off this model.

These are not high-end over-ear headphones. If that is what you are looking for, don't get in-ear headphones.

product_title: Satellite Speaker Stands
review_headline: Works great for the VIZIO S4251w-B4 5.1 Satellite Speakers
review_body: I was able to get these installed in about an hour, from unpacking to clean-up. Overall they're well-built, with very sturdy bases and vertical tubing with a diameter large enough to fit the cabling through (though you'll need a thin, long rod to help coax the wire). The L bracket doesn't have enough space to fit the angle RCA connector, so you'll have to:  1. Wedge the angle RCA into the L bracket. 2. Use the flat washers to modestly hold down the L bracket. 3. Grab the satellite speaker and position the angle RCA and L bracket to your liking. 4. Remove speaker, tighten everything down, bend L bracket forward a bit, and attach speaker for it's final home.  Routing the cable was a little confusing, but the easiest way is to have it come up the tube, through the base plate, OVER the rear flat washer and then parallel with the vertical part of the L bracket. You'll need to pull a bit of slack through in order to get access to the rear screw for the base plate.  I used a Dremel to remove the excess L bracket that pokes out the front of the stand.  Honestly, most of the install time came from me looking for a dowel rod to get the wire poked through. If all your tools were available, you'd be done in 20 minutes.

I love the Monster line of audio products. These are no different. Keep in mind that these phones are squarely placed in the "mid-range." In my opinion, they exceed mid-range quality.

The control talk worked perfectly and people on the other end reported incredible clarity (I can report the same on my end). The microphone and phone controls are placed very well on the cord on a flat cord (not round like most). These seems to help keep the microphone well placed. Unlike many other in-ear phones, these do not fall out even under vigorous conditions. They are also very comfortable.

These phones provide exceptional sound quality in my opinion. Noise cancellation is very good. Bass response is very good. While sound quality does not compete with the Monster DNA version of phones I have, they are still great in every respect.

Bottom line, these phones will not standpoint.

product_title: Fusion4K High Speed 4K HDMI 2.0 cable - Professional Series Ultra HD
review_headline: Best HDMI Cable on the market!!
review_body:
The QUALITY of the HDMI cable you use in your setup matters. To verify the quality of a HDMI cable, one test that is performed is called the "eye" test. I bought the Fusion4K cable because they proved their quality by showing their eye test results.
Doing a fair amount of research on this topic I learned the following:
As the length of the cable increases, the signal interference also increases. Think of this like the "resistance" of the signal in the cable increases the farther it has to go. Also, the more data you pass through the cable (bandwidth) the more interference you'll see as distance increases until the cable fails like cheap cables will.
The Fusion4K eye test shows a clear area around the "mask" (the middle shape in the eye) in their results. This means that there is no signal loss in the cable and that tells me that the materials used to make the cable are top notch. I found this information with simple internet searches and you can too.
My point is that better cable materials make a better cable and I want the best to future proof my setup. That's why I went with this cable. Also, the cables look great and "feel" well made when I held them next to my old cables. I'm very happy with my purchase.

product_title: Sony MDR10RNC Premium Noise Canceling Headphone
review_headline: Is it a sin to love my Sony headphones?
review_body: An incredible deal on spectacular technology. Bought these for $99 -- new but without original packaging -- from House of Electronics. One of the few times I took a chance with one of Amazon's alternative sellers. And I couldn't be more pleased.  Push the button near the on switch and the noise cancelling technology takes a sip of the ambient noise, then automatically selects the most effective sound-deadening protocol. Nothing is 100%, but I couldn't hear a word the flight attendant said in the pre-flight safety performance. It almost feels like you're in a vacuum.  But that's not the best part: The music sounds delicious. Ample bass, crisp highs. Mellow middle. Yet they are so incredibly light and comfortable, you just become completely immersed in whatever you're listening to.  One nice feature? The wire(s) are separate. Nothing sucks worse than snapping a headset wire. So, just in case you forget you're attached to your laptop or whatever, you're not jammed up if you break the wire. Oh, and if you simply want to use the headphones to block out noise, no need to be dragging around a wire.  It also comes with a cell phone wire that allows you to push a button to answers calls along with a mic. I haven't tried using that wire yet. I've only used these cans on jets. And I have no friends or family I need to talk to that badly I'd be willing to interrupt my music...or audiobook.
