product_title: Amplified HD Digital Outdoor HDTV Antenna 150 Miles Long Range with Motorized 360 Degree Rotation, UHF/VHF/FM Radio with Infrared Remote Control
review_headline: If at first you don't succeed......
review_body:
Got this to try in my attic for metro area stations whose transmission tower farm is about 35 miles away providing about 30 over-the-air channels. With my antenna aimed precisely at the tower farm, the signals were mostly intermittent, oscillating from strong to almost nothing over a few minute period. I was about to write off the antenna when I realized that a neighbor's house that was about 100 yards away was directly in line with the towers I was aiming at. Notably, this house was three stories high with a steep pitch all metal roof. In desperation, I moved the antenna to the other end of my house's attic hoping it might give me enough offset to shoot to one side of the neighbor's house. Luckily, all the station signals now came in with steady high strength signals. So given a more unobstructed view, this very simple antenna is doing the job for me.

On the down side, there are a couple of shortcomings. First, the rotating drive 's tendency to randomly start in either direction doesn't make it effective for jogging the position to refine the aim. Another problem I had was an audio hum in one of the TV's that was running off the antenna. It appeared to be feeding into the TV on the cable shield from the antenna control box. Suspected it might be an artifact of the rotator's AC power being fed to the antenna on the cable itself. By putting a direct earth ground on the control box shield side of the F-connectors, I was able to eliminate the noise that caused the audio hum.

Apparently, the control box antenna signal circuit is more than a simple boost amplifier. If the control box power is off, there is virtually no signal available on the outputs to the TV. So even though the control box rotator function isn't much use, reliable AC power and amplifier circuit operation is necessary for this antenna to perform suitably. This along with my doubt that the antenna is durable enough for outdoor environment lowered my rating to OK (3-star) even though I'm getting the performance I need for a strong signal.

product_title: Grace Digital GDI-IRDT200 Hi-Fi Internet Radio Tuner
review_headline: Close, but misses the mark, sometimes badly

Tech support says Rhapsody 'limits their access', but I always get to my personalized content with the other media players I've had. No Spotify at all, and no commitment as to when, if ever, they will have it. I've had the unit for 2 days, and for much of that time, couldn't even connect to Pandora or Rhapsody because of server issues on their end. When I could connect, there were drops and long lags between songs, even using a wired gigE connection. None of my other players ever had a problem using the exact same connection. It's possible it was related to their server problems. As others have said, the UI is terrible. The iPhone app is much better, but still is cryptic, sometimes complex, and poorly documented. On the plus side, it connects perfectly to my 3 media servers, Logitech Media Server, Mediatomb, and Plex. No skips or drops. Logitech's bean counters should all be fired for killing the Squeezebox, still nothing comes close to them (except now they can't handle the new stream encryption services are moving to). Unfortunately, this is going back.

product_title: B&O PLAY by Bang & Olufsen4
review_body:
Where to start...I researched online between these, the Bowers & Wilkins P5 Wireless and the Sennheiser Momentum Wireless and ended up purchasing the H8's due to their relatively good reviews and super looking design. I have the original Momentum wired headphones and love them but they are still a bit to plastic like and I don't like that they don't fold flat. When around your neck I like the headphones to rest flat against your body so you can easily move your head left and right without chin interference of the headphones. Upon arrival and unboxing I was very happy. These look and feel top notch in every way. I really liked the color combination, the brushed metal is gorgeous and also extremely important they looked great on my bald head while feeling comfortable. The style part is A+, no doubt about it.

I have the Galaxy Note Edge and the bluetooth pairing was easy. The touch controls are average in functionality but a great idea. I had no trouble circling the ear cup for volume up and down, no trouble pressing the middle for play/pause but I had all kinds of trouble swiping up and down to activate and deactivate the noise cancelling function. It worked about every 5 swipes in either direction and more often than not paused the music instead of doing what it's supposed to. This part was very annoying. At this point I am still liking the headphones.

Music playback initial impressions we very good. I played Today's New Hip Hop music station via Google Play Music and they sounded really good over bluetooth. Punchy bass and wonderful clarity, I couldn't ask for more...until I started walking. I'm a Realtor and like to listen to music while I measure a home and photograph it, makes the time involved more enjoyable. Having no wires to trip you up or get caught while moving around is even more enjoyable. So when I began to walk with these I noticed immediately a thumping sound that coincided with my steps. Surprised at first thinking it must be something simple or will go away and it never did. With each step I got a thumbing feedback through each ear cup and it ruined the experience. Sure if I cranked up the volume it overcame the thumping but for $500 this wasn't going to cut it. I asked for a replacement and one was sent out while I shipped these back.

The 2nd set arrived and within 15 minutes the exact same thing was present. One reviewer who rated these very well said they aren't for walking about halfway through his review and had I known this I wouldn't have wasted my time. What's the point in my opinion to have a convenient bluetooth headphone if you have to remain stationary? I cannot recommend these for that reason alone. I will also add I experienced some pretty severe distortion during J. Cole's G.O.M.D. at 4:00 through the song.

These are really gorgeous headphones but the odd thumping feedback while walking and their distortion are not acceptable for the price point. I think for now I will stick to wired until manufactures get the kinks worked out.ething simple or will go away and it never did. review_body:
I had high hopes for these -- I hate constantly dealing with tangled headphones -- but they just won't work for me.

1) The cord that goes from the clip on part to your phone is very short and not retractable. Therefore, if you have it plugged into your phone and are walking/running (my primary use for headphones), the only way to clip it on is if you have your phone in your pants pocket. As a female who often doesn't have pants pockets, this is not helpful. So for me, the clip on part just swings freely, banging into my chest as a move.

2) The retractable function is cheap. Sometimes takes a few tries and seems like it could easily break.

3) Lastly, this may just be personal preference, but if your primary purpose for headphones is to use while exercising, know that you can hear each step you take reverberate through the ear buds.

Sorry, but this ones going in the trash.

product_title: Cootree C250 Lightweight Sweatproof Earbuds
review_body:
This headset is by far one of the most comfortable headsets I've had! This triangular design really does allow these to stay in place. Keep reading for a more detailed review!!

Design: Out of the box, the design is a unique one. The triangular shape to the ear pieces are so comfortable! I have fairly delicate ear lobes and my ear shape is small. Normally I have a mess of a time getting the In-ear style headphones to stay on and in my ears. But not these! They fit perfectly in my ears and my hubby's ears too. ( He has good normal size ears) The back wiring goes above the ear and behind the head. I love this because it's not so big that it dangles down my neck but it is tight and hugs my head so that it can easily be hidden! I just part and lift my hair in the back, put these on and in my ear and they are hidden and good to go...I even forget that I'm wearing them after a few mins. Fabuloussss!!!

Controls: This aspect took some getting used to. At first there just seems to be too many buttons and it gets over whelming...however, when you realize that 90% of the time you just need the main function button it's not that scary of a monster. Then, it's just a matter of remembering which side has volume up and down and which side has forward and backward...your good to go. Be patient and take time to play, don't try to attend a meeting without experimenting with these first...you may get frustrated and switch back to your phone instead.

Sound Quality: Talking on the Phone: Well, I think it's as good as it could get. Many times there is a mysterious static that appears and it's hard to make out what the other person is saying. Sometimes, there's a lag in communication, at one point a friend and I were having 2 different conversations at a time without realizing it! Lol! Imagine that! But for the most part, it gets the point across.

Music: It's got a lack luster bass. Songs that really go BOOM BOOM go booo booo ...mmm...So, if you're looking for a great sounding headset for music...these are not your best friend...but the music does come across clear and crisp. Just no BOOM :(

Now, just a little note on this sound quality part...I must say that after reviewing so many of these types of headsets, I really do believe that all sweat proof options are low rated on sound quality. Maybe it's just the extra protection from the moisture that blocks out some of the sound quality so I can't punish Cootree for this...It's just a mid-priced headset sweat proof sickness...***sigh***

and finally...

Range: These headphones I have to say are a bit disappointing when it comes to how far I can travel without my phone. I can only go about 10 feet away and the static starts to take over. So, this works well if you are cooking in the kitchen and just want a hands free device but to travel about the office or house without your phone with you...good luck.

Summary: In summary, These are a keeper for their comfort and simple functionality. If you're looking for a stable and reliable option to stay in your ears while you're working out, running, jumping, doing cart wheels...twirling around...these are for you! You will get clean clear music and your point across if someone calls you...However, if you want exceptional sound quality and say...dance to the beat...well these have little to no bass...so just sway from side to side.

review_headline: Poor build quality, average sound quality, biased reviews (paid)
review_body: Background: Unit bought during the Kickstarter campaign.  TL;DR: Don't buy it. Poor build quality (loose rubber band), poor battery life (3-4h max at low/med volume), sub average bluetooth range (10ft), lack of basic functions and sound quality issues.  Disclaimer: Many of the reviews here, especially from mid december to mid February were made from Kickstarter backers in order to get a $20 discount code towards an additional unit. Deception is also used right here with a fake MSRP of $150 (real MSRP is $99 as you can check on nudeaudio website, leading to a false 33% discount claim.  Details: Scheduled for delivery on September 2014, then Christmas and finally between January to not "delivered yet" to a lot of people who ordered on KS I was one of the lucky ones getting mine in the ordered color on January. Then problems started. This speaker is pitched as a fancy "design", waterproof and hand free phone handset. But is it really?  - Fancy design speaker: no. Everything come down to the loose rubber band, supposed to be a feature, not a bug. It may be right, but it's annoying as hell to have to put it back together every time you fetch the speaker from your bag. - Waterproof: not really. Projection and splash proof rated. But, at least on the kickstarter packaging, the warranty state that the unit is not waterproof and should not be exposed to water. So copy paste error, or way to screw you if any water damage? Hard to say yet. - Hand free call for your phone: not at all. Mic quality is horrible. Don't even hope using it for anything. Never. - BT Speaker? Barely. Sound quality is average. Not as good as it's pitched for. Battery life is poor. Can barely reach 4h when playing at mid/low volume, far from the promised 8h at 70% volume. My unit also have intermittent problems where sound levels are not similar on both side of the unit. BT range is mediocre in comparison to other speakers I own, but in the low BT specification range. Finally, a big problem is the lack of basic functions than every other speaker seems to have like: skip track, play, pause, or answer the phone. What is the point of having a waterproof BT speaker if you have to get your phone out in a wet environment to change the song, or to answer a call?  So overall a bad experience with this speaker. For now I'm still waiting for a replacement or refund of my unit, but so far NudeAudio people are playing dead. So I would not expect a lot of customer service here neither.  Depending on your use I would rather recommend: - a cheap waterproof speaker to bring to the pool/beach like [[ASIN:B00RBIC1IS Omaker M4 Portable Bluetooth 4.0 Speaker with 12 Hour Playtime- Rugged Splashproof and Shockproof Wireless Bluetooth Speaker for Outdoors/Shower With NFC Tap & Play Technology (Army Green)]] or [[ASIN:B00MYYCGKW VicTsing Wireless Bluetooth 3.0 Waterproof Outdoor / Shower Speaker, with 5W Speaker/Suction Cup/Mic/Hands-Free Speakerphone - Army Green]] - a good quality speaker like [[ASIN:B00E9YIFQO Ultimate Ears MINI BOOM Wireless Bluetooth Speaker/Speakerphone - Red]] - a high quality speaker in the $200 range such as [[ASIN:B00CM0XHNS Ultimate Ears BOOM Wireless Bluetooth Speaker - Black]] or [[ASIN:B00D5Q75RC Bose SoundLink Mini Bluetooth Speaker]]

review_headline: Year and a half.  Repaired through warranty.
review_body: Year and a half.  That's what I got out of mine.  It's too cheap to think about repairing, really.  Good value for the money as long as it worked.  Some people have asked about replacing old/classic era amps with this and I did that.  Having the remote was really handy.  On the other hand, it just lacks something that the old solid state amps delivered.  It's just a little lifeless somehow by comparison.  Actually, I have an older model solid state amp that I bought on ebay recently because I wanted to set up another pair of speakers so I could enjoy the full bodied sound sometimes and other times just be lazy and work this Sherwood amp via the remote.  My Sherwood still plays through the headphone jack but no sound from the speakers.  Capacitor?  Short?  I dunno and for the price it's really not worth digging into it and certainly not worth taking to a repair shop.  I noticed some of the other reviewers say they're getting longer life out of theirs so probably just luck of the draw with me but for whatever reason a year and a half of intermittent play is all I got out of it.  Update:  Usually I seem to see 1 year warranty on just about everything.  This amp has (or had when I bought it) a 2 year warranty.  At a year and a half it developed a problem.  I sent it for repair and they did honor the warranty.  BUT at the (low) price of the amp, the shipping for this large and heavy of a box is a very large percentage of the original purchase price.  Took over a month.  It's still a very good deal if you get one that works properly for the long term.

product_title: GE HD Bar Indoor Video Antenna , (33683)
review_headline: save your money its no better than a coat hangar
review_body:
My friend purchased this, she lives in el cajon CA which isn't far from a dozen stations but its surrounded by mountains between it and the xmitters. She has also had several antennas I gave her including amplified rabbit ears and a 10' piece of buss wire I formed into a loop about 30" diameter. I told her she needs a winegard amplified flatwave like I have but she won't listen and wants to try every sub $20 antenna she sees at big lots including this GE piece of dung. This antenna gets half the stations my $1 piece of wire did. GE must be laughing their way to the bank with this truly shameful performing product.
I give you my word purchasing this product is no better than using your money for toilet paper. You've been warned.
A decent antenna has to be larger than this it's a matter of physics having to do with the wavelength of the frequency you are trying to capture. The longest vhf wave is around 9 feet and if you aren't at least 1/8 the wavelength there's little chance of capture. 1/4 or 1/2 is better.
Spend s little more and accept that it's going to be something you see. Not tiny and cute. As stated I think the winegard flatwave amplified is a good choice. Very few antennas in the sub $20 range are acceptable, those that are will usually be the double rabbit ear type which are physically obtrusive but that's why they work.
Summary: GE antenna: Dung in a box that a monkey probably engineered by throwing darts at a board blindfolded.

product_title: Best Wireless Bluetooth Earbuds, Atlas Media Headphones - Atlas EarBuddy, Secure Fit NFC Premium Earbuds with Mic - iPhone - Android - HTC - Galaxy - Samsung - T-Mobile- AT&T - Sprint - Verizon
review_headline: What you get for the money is not worth the price.
review_body:
I am going to set aside the fact that I purchased these as a birthday present for my wife and they showed up cosmetically damaged. This review will focus on the sound quality and product build which all the time I had to observe before returning them. Sound quality is not comparable to anything else in the price range and I do not mean that as a compliment. I have heard better sounding $15.00 earbuds. The are flat with no sense of depth whatsoever. They lack luster in the high frequency range and bass response/frequencies are no where to be heard. It felt somewhat like listening to a FM radio station that was not receiving a clear signal. The sound quality would have been considered acceptable had there not been a $100 price tag attached to it, but given that price do yourself the favor and purchase something that has earned its reputation and right to price there products in this price range.
As for build quality and materials; They surprisingly had a little weight behind them, my guess due to the fact the battery and charge receptacle are in bedded in one of the earbuds. The outer housing is made of a very thin plastic that does not hold up very well as I have seen first hand. The earbuds I had purchased for my wife were already damaged upon initial opening. The backing of the earbud that did not contain the charge station just fell off in the packaging. Apparently they should use better glue.
I did not have a lot of time to thoroughly examine this product but I can certainly tell you, having owned numerous expensive(ranging from $150-$1500) In-ear monitoring and listening devices similar and much better than these, I will be saving my money for something better and deserving of that price. If you do not need bluetooth, consider Westone or Shure, if you do try Bose or JBL. These are not worth the money.

product_title: La Crosse Technology BC-700 Alpha Power Battery Charger
review_body:
I used this for 8 months, and it worked great until one day it started overheating the batteries in one bay.

I put 4 eneloops in to discharge/charge on the lowest setting. A little while later, I hear a hissing and popping sound coming from the unit. The battery in bay 3 was EXTREMELY hot, so, I unplugged the unit and removed the batteries. The hot battery had popped its casing from overheating and was releasing gas through the safety vent. Thinking maybe it was just a bad battery, I put 4 other (depleted, not charged) eneloops into the charger on the lowest setting. 10 mins later the same exact thing happened in the same exact bay. Obviously, this charger is defective, and it destroyed two of my eneloops.

This was extremely disturbing as I often charge my batteries overnight and wouldn't usually be near enough to them to witness this happening. I worry about what would have happened if I hadn't been there to quickly shut it down.

I bought this highly reviewed smart charger because it was specifically supposed to prevent overcharging/overheating. I am tossing the whole thing and buying a Maha MH-C9000 instead.

product_title: SoundMAGIC ES18 In-Ear Earphones
review_headline: These aren't the bargain phones you're looking for
review_body:
Ugh. Not sure where to start here. Look, there's no denying everyone loves a bargain, especially an incredible bargain -- myself included. After reading numerous other reviews of these headphones here on Amazon, my expectations had been raised to the point where I actually believed SoundMAGIC may be offering that elusive bargain. Sadly yet unsurprisingly, there's no bargain to be found here. While these SoundMAGIC in-ear headphones might be worth every penny of the $12 that I paid for them, make no mistake: These headphones dishonor the music they purport to reproduce, especially if you like vocals or acoustic music.

I compared these headphones to my bargain reference, the Shure SRH400 over-the-ear headphones, using numerous uncompressed CD-quality recordings. The first thing that struck me was the similarity in overall frequency response. From deep acoustic bass notes to the overtones of a high-hat cymbal, the ES18s seemed to reproduce the entire frequency spectrum with a very balanced presentation that surprised me at the price. I also felt the build quality was quite high, with well-reinforced rubber (not plastic) cables that seemed like they'd last a reasonably long time. The provided assortment of three ear cushion sizes was an unexpected surprise, as was the quality of the "L" shaped plug.

But when I the first word I uttered was 'ugh', I meant it. To me, the most-important midrange -- male vocals in particular -- were nearly unlistenable. Rough, harsh, and gritty, voices were poorly reproduced, sounding nothing whatsoever like the real thing. The best way I can describe this is to imagine listening to live music mixed equally with the sound of a large grille frying a dozen bacon cheeseburgers. Sure, there's music happening, but riding on top of the music was a harsh, splattering component that made it impossible for me to "relax into the music" the way I could with other headphones. I could also describe the sound as AM-radio tinny, augmented with excellent bass. For now, let's just call it a distinct lack of refinement. Simply put, these $12 headphones sound like $12 headphones. Yeah, I'm kept them and gave them to a teenager.

product_title: HomeSpot NFC-Enabled Bluetooth Audio Receiver for Sound System
review_body:
I bought this to replace another bluetooth receiever that I have had for a few years. I previously had purchased the cheapest one that I could find on amazon (made by Vibe). The rechargable battery in that one failed, and now the unit has a background hiss - even with direct power, and the battery removed. So, I wanted a new one without a battery since it will always be near power when I use it.

The Bluetooth range on this unit is very poor. It states that you can have up to 66ft of "line of sight", but that just is not true. I do realize that the 66ft number probably was achieved in a lab, using a super powered bluetooth transmitter, but not even close with normal MP players, phones, etc. I got maybe 15 ft. before it started dropping signal. That is likely good enough for a room, but not outdoors where I intend to use it. Even worse, the distance dropped to about 5 ft if you stand between the unit and your phone (ie, turn your back on the unit). No Bluetooth unit I have ever owned failed when someone walked between me and the unit. It behaves more like infrared and not Bluetooth - it requires line of sight.

The sound coming from my stereo system is very good with this, indicating that the frequency response of this unit is very good. Some of the bluetooth units I have had in the past did not have a very dynamic range so a good stereo would always sound crappy. But, this one does sound pretty good.

product_title: Cable Matters 4 Port 4x1 HDMI Switch with Toslink and Digital Coaxial Audio Output
review_headline: It does the job, but I was hoping for more
review_body:
It works well. I purchased this model because it has the separate audio output which allows me to listen to music on my various devices without having to have the TV on to pass the sound to my receiver.

While that works, I think it might be causing a problem for audio from my AppleTV. Movies and some TV shows (especially via Netflix) only have the audio on the Toslink and not the HDMI which means I have to turn on my receiver for sound. For the most part, we don't need the full surround sound experience and having the TV's stereo speakers is preferred. This does not happen for all content on my AppleTV; nor does it happen when we play the same movies/shows via our blue-ray player's Netflix. The main downside to this is that somethings work better on one device than the other and therefore we have to switch between them more frequently than we'd like -- which leads me to my next problem...

I was disappointed that the automatic switching does not work. I have a Samsung Blue-Ray player, an AppleTV, and a WDTV connected to it and I'm not sure if its them or what, but this stated feature does not work for me. Powering on the BR player (regardless of which input is selected or if the switch is even on) does cause my TV to automatically switch to this input, though.

In addition to having to switch inputs manually (I know, FWPs), the LEDs are very bright and distracting. I cannot overstate that. I solved this by fitting a dark piece of card stock to the front of the device -- the LEDs show through and I cut a hole for the IR from the remote.

All said and told, though, it does the job and when compared to other similar devices, it seems like there is no clear choice -- all of them have their issues. I like Cable Matters and they tend to make high quality products which last.

product_title: H2O Audio Amphibx Fit Waterproof Armband for Smartphones
review_headline: Great Idea, Sometimes Works Great, Sometimes works badly, likely to destroy your phone with enough use
review_body:
This product is a great idea, with some critical flaws in execution. As far as I can tell this is a one-of-a-kind product. I wish there were something competing with it so that I could buy the competition, but I can't find anything else. It would be easy to make some incremental improvements to this and make it much better. I've used it on-and-off for about a year, and I'm really grateful when it works well, but it fails somewhat frequently, and that is extremely frustrating (and costly when it damages your phone).

Before going any further, let me emphasize that I would not advise anyone to use this with their primary phone. I only use it with my old smartphones, because I'm not willing to risk taking my primary phone underwater, and experience has shown that to be a wise choice.

I use this to listen to music while swimming laps. All my music is in Spotify, so I need a full-featured smart phone to play the music. This seems to be the only item that will enable me to listen to my iPhone while swimming, but it is somewhat inconsistent. The arm-strap doesn't work for me. I generally don't like those things, even when I'm running, and when I'm swimming my arms are moving so much that it is totally impractical to use an arm-strap. I also find that it cuts off the circulation to my arms a bit, so wearing that is out of the question. Instead, I just plug the thing in and then stuff it down the side of my jammer, which works quite well. The jammer is very elastic so it effectively holds the phone in place against my thigh. (This would not work with swimming shorts.) I also bought the waist strap to try that out. That certainly worked better than the arm strap, but it would move around a bit while swimming, so jammer was more effective. That's too bad because it is a little awkward to be shoving this thing down your pants (and might now work for women). If they could get this thing right it might actually make sense to sell a jammer with some kind of pocket to hold it.

When this works it's pretty great to be able to listen to Spotify while swimming. I've had it fail in two separate ways: (1) it does not play the music properly, and (2) the locking latch comes undone and water gets inside and damages the phone.

The first type of failure I experienced from fairly early-on. I'm not sure what causes it but it seems like the audio connection to the phone sends a "fast-forward" signal, and the music basically plays at about 4 times the speed at which it's meant to. It's sort of a bizarre error, and I don't really understand what could be causing it, but I've only ever had the problem while my iPhone is in this case, so it has something to do with this case. You'd think this would be easy solve by pausing the music and pressing play again, but that has generally not worked. Disconnecting the phone from the case and reconnecting works better, but that is very time consuming, especially given that you're in pool to swim, not fiddle around with electronics. It's also kind of dangerous to be trying to fix this thing while in (or around) the pool, given that if you drop it while the case is opened then your phone will get wet and no longer work.

The second type of failure seems to be associated with age. For the first year that I owned the case, I never had a problem with water getting inside. Over the last few months I've had the locking-latch come undone on 4 separate occasions and water has gotten inside and damaged my phone, so that I had to have the motherboard or battery replaced. Given that it had worked so well for me for so long, I thought that I must have done something wrong after the first two times. After four times (and a lot of effort to be very careful) I'm convinced that the locking-latch has deteriorated with time and the seal also seems to have deteriorated a bit. Clearly, this is a pretty serious problem. I'm glad I never use this with myprimary phone.

It would be really easy to markedly improve this in several ways. 1) fix the issue described above, 2) Add some kind of secondary safety latch, to either reinforce the first one, or somehow provide a safety measure. One of the things that is nice about this is how much less of a hassel this latch is compared to some comparable products, but it should be easy to come up with something that is both more secure, and still easy to use. 3) This should have some sort of "remote" feature built in, for both volume control and for play/pause/next/back. Some underwater headphones have that built in, but most don't. The biggest frustration when this thing did work was not having anyway to skip to new songs, or adjust the volume (swimming turns out to be a louder activity than you would guess). I've tried some of the other headphones by this brand and others. I've generally been disappointed. They generally work fine underwater, but there seem to always be other critical design failures.

A final point about this is that the current picture attached to this product is misleading. The product did not look like this picture, but Amazon is telling me that this is product I bought. The product that I bought actually looks a lot more like the other X-1 product, than the picture here. I'm worried the seller is intentionally being misleading. The selection on Amazon, make's it seem like there is a newer model that is materially different. I've bought both the newer and older model and have them both in front of me right now. The differences I can see are in some of the logos. This is important because I knew that the older model was flawed, but bought the newer one expecting it to be different and better. It is neither different nor better.

product_title: Connectland Headset - Stereo - Over-the-head - Binaural - Ear-cup
review_body:
I have always liked neon and pastel colors. The reason being that they're different and mellow. With that said, this pair of headphones definitely caught my eyes while I was browsing for a new pair of headphones. The funny thing is that I was looking to purchase the Beats by Dre but eventually, settled for this. My intention was to purchase a decent pair of headphones that has the right color and style. The beats did fit the bill but I realized that if I were going for style, ConnectLand Stereo definitely takes the cake. I asked myself "How many people have I seen with the beats?". I knew from the get-go that the sound quality might disappoint, however, I was surprised to see that it has outlasted my friend's beats headphones! In addition, the sound quality might not be as comparable to the beats but it does its job. I've used it during my commute to work, gym and study. After 6 months of usage, here is my review:

Usability: 10/10
Plug and Play

Style: 9/10
It's pastel color definitely caught my eyes. The beats only has two colors; they are white and black. If you are looking to get noticed and can settle for mediocre sound quality, this is it.

Affordability: 10/10
It's a fraction compared to how much the beats by dre costs.

Overall, I highly recommend this pair of headphones if you are looking for an inexpensive headphones with style and mediocre sound. Again, i've used it for the gym and studying. It's versatile for every occasion and looks as expensive as the beats.

review_headline: Only suitable for use in US and countries with 110V supply
review_body: The transformer is an automatic voltage step up transformer as well, a fact not clearly highlighted by either the manufacturer or amazon. The manual that came with it is barely a single page of printed material and is not even specific to this product. When plugged in to 110V it automatically up-scales the voltage to 220V and vice-versa. So far so good, but the issue comes when the unit is used in a country with 220V supply. When the unit is switched off, the red light (indicating 220V output) turns on for 1-2 secs, before turning off again, which should never happen as the unit is not supposed to output 220V. The odd behavior can be explained by the following: When the transformer is turned off, the input voltage drops from 220V to 110V and then eventually to 0V. At 110V, the step-up circuit activates itself, causing the 220V output for a few seconds, which is enough to blow any 110V appliances connected to it. I would refrain using this transformer in a country with 220V supply. I must highlight that the manufacturer did not bother to respond to any emails but I'm glad Amazon agreed to refund me the entire cost of this worthless product.

product_title: Sony MDR Premium Over The Head Headphones
review_headline: Gorgeous, But Be Prepared To EQ The Heck Out Of Them
review_body:
I've owned a lot of headphones and this is the most impressive initial experience I've ever had. The packaging is almost unbelievably nice. I felt like I was unwrapping some kind of religious artifact. The headphones themselves are gorgeous and extremely comfortable to wear. Sony's design team is still one of the best in the world.

The actual sound, though? The sound quality is kind of baffling. I don't know what they were going for here. There's a decent amount of bass but it doesn't go very deep, and frankly doesn't sound good. The mids and highs are okay but not exciting.

These headphones can sound pretty decent if you adjust the EQ in your audio software. That and the comfort level are their saving graces.

review_body:
I received a defective unit at first, but the seller promptly emailed me a paid UPS return label. I ordered another of the same model based on the near negligible chance of getting another Lemon, and because they felt so comfortable! I already know that about this product, whereas if I go with another model, there is a chance of a bad fit.

I tested the range outside in open space and got 43 feet out is where music starts cutting out. I also tested it by leaving my phone on the second floor of our house and walking down into our basement level garage... This things Bluetooth signal penetrated through 2 stories of house without missing a single beat!

I don't know what exactly is causing it, but almost every time I listen to any kind of music on these for more than 15 minutes, I get a pretty bad headache. I compared it side by side with a super old but mid-upper end quality Sony wired on-ear headphones, and I have to listen with the volume up twice as high and for twice as long to start getting a similar headache. It took me a couple weeks to really connect the dots and fully come to terms with the fact that I have to continue hunting... that is why I had reviewed it with a 5/5 initially.

I was in love with these when I first got them, but this headache issue is bad enough that I am going to continue the quest for my dream headset.

Oh and one more thing... these leak a TON of sound! Like a person 30 feet away can hear the music at above 50% of the volume the wearer is hearing!

review_body:
I have the "ultimate set of tools" and have been working with electronics for 45 years, so I was not afraid of the tools required. These use a 1.5mm hex key. Not that popular, but I have them.

What is a total fail is, while the center conductor screw clamps onto the conductor, the ground/shield is a totally bass-akward design that could only possibly work for coax and only partially. The set screw for the other conductors screws against the first wire. This will never work with a speaker cord which is what I was using it for (longer wires for some computer speakers). In the case of a coax conductor it will also just split the shield and cause a flaky connection and pierce the insulation into the center connection if you would go any further (as in enough to get the housing over the set screw).

I short, I have no idea what they were thinking when they designed this. It is a total fail and just needs to be withdrawn from the market.

product_title: SoundBlock Bluetooth Wireless Stereo Speaker for Computers & Smartphones - Bluetooth 3.0 Technology with Built-in Speakerphone and 10 Hour Rechargeable Battery
review_headline: Static/White Noise When Playing, Gets Much Worse When Charging
review_body:
Bought two of these, returned them both. Here's why:

The good - the sound quality is excellent. The clarity and depth of the sound are amazing. It gets very loud without any distortion even at maximum volume, which is very surprising for a speaker this size. It paired instantly with both my Note 4 phone and my iPad Mini 2 Retina tablet.

The bad... the static! There's a constant low hiss/white noise when playing sound through the speaker, and it's very audible at night when listening at low volume. But when you plug it into a charger, the static gets so loud it overpowers the audio material being played!

I tried both of my iPad chargers (genuine Apple 10W and 12W units), my Note 4 charger (genuine Samsung), my LG Watch R charger (genuine LG) and a genuine HTC charger from my old phone. As soon as I plugged the speaker into the charger, the static would get unbearably loud and continue until I stopped the music on my iPad or my Note 4 phone. This was happening on both speakers I bought, so I returned both of them.

Another deal breaker... the power-on tone and the volume setting tone plays at maximum volume which can easily wake up someone sleeping in the same room or even startle an awake person... it's LOUD. Even if I set the volume on the speaker itself to minimum, the tones still play at maximum volume, which is mighty annoying.

Finally, one of the two speakers I bought came with a dented corner. The box was factory-sealed, so it looks like someone at the factory dropped it before putting it in the box.

Overall, this would have been a great speaker if the static and the tone volume had been fixed. But as such, it's only suitable for playing music loudly, like at a party, and only when not plugged into a charger. No good for listening at low volumes late at night.

product_title: Etekcity hdmi splitter 2port
review_headline: Picture good, but the value differentiators do not deliver
review_body:
I have been through a few HDMI switches, most of which work very well and I just wanted more ports/functions. The last one I tried (not this model) cost less and had fewer ports but had dual output and TOSLINK output. It cost half the price of this one, but switched really slowly and didn't recognise my devices properly, so I wanted to step up to solid features.

This 6x2 from Etekcity was that step up. I deliberately spent more and looked for Etekcity given I've had a previous unit from them which worked well.
All was good initially. Picture was good, I plugged in DirecTV H25/100, a Matricom G box Q and my Linux PC. Picture from each was great, resolution detection great.

Expecting my DirecTV H25/100 to be least troublesome of all, I started trying it on In1 and OutA, with TOSLINK audio 2ch. No audio. After much replugging, I unplugged the monitor on OUT-A and suddenly- sound from TOSLINK now I'd unplugged the monitor! I plugged the monitor back in on Out-A - no sound again after the video selection completed.

I have not been able to reproduce that one fleeting sound moment. But Matricom sound is perfect; switches every time. I've made very sure DirecTV is set to 2ch to match the EDID output - again, Matricom works fine, DirecTV nothing.

I'll also add that PIP is not what I expected, though it was a feature I wanted. When you press PIP, you get thumbnails of all the 5 other inputs on the left of the current main selection. One is offset, indicating that if you press Enter it will become 'main'. Each thumbnail updates on a timeslice - ie each does a jerky update as the software scans around them.
I expected to be able to select a single PIP, maybe 1/6 or 1/8th full size, in a corner, which would be live - ie continuous/fluid and not jerky updates - which would be my definition of PIP. This seems the be a thumbnail selection utility, not what I call PIP.

DirecTV is a key part of my setup, hoped to get within a PIP or on main screen depending on my current work mode, but is out of the question with no audio.
Skype/Zoom on the Matricom was another key part, and while audio is good, a fluid video within a single PIP while I work on the PC outside the PIP does not happen, so this option is not good also.

So frankly it's next to useless for any single option I was looking for.
Without the audio switch, I can revert to my video only 5 port switch which was 1/3rd the price.
So while I can't fault the full screen picture quality and switching, the key differentiators which make this unit cost 2x more than others don't work effectively, so I can't honestly give it more than 2 stars.

review_headline: PURELY a SCAM and a FAKE product. Shame and sad.
review_body: This is PURELY a SCAM and a FAKE product:  This device simply does't work with any of my several monitors and PC's or tablets. Tested it both ways: - from PC's VGA out to monitors' HDMI in and vice verse from HDMI out to monitors' VGA in. I was naive last time, hoping that HDMI signal can be converted to VGA video signal and separate audio output. That is simply false. It has been explained many times: there is no simple, inexpensive HDMI to VGA video conversion coupler or converter. My opinion is that Amazon and any sellers should test every single item for its designed functionality and specifications or at least follow up when negative reviews are posted and refuse to advertise and participate in selling faulty or imaginary products. There is, it seems like, many manufacturers and sellers that make possibly big bucks by selling fake +/_ $10 products which are not returnable purely from economic reasons. This is very dishonest and going on perhaps on a huge scale. Frankly this is robbing and stealing in a "legal" way, in bright daylight and on many corners. Huge profits for fake products. Really sad and shameful. "HDMI contains no analog signal so it is not possible for any combination of passive adapters and/or cables to convert it to VGA. http://superuser.com/questions/225721/how-can-i-plug-my-hdmi-device-into-a-vga-input  : There is no easy way to convert HDMI to VGA, as VGA is an analog signal. What this means is the powered digital signal of HDMI has to be actively converted to VGA's analog signal. On amazon you can see plenty of 10 dollar "conversion chords" that claim to convert for you. THIS IS A SCAM. somebody has simply glued a VGA connector to an HDML cable. THESE CANNOT POSSIBLY WORK". "The only way to convert HDMI to VGA is with a powered converter box like those you can see on http://vgatohdmi.com/ (found by google, I do not endorse them as I have no experience with their product). Even when using the converter box you maystill run into another problem: HDMI signals are encrypted for DRM. The converter will not decrypt the HDMI signal, so you may have trouble with that. I am not aware of whether or not Boxee encrypts the output, however if they do not then you will be able to use the converter".

product_title: Logitech Harmony Ultimate Home [Discontinued by Manufacturer]
review_body:
3.75 stars

I've owned Harmony remotes for about a decade now. My first one was an 880, and then the previous version of the One. The Ultimate Home is a good product, but needs some work to be great.

Pros:
-Can control Nest thermostat.
-Updates through the network hub instead of plugging into the PC.
-Works from just about any angle or facing away from your devices.
-The usual Harmony functionality and custom set up. The ability to set up any remote devices you have in almost any way you like.
-The addition of the colored buttons at the bottom are a nice touch. BluRay and DirecTV both use colored buttons for certain features.
-Can control your entertainment network through your smart phone without the remote. In the back of the house and need to raise the volume when you left your remote in the living room? Done.

Cons:
-The ergonomics/layout is kind of backwards. Buttons that you use often are at the top and out of easy thumb reach. In my opinion, the touch screen should have been placed at the top with FF/REW buttons in the middle. I use these all the time to jog my DVR forward skipping past commercials, to puase a program, and start to play again.
-Touchscreen menus aren't easily navigated when you need to get to your devices for individual control.
-The "touchpad" to use motions for commands is pretty much worthless.
-The ROUNDED bottom. This has to be the single most thing I hate about the remote. Why, oh why, did they not put a flattened area so this thing would sit still on a table. I have a smaller table that sits next to the couch for the remote and if the dog hits it this thing can rock right off the table.
-I had some trouble setting up my delays between turning on devices. The computer interface wouldn't allow me to move things around with the proper delay. I use an AVR that has to be turned on first, which clicks on the power management unit, which turns on everything else. It kept trying to turn on my TV too early (meaning it wouldn't turn on due to not having enough delay), so I had to add in an additional command for TV on to make it work.

Bottom line: This is a cool remote and has a lot of features. I haven't even tapped into all the things I can do with it yet, and not sure if I'll need to. If my previous Harmony One hadn't died after several years of use I wouldn't have upgraded. The ergonomics need a little more thought to them and they need to add a flat spot so this thing sits flush on a table instead of rocking around.

If you want/need the ability to control Hue lighting, Nest, and other non-entertainment stuff I'd say grab one. If you're looking to upgrade an existing Harmony that works fine, keep what you have. I took advantage of a rebate that was offered and needed to upgrade my old model One remote that was broken.

product_title: Mini HD Video Converter Box HDMI to AV/CVBS L/R Video Adapter HDMI2AV Support NTSC and PAL Output
review_headline: This Device is NOT Reliable - will be a waste of your time and money
review_body:
I originally bought this device to convert a HDMI signal from a computer into a composite video display, this did NOT work... I tried it on two low wattage HTPC's, one being a very low wattage atom based computer, the device could do nothing with either one of them... Then I tried it with an Ouya I had, it worked well with that, at noticeably different resolution and screen aspect of course...

However after 10 days of having it connected to the Ouya, it began to have problems... The audio has begun to cut out briefly every 1-2 minutes... Luckily mine crapped out within 30 days, so it was easy to return through Amazon...

Bottom-Line: Based on the reviews I've read and my own experience, I would NOT recommend this product... It may or may not work for your desired application, but even if it does, it is totally unreliable! Mine only worked properly for 10 days, maybe you buy it and it works properly for 3 months, but then what? Sooner than later this thing is gonna crap out on you, and it might come at a very inopportune time... Either way, there's a good chance this device will leave you feeling burned... Especially when it goes out 45 days after you bought it, it's too late to get your money back, you're already out $15-20, and it would cost at least half that much to ship it back under some sort of warranty... So in the end you've lost your $15-20, you still have the same problem you wanted this device to solve, and when you look for an alternative solution, damn near the only option you have is to buy another crappy Chinese converter that is exactly like this one, and it too will soon fail...

PS - Why would anybody still need RCA inputs, just get a new TV???

Though I tested this device with my home entertainment system, my true intended purpose for this unit was to eventually go into my car to convert a computer's HDMI output into a Composite Video (RCA) output to feed my head-unit and other monitors in my vehicle... MyKenwood DNX571HD head-unit does have a HDMI port, but it wont feed that input to other monitors through HDMI input, it is only capable of that using Composite Video, so I wish this would have worked... Once I finish my install, I want it to be a reliable setup, and needless to say this device did not fit the bill... I am now forced to move on to testing a different solution of using a MHL capable HDMI Matrix with 3.5mm audio-out in my vehicle, it's a lot more expensive way to go, but hopefully it will actually work...

So you see I was pretty much forced by car audio/video standards into using Composite Video, which is why I needed this device... But if you're buying this device to use on an old TV in your house, I would recommend saving your money and putting it towards a HDTV...

product_title: Ivation 1000mAh Rechargeable Bicycle Speaker and USB MP3 Player With External Audio Controls
review_headline: DECEPTIVE LISTING, POOR DESIGN, MISSING PARTS & TERRIBLE SOUND - BE FOR WARNED!
review_body:
** DECEPTIVE LISTING: As this review is written the bullet points of the product listing reads (just below color choices): "Connect any MP3 player or phone VIA the 3.5mm AUX cable". In the product description further down it reads: "To stream audio from your iPhone, connect it with the auxiliary cable." There is no auxiliary cable included despite their listing leading one to believe it is part of the item one is buying. The product listing will lead one to believe there is a 3.5mm cable to connect your mp3 or smart phone to but there is none and the company will not send one despite the deceptive listing.

** POOR DESIGN: Why this was produced and shipped with a USB port makes little sense when instead what it really needs is a built in 3.5mm cable to plug into an MP3, iPod, iPhone, or any other brand of smart phone on the market. After all, this is going on a bike and one would buy this to store their phone inside while riding. It only makes reasonable sense to include the cable to plug into your phone or mp3 device while its inside. Its like buying tennis shoes without including the shoe laces. So be warned you will need to spend additional time and money finding the correct cable to get this to work. When you do find a cable, make sure the end is a 90 degree and not straight because if it is straight it will protrude into the fabric which separates the internal connections from the cavity which is used for storage. Bouncing and jolting of the bike with pressure on the connection from items stored inside could also cause a failure in the connection over time.

** ADDITIONAL MISSING PARTS: The unit received was also missing 1) the lithium battery and 2) the charging cable. Unfortunately the charging cable connection isn't the standard phone style connection either, so if yours actually comes with the cable be careful not to lose it because you may not have a similar one around and will have to buy another cable tocharge it.

** SOUND QUALITY: If you like the scratchy, hollow & barely decipherable sound of a subway conductor and want it on your bike, by all means buy this product! This unit was also a huge disappointment in sound quality but as others have said, it can be loud..... screeching loud!

SUMMARY: Deceptive Listing, Poor Design, Missing Parts & Terrible Sound, make this a loosing option as a bicycle speaker. Don't waste your money on this item.

As of this writing, Rome 2 is well over a year old and the digital download on Amazon is being offered for $60. I managed to snatch it for $15 during a holiday sale, and even then I'm still disappointed with this game.

THE GOOD
+ Looks very pretty.
+ It actually runs well (an issue this game had at launch).
+ Steamworks community.

THE BAD
- Very simplified and boring game mechanics compared to its predecessors, and especially compared to other games in the genre.
- Predictable and unengaging AI.
- Battles, though pretty, are still very fast. You'll spend more time in empire management, again a concept other games do better.
- Limited multiplayer population. It takes forever to find a game.
- Still prone to performance issues and graphical glitches.
- Unsatisfactory DLC experience. Be prepared to shell out cash for additional repetitive campaigns, reskinned "official" factions, and the privilege of portraying blood in a war game.

Rome 2 was plagued with issues at launch, that's documented. This is the "revamped" Emperor Edition. It optimizes game performance, fixes the majority of bugs, and provides an additional "Imperator Augustus" campaign. The latter can basically be viewed as a save point where you can take command of a large and already established Roman faction at a later point in history.
If you've never played a Total War game before and are very interested in the setting, do yourself a favor and wait for a sale. And do us all a favor and avoid pre-ordering Attila for that matter. Don't expect historical accuracy here, history buffs.

product_title: Monster Cable Diesel In-Ear Headphone with Apple Control Talk
review_body:
Price:
Bought these Diesel headphones for about $40.
I wouldn't consider myself an audiophile however I have spent big money on premium headphones. More specifically on in-ear noise isolation headphones.

Sound:
First off, the sound quality is subpar which was kind of unexpected from the Monster. I used to own some Turbines a long time ago and they were one of the best headphones I have ever used of all time. I'm not overly obsessed with bass but even these are lacking. Overall is just muddled and I've gotten better sound out of cheaper headphones. One aspect I was very pleased with was the microphone. I hardly use it but I asked during a call how my voice sounded and was told it sounded clear. Leakage was no issue at all too.

Design and Comfort:
They look stylish with the black and yellow color scheme and they do have a unique pyramid-like shape. The unique shape however works against it at least with regards to my ear fit. I have fairly big ears but that doesn't stop the top from prodding my ear every now and then. I use them while running and it's more frequent when I am. However if I am in a stationary place, not so much trouble with pokes and prods. The in ear buds were also very uncomfortable. I went through the entire set of buds in the package and wasn't comfortable with a single pair. Fortunately I've acquired a huge number of buds through the years and found a nice set for them.

Conclusion :
Honestly at the end of the day, I was swayed by past experience with previous Turbines. I've probably had these Diesels for about 4-6 months and I really only use them when I know I will be making calls or I can't find my much better quality (and cheaper $) jLabs. I really wanted to like these but i can't give them anything more than 2 stars. Would have liked to give 3 stars but I couldn't justify the $40 spent when not one pair of the buds included didn't fit comfortably.

product_title: Omicron TURENO HDTV Speaker subwoofer
review_headline: Loud and boomy, lacks definition in music sound quality. I'd rather go subwooferless.
review_body:
It's great at being loud, boomy, and obnoxious. That said, if you're looking for sound quality and definition in music, go elsewhere. I use a receiver and connected this via the sub line-out, set crossover on the receiver to 60Hz or 80Hz (played around with it), and adjusted the volume on this sub to blend in. The bass that I sent to this instead of my bookshelf speakers (using the crossover) was deeper, but much muddier. And I'm talking 60-80Hz bass, not higher stuff. Even though having a sub means my main speakers don't need to do bass (and can thus do midrange and highs better), I found the overall result was a system that has muddier lows, and that makes the particularly low bass too loud. At best, it gave the system a little more kick, at worst, it muddied it up.

All in all, this might work if you want explosions in movies to boom, or electronic bass in music to be loud (a friend with one of these loves it for that). But if you listen to other genres of music and want a sub that will add to the system overall, look elsewhere. The space this needs and the cost of it just weren't enough for me to justify keeping mine.

product_title: HDE VGA w/Audio to HDMI 1080p UP Scaler Converter Box w/DC Adapter for TV
review_body:
I purchased this to play my Dreamcast on my relatively new Samsung TV. I had to first buy a VGA Cable with RCA Sound adapter for the Dreamcast first, and then plug all that into this device. After plugging everything in, my TV could not find the HDMI source that this was plugged in to. I switched it around a few times, each with the same result. Finally, after messing around with it for over an hour, I got it to work. I played a game on there for half an hour and felt pretty pleased and decided to restart the system, as I wanted to check out the Dreamcast boot up sequence. When I restarted it, the last frame/image of what I was playing remained on the screen, with static, and all in purple. Confused, I turned off the system, and turned it on.. only to find the same exact thing displayed on the screen.

I even powered off this HDE box, but nothing seemed to work. I unplugged the cables from this HDE box and plugged the VGA cable in to the TV directly, and the picture was perfect. Now, I just need an extension of the audio cables so I get audio. This HDE box, when it worked, was wonderful. I was thrilled when it worked, but for some reason when it doesn't work, it's near impossible to figure out exactly why it suddenly doesn't work. I'm up for suggestions as to how to get this to work, but right now I'm switching back to the VGA connection and doing it that way.

product_title: Clip Plus 4 GB MP3 Player (Black)
review_body: When I purchased this item, my sole intent was to use it for my wedding. We planned to hook it up with aux cord into a PA system to play our reception music; a preselected list of MP3s. I charged it that morning, brought it to the reception, plugged it in and...didn't work. Yes, this was the first of many surprises with this player.  PROs: 1. Small, durable 2. Easy to understand settings and prompts 3. Built in clip is great for any kind of workout, or even just sitting in the office. 4. While not loud, this does achieve a decent volume. 5. Once software is loaded onto computer, and after you've navigated to the Tracks area a few times, loading music is relatively simple.  CONs: 1. Shorter battery life: 10 hours max, and often less, depending on volume level. The battery indicator shows 1/2 charge when it abruptly (and automatically) powers down. This wasn't just some one-time glitch, this was standard operating procedure. I had the screen light on the lowest, and the shortest say-lit time. 2. Strange glitches: search troubleshooting guides and you'll see complaints about this player turning itself off randomly (for me, this happened roughly once a week with normal use). The fix is to hold the Power button for 10-20 seconds, which somehow magically resets it. Then pushing the power again turns it on. The player resumes on the song you started with when you first turned on the player (so could be hours ago). 3. Charging the unit turns it on: You're thinking, "Who cares?" While the unit is charging, it is turned on and in a static mode showing a few graphics to indicate a charge is taking place. However, as soon as you unplug it, the unit remains on. If you're not used to this, you might put the unit away allowing it to drain itself of battery within the day. Once you're used to this issue, it's not a big deal to turn it off. Guess how you become used to it? By forgetting to turn it off a few times and finding the already-short battery life drained. 4. Last less than two years: Look folks, I work in an insurance office. I sit in front of a computer. We're not talking rugby, we're talking paperwork and mainframe screens. One day, my unit was working, the next day, kaput. No explanation, no fix. Less than two years. I don't care if everything is built to break - this lasted less than a fifth of my 10 year old crappy flip phone, c'mon. 5. This accepts a MicroSD card, but from the literature I've read, it only allows pre-paid/pre-loaded music. Maybe I didn't understand what I was looking at, but without additional storage, the 4gb version is only just big enough.  Overall, this is an ok purchase if you don't mind dropping a little cash on a mediocre MP3 player. My bet is I could have received much more bang for my buck elsewhere. Now I have to run out and purchase a new one (different brand, of course) because this Sansa didn't even last as long as the Sony headphones I bought for it two years ago. Shame.

product_title: FiiO X5 High Resolution Lossless Music Player
review_headline: Could be great, were it not for serious design flaws.
review_body:
UPDATE: FiiO has already released their "2nd gen" X5 and given up on this bug-laden device. Changing review to one star and hoping that I someday forget that I ever wasted money on this thing.

Below is a modified version of a letter / review that I recently wrote to FiiO support. I'm hanging on to my X5, with the hopes that they'll resolve some of the issues I've outlined in future firmware updates.

I purchased a FiiO X5 back in December 2014, shortly after Apple announced that it was discontinuing the high-capacity â€œClassicâ€ model. Like many former iPod owners, I wanted to get a replacement portable digital audio player that could hold my entire music library (which, in my case, is nearly 200 GB). After a thorough online comparison of alternatives to the iPod, I chose the FiiO X5, mainly because of the dual-TF card storage that allows for up to 256 GB.

After using the X5 for a few months, I had some thoughts on whatâ€™s working and what could be changed in terms of user interface. Right now I wouldn't to recommend this device to others; with a few changes to the firmware I think this could be an outstanding portable audio player that I would recommend to anyone.

First, things that the X5 have over other portable audio players:

- The dual-card storage setup that allows for high capacities of data. Like I mentioned, this is the main reason that I bought the X5, and I imagine what other former iPod Classic users are looking for. This immediately puts the X5 ahead of other lossless digital audio players such as the Pono. Iâ€™ve heard that FiiO plans to allow larger capacity TF cards in future firmware updates; hopefully they plan on following through with this.

- High resolution audio options. This is becoming increasingly popular among the audiophile market, so itâ€™s good that FiiO is ahead of the curve by allowing pretty much any type of audio file on it. The USB DAC option, although not necessary for me, is a worthy feature to offer as well.

- No-nonsense drag and drop interface. This is actually both a positive and negative feature, which Iâ€™ll get into later.

Now, on to things that I think could use improvement:

- The slow scroll speed. This is, in my opinion, the biggest setback right now in the X5â€™s interface. With my library of over 1600 artists, it takes three and a half minutes of constantly scrolling the wheel to get from the first artist in my list to the last. Three and a half minutes. This makes casual listening to the FiiO X5 pretty much impossible. Yes, I am aware that it is possible to scroll backwards and instantly go from the first A entry to the last Z entry, but itâ€™s still not a solution, since weâ€™re still discussing the scroll time in terms of minutes. From a customerâ€™s perspective, fixing the scroll speed should be the number one priority for FiiOâ€™s software developers. Itâ€™s the one major issue that makes using the X5 a chore, without any workaround available to the user. My suggestion â€” keep the speed of the scroll wheel the same, and have the top and bottom right buttons (which currently serve the same purpose of the scroll wheel) jump up and down to the next letter, respectively. Example â€”

Scrolling through the artist list in the â€œAâ€ section when I think, â€œI want to hear some Devoâ€. Click the bottom right button three times, skipping to B, C, D. Then I can scroll from the first â€œDâ€ entry to Devo. This would only take a few seconds, rather than nearly a minute of scrolling.

Barring that example, just take a cue from the iPodâ€™s design and have the scroll wheel automatically switch to scrolling by letter once you scroll long and fast for a couple seconds.

I cannot stress the scroll wheel issue enough. If I had to give the FiiO X5 a letter grade in its current state, it would be â€œC-â€œ, for all the issues Iâ€™m discussing in this letter. Just by fixing the scroll wheel speed issue alone, I would change the grade to â€œB-â€œ â€” not great, but worlds beyond how it used to be.

On to the other not-as-critical (but still important) issues:

- The media library update. Every time I add new music to the FiiO, in order for the FiiO to recognize the new tracks on the drive I must go into the settings and manually update the music library. My current music library totals at over 31,000 songs, all of which I have copied over to the X5. I just ran a media library update, and it took just over 34 minutes. This is unacceptable for obvious reasons (especially considering that the flash card storage should mean faster processing speeds). Itâ€™s a design flaw thatâ€™s nearly as bad as the aforementioned scroll-wheel issue. The only reason that itâ€™s not as critical an issue is that this process only needs to be run every time new music is introduced to the X5 (which, for some people, is quite often).

- Syncing. The drag and drop feature is convenient in some cases, but can be tedious for those of us who are used to iTunesâ€™ sync feature. Jeremy Lawrensonâ€™s â€œDapperâ€ app is absolutely necessary for any user of the X5. It would be great if FiiO developed a similar program, rather than necessitating the need to drop $20 on a third-party app.

- Interface issues. I try not to get too hung up on things like this, but there are a couple issues UI issues that make using the X5 tedious:

- Itâ€™s irritating how every time I start up the X5, in order to listen to music I have to scroll to â€œPlay by Categoryâ€, click, then scroll to â€œArtistâ€, then click again. It would be great if the X5 remembered this choice, so when it starts up Iâ€™m immediately presented with my list of Artists.

- The alphabetization of definitive articles (The, A, An, etc) â€” this one is a no-brainer. The Descendants should appear under â€œDâ€, not â€œTâ€.

Iâ€™ve composed this with the hopes that someone on the FiiO development team would understand the X5â€™s issues on a consumer level. Like I said, the X5 has potential to be the best affordable high-storage DAP on the market, but right now the interface needs a serious redesign.

UPDATE: FiiO customer support was nice enough to get back to me re: the list of complaints above. Turns out the scroll wheel is an issue that they've been working on, and plan to address in future updates. product_title: Winegard HD7697P High Definition VHF/UHF Antenna
review_body: I had a 35 year old antenna in the attic that had caused me some grief since it was rather large.  Climbing in the attic was made more difficult because it was just in the way much too often.  Since the present day digital stations do not use low VHF, the elements on the antennas can be much shorter.  With this in mind, I bought the Winegard HD7697P to replace the old antenna.  Aside from the shorter elements, it is clear that the old antenna was of much higher quality.  Every part just looks better made.  Does an antenna have to look good?  Not necessarily, but having a well made antenna gives one confidence that it would preform well.  I carefully read the instructions and rehearsed in my mind what I would do in the attic, which is not a pleasant place to stay for long.  Straightening out the elements was rather easy, just as I expected.  The problems came trying to align screw holes.  I had previously read some nasty comments on the web about holes not lining up.  They were right.  Apparently, Winegard engineers never heard of mechanical tolerance.  I've designed plenty of parts during my career to know parts typically do not line up, and hence some slack must be built in.  Well, there was none here.  To remedy the situation, I had to enlarge the hole connecting the brace just to get the screw to go through two parts.  Actually I should have made the hole a bit bigger because the antenna is now a bit distorted from the high tension put on the joint.  By the time I had to attach the front end to the rest of the antenna, I was too tired to even enlarge that hole.  Instead, I just stuck the screw through one set of holes (It has to go through two sets to penetrate the top and bottom of the parts.) and gave up.  Since the antenna was in the attic, there was no worry that the front would fall off from wind storms.  So partial assembly was OK.  The cable box was received with one of its four sets of V-connectors bent.  I e-mailed Winegard to see if the bent ones neededto be straightened out.  They did not reply for a couple of day.  So I went ahead and put the box in place.  The actual answer was that it should be straightened out.  I asked if removing the box would cause damage, and the answer was "no."  So based on this information, I went back up to the attic to take out the box and fix the defect.  Well, they were wrong.  One of the connectors had stuck to the wire connected to one side of the high-VHS elements.  When I pull out the box, the wired came with it and bent sharply at a large angle.  Fortunately, I saw what happened and bent it back.  On my old antenna, the connection was made with a springy contact, which can be removed repeatedly without damage.  It also used screws to pull the box onto the antenna base, a very secure situation.  In contrast, the Winegard merely had tabs on the plastic box, which can easily loosen over time.  Needless to say, I was not impressed.  Of course, the true test of an antenna is whether it pulls in more stations.  In my case, the one iffy station was 7, which I can get on a rare occasion with the old setup.  With the new antenna, 7 came in more often, but is still occasionally lost.  I had not necessarily expected to get more stations since the old antenna received every station expected from my location in the SF Bay Area.  And I did not.  So for my efforts, I had marginal gain in performance.  But I may have been able to do the same with a UHF style flat antenna that is prevalent today.  That would have been much easier to install.  The bottom line is that the 7697 is OK, but I would have much happier if the mechanical design was better and the antenna was better built.  As for signal gathering, I just wonder whether the flat antenna would have worked just as well without all the effort of moving element and the rest of the assembly.

The only way I can bear listening to the classics on this thing is to keep the volume on the bare minimum, so the speakers won't hiss at the crescendos. product_title: Yamaha CD-S700BL Natural Sound CD Player (Black) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Good player but seems over-priced compared to some other players............You decide whats best for you :)
review_body:
I didn't keep my Yamaha S-300 but I did give it a good 20+ day trial before I returned it.

This is a very well built and nice sounding CD player but it has a few limitations that the Onkyo C 7030 that I ended up keeping does not have.

This Yamaha will "NOT playback" (.Flac files) but will playback MP3s if that's your thing. I just never use any source that's that compressed as it defeats the reasoning for owning a CD only player.

This Yamaha is a nice player but is not worth the $300 price tag in my opinion. I love Yamaha products and own a 7.2 Yamaha receiver and a Yamaha Blue Ray player that's still going strong 4 years later.

I have a separate component system for music playback only in a 2.2 stereo analog only setup. It's all vintage equipment that's been upgraded to last for a very long time.

So if your not planning on using this players USB/MP3 playback option all that often then the Onkyo 7030 would be a better choice.

I like the Yamaha's Burr-Brown DAC and its nice look but it's cost is just too high when the Onkyo 7030 is available for almost 50% the cost.

I did many A/B comparisons between this Yamaha and the Onkyo as I thought the Onkyo was just too cheap to be any good.
Well I was wrong about that and the tests proved it as I had several friends also listen blindly during A/B testing.

The Onkyo has a 11.7 LB weight and the ability to playback .Flac files which made it the player for me. This Yamaha is a very good sounding
player but at 7.7 LBs it's not built as well as the Onkyo with it's very high end power transformer.
Weight really matters with CD players and even Blue Ray players like the Oppo home blue ray players that weigh about 10.5LBs with it's shorter total height similar to the Cambridge Audio CD only players.

If you start checking the weight of CD only players you will see how the more heavy units cost a heck of a lot more. This is do to the power transformer, the DAC or DACs, and the overall build quality of the player. The higher the weight the better the player is with reducing vibration and giving you skip free playback.
The players transport is also very important as it actually lifts the disk up and spins it up to playback speeds. The transport on both the Yamaha and the Onkyo are basically equal center mounted transports but the Yamahas tray only comes out 3/4 of the way forcing you to angle your CD for insertion.
Not a deal breaker for me but it could be for some people.
If I were interested in buying a new CD player I would simply do what I did. Simply just buy both and take a solid 20+ days to compare them and then decide and return the other.
The Onkyo with it's Woflson DACs and high end transformer is a great sounding and well built player. The Yamaha is also a very good sounding player as well, but light on the overall weight partially due to it's shorter overall height. That said the Cambridge Audio 640CV2 that my friend owns weights about 10.5 LBs and is the exact same height as this Yamaha.

I am a budget audiophile since I was a teenager back in 1982. I learned at a young age that it's not always the component with the higher price tag that's the best.

If you are really looking for a nice sounding well built CD player you cant go wrong with either player. In fact at one time I was still going to buy the Yamaha as my secondary CD player since it has a Burr-Brown DAC and would just barely fit on top of the 7030.
I since bought a Denon910 DVD/CD player that also had a Burr-Brown DAC for $48 used but in mint condition on Ebay.

Here's my system:
Carver C-1 preamp(Mint and upgraded) Carver TX-2 Tuner (Mint) Hafler DH-500 amp (Mint and upgraded) with it's 255+
watts of super clean power, Onkyo 7030 CD player (New), Pioneer PL-7 (Mint condition) Shure M97XE Cartridge(New), Adcom ACE 515 line conditioner and component On/Off timer. Definitive Studio Monitor 450's (Front speakers) SVS 12" powered subs x 2 hooked up to the secondary pre-outs.(One for each channel)

This system may be using dated equipment but as all of the vintage equipment has been upgraded the Carver C-1 preamp and Hafler DH-500 amp have had all available upgrades needed. The C-1 preamp has new resisters, caps, and Op-Amps that put in a class by itself with only the best top of the line new preamps being competitive with it. The Hafler DH-500 amp has had the rear RCAs replaced and the speaker binding posts replaced as well.

So after running this equipment with both CD players I found the Onkyo 7030 to be the best in build quality and sound. For the record I have never owned any Onkyo equipment before so I'm not a Onkyo brand nut. I'm actually big Yamaha fan but simply could not justify the $300 price point compared to the $160 Onkyo C 7030.

I don't like to act like I know it all and thus I would simply let it be known this is just my opinion, although a educated one.

That said, I would order both and decide for yourself after a good A/B comparison. After all everyone has different source playback equipment and please understand how important that equipment is when listening to a new CD player.
