product_title: EarZonk Premium Long-Life Leatherette Ear Cushions for Grado Headphones
review_headline: They look and feel nice, but ruin the Grado sound
review_body:
I rarely write reviews, but I figured I would share my experience with these pads as I have had mostly good experiences with other EarZonk ear pads for my Grado 225i's.

On the plus side, they are pretty comfortable and seem durable. They also are easy to install and do not fall off (as some EarZonk pads do). That's about all I can say that is positive.

Simply stated, these things completely muddy up the normally tremendous sound of Grado headphones. I cannot imagine how anyone that actually used them would ever give them a positive review. Still, I see some people saying how they actually improve the sound. I get it that acoustics are a little subjective, but you would have to be completely tone deaf to like how these make Grados sound.

I tried, as some had suggested to pull off the mesh from the inside (not an easy task to do without messing up the pads, but they sounded so awful that I did not care if I messed them up). This improved the sound a little, but they still honestly have terrible sound. I put my old worn out L cush pads back on and it was like night and day. I ordered a new set of genuine L cush pads from Grado. Ear Zonk makes a decent knock off, but they were still a little off in how they were cut (one ear pad falls off sometimes).

product_title: RBC6 UPS Complete Replacement Battery Kit for SUA1000
review_headline: Battery is slightly too tall to fit easily in my APC BackUPS Pro 1000
review_body: Battery started up in my old APC BackUPS Pro 1000 with no problems. But installation was a hassle. As some other reviews have noted, the Chrome Battery RBC6 is just slightly too tall. You need to use a lot of force to slide the RBC6 into the APC UPS case (I'll note here that the battery I'm replacing, an ABC-branded battery fit just fine in the BackUPS Pro 1000, and removal was also easy -- the battery didn't swell). Most likely, if there is any battery swelling at the end of battery life, you may not be able to remove the battery to replace it. As it was, sliding it in took way too much force for my preferences. I used some hand tools to bend the L brackets to add some clearance over the top of the battery. That allowed the Chrome RBC6 to slide in relatively easily.  The battery's Positive connection also seems to be out of spec dimensionally (too thin). The UPS's Positive (red) female connector fits very loosely on the battery's Positive tab. Some slight bending of the UPS's female connector fixes the issue.  Fuse on the jumper cable is 60A, which matches what APC uses. The fuse is properly secured to the battery using double-stick tape, just like with APC. The RBC6 consists of two 12V batteries connected in series, and the two batteries are also properly attached to each other to form a single unit.

product_title: Philips AJT Bluetooth Dual Alarm Clock Radio iPhone/Android Speaker Dock Speakerphone Microphone â€¦
review_body:
This is okay, but not great. I previously had an iHome for an alarm clock, but, as I haven't had an apple product for years, I only used it as an alarm. I have a Samsung Galaxy s3 and since my iHome was dying a tragic and annoying death, I wanted an android compatible product. This is not it. It will charge my phone, but only with a charging cable that needs its own outlet. It doesn't play music directly through the unit, only through Bluetooth. Also, the alarm is the strangest thing. First of all, it doesn't let you control the alarm volume. I don't need a lot to wake me up, but my husband requires an air raid siren to stir him in the slightest. This alarm starts very quietly and then escalates to a slight whisper. That just won't wake him up. Then, the snooze feature doesn't go of every 9 minutes, like every other snooze in the world does. The alarm goes off, and you hit snooze. Then it goes off in four minutes. Next time it goes off in 6. Eventually, it will go 9 minutes between alarms but by then you really need to get up. This is at most an adequate alarm. I wish someone would make one that is just like the iHome but for android phones.

Also, the cord puts out a high pitched whine like a ringing in your ears. This is quite annoying.

product_title: CyberPower Standby Desktop UPS
review_body:
I could not find software or any instructions how to disable the alarm for a power outage. The alarm is super annoying goes off like every minute. Also, even if there is a minor power outage overnight this thing can wake you up pretty easy.

You can disable the alarm by gently prying off the motherboard speaker inside. You need a precision star screwdriver set (for a long narrow T10) and a long narrow #1 philips head to get inside the case. Then use a small flat head to gently pry the speaker off of the motherboard. I did this and it works fine and now does not beep. Search for \\"motherboard speaker\\" so you know what it looks like (it is a black round piece with a circular hole in the center and it was in the upper right hand corner of the motherboard). Of course the manufacturer wont like this but they dont have to live with the annoying beep now do they.

Unit otherwise works fine, it is an economical battery backup, this wont keep things running long, definitely not meant for a big TV, but its fine for a small TV and game console or a satellite reciever.

product_title: iHome iDL91 Dual Charging Stereo FM Clock Radio with Lightning Dock and USB Charge/Play for iPod/iPad and iPhone 5/5S and 6/6Plus
review_body: This clock radio has some nice design features, and some glaring weaknesses.  Pros: * the speakers have enough low-end to sound pretty good * detailed alarm settings include setting of Mode, FM station and volume for both alarms   (independent of the 2nd alarm and current listening settings) * time display is easily readable and adjustable, includes date or current mode in display * build-quality seems good * aux-in and extra USB port are useful  Cons: * the buttons are impossible to feel in the dark as they are perfectly flush with the surface * the built-in lightening docking connector is a bit vulnerable if the iPad is moved incorrectly * the iHome Set app for iOS is intended for updating firmware & access features.   but the app is non-functional and has not been updated since 2013. * the USB mode doesn't allow you to select mp3 files for playback (from a non-iOS device, like a thumb drive)  I think it is a decent product. But I'll have to do a few things like putting textured tape on some buttons to make them easier to find in the dark, and being careful not to let the iPad tilt forward when docked. These things could have been addressed easily in the design phase. It is surprising they weren't addressed since other features do seem pretty carefully implemented. Having a broken app for more than a few months is pretty weak.  Despite the above issues, I didn't see any other products that matched its quality, features and price. Too bad iHome didn't go the extra mile to make this a great product.

product_title: Yamaha RX-V675
review_headline: Pretty easy to use. But got Access Error when using Pandora (even on replacement unit)
review_body: I currently have a Pioneer Elite SC-55 and it's outstanding except when it comes to programing the darn thing. You need a PhD to do anything with that thing UI is pretty dismal. I am adding another TV in another but I don't need all the bells and whistles so got the Yamaha 675. The Yamaha user interface is a welcoming relief. Pretty easy to program and set up. Hook up the ethernet cable and you're set to you.    Unfortunately Pandora streaming was another story. Every 5-30 min I would get a pause. Then half the time an error message on the screen saying ACCESS ERROR. So I hook up the Pioneer to the same router and stream Pandora as well just to make sure it's not my router. The Pioneer had no problems. I even switched the two wires making sure it's not my router. And same thing. So I'm returning this thing hopefully the next one does not have a faulty ethernet card, apparently happens to some of these receiver. Crossing my fingers.    12/8/2014 Update:    Just got the second receiver today. Plugged it in and did the update via ethernet. Started Pandora and within 30 seconds the music stops playing, same problem as the first receiver. Just to be sure I restarted the receiver and let it play a bit longer, this time it paused playing and the receiver displayed the ACCESS ERROR message. What's the chance that both of these receiver have a faulty ethernet card. For the last couple days while waiting for the replacement receiver, I've been plugging my Pioneer Elite and streaming Pandora. It plays without a single pause this weekend. So I'm pretty convince Amazon had a bad batch or something. So if you just got this you might want to set Pandora up and make sure your unit doesn't have the ACCESS ERROR.    I'm going to give Amazon one more shot at it. I'll call it quit if the third unit also has this defect.     12/9/2014 Update:    So Amazon is not sending me a replacement unit wants me to call Yamaha. This is odd I would expect them to just replace the unit. Not sure if Iwant to deal with customer service at Yamaha. This is a brand new unit it should work that way. Bummer cuz I really like this receiver.    12/22/2014 Update:    Amazon finally sent me a 3rd unit. Sadly after listening to Pandora for 10 minutes on the 3rd unit it does the same thing as the first two units. It paused Pandora streaming and then it displays \\"Access Error\\" on the front display. So perhaps it doesn't work with Pandora. Nevertheless I'm going to keep the unit since I have work around by streaming Pandora with my phone. I'm hoping this problem only occur with Pandora and not Airplay or something. So while the unit advertises that it streams from Pandora, it doesn't actually work. Now my internet connection is via ethernet wire, not wireless. As I said previously, I connected another receiver to the same ethernet wire and it streams Pandora fine.

review_headline: Brain Dead Design, which malfunctions â€“ 1*
review_body:
Update â€“ I have had to stop using this clock after several months of operation. The clock just stops momentarily, resetting to 12:00 midnight on Jan 1. I initially thought that the AC power was being stopped because the input from the transformer might have come loose, so I arranged to it to be attached more securely, but the same thing still happened, even though there was no one near the connection when the interruption occurred. I then went to battery power, but the projection system does not work on battery power, so I used both the battery and AC in hopes that if there was an interruption in the AC then the battery backup would prevent the clock from resetting, but it does not. Even a broken clock is right twice a day, but when this clock resets it is never right, and gives an erroneous time. I have therefore had to downgrade from two to only one star.

Original review
I do not recommend this clock for the reasons described below. The clock worked and I purchased it on a half price closeout, so as a clock it was OK, but overpriced if you just operate it as a simple digital clock, hence two stars instead of the minimum one.

Why do I call this a â€œbrain deadâ€ - described below in order of the most annoying features first:
Â· The projector feature is poorly designed. When you face the clock, it projects the time on the wall behind or above the clock upside down and backwards. The time is projected correctly on the wall facing the clock and can therefore be read when you are facing this wall and have your back towards the clock. However, this most likely requires projecting the time more than the six foot focusing distance, as it did in my case. The result is a large somewhat blurry image. The correct orientation is also displayed when you turn the clock with its back facing you, so you can only read the projected time on the wall facing the clock. BETTER PROJECTOR CLOCKS HAVE THE ABILITY TO FLIP THE IMAGE IN ORDER TO CORRECT FOR THIS, and give you the ability to view the correct image with the clock in a different orientation relative to the way that you are facing. Also, while the projector can be rotated about one axis, that is all. Therefore, I found it impossible to orient both the clock and the projected image to optimum orientations.

Â· The clock face is tilted backwards at a fixed angle, which cannot be adjusted. This made it difficult to read the clock while lying in bed, and required me to make a jury-rigged system to keep the face at an orientation where I could read the clock. Unfortunately, the clock was less stable in this position, requiring still further modifications. Even a moderately thoughtful deign would have eliminated this problem without adding to the coat of the clock.

Â· The temperature readings were three degrees high (compared to two other digital thermometers in the room). This may seem petty, but if you are interested on knowing the temperature and its changes over a period of days you should at least see the correct value. This incorrect value may be due to the heat given off by the projecting LED and there is no way to turn off the projector, except to run completely on batteries. (The clock can be run completely on battery power, or with the batteries as a backup for a power failure but unused when the clock is running on AC.)

Â· The clock is very bright, perhaps too bright when you are trying to sleep and there is no way to reduce the brightness. The numbers are 1/2 an inch high as opposed to Â¾ of an inch on other clocks. Instead of a larger image this clock has color bands that go up and down and cycle, illustrating the temperature changes over the last five days. The bands take up most of the lower half of the clock face and I found them to be distracting, so I had to cover over this feature, as there is no way to turn it off.

Â· Setting the clock up was a pain â€“ not at all intuitive and probably almost impossible without the instructions, so if you lose them the clock might become useless.

All in all this is a prime example of a poor (brain dead) design. The clock would have been more useful as more than a simple clock if the clock face could be tilted and more useful as a projector clock if the projected image could be rotated about more than one axis and flipped so that it could be read when one was facing the clock, instead of only when the clock face is not also visible. Rather than having these features, the clock has multiple alarm choices, which were difficult to set up, and the ability to set up a â€œspecial dayâ€ setting, which is very confusing to set up as it is easily confused with the actual date setup.e them the clock might become useless. product_title: Onkyo TX-NR626 7.2-Channel Network Audio/Video Receiver (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
Disappointing.

The general features work as advertised, however there are two "features" which do not make sense and degrade the quality of the otherwise good product.

1. You can have one source be the video for the TV, while and audio-only source play through the speakers. However, apparently bluetooth audio is considered a video source as well, and takes over the TV. What does it show? The name of my phone. That's it. So rather than being able to watch the game and stream music from my phone, I am reminded of what my phone broadcasts itself as to connected bluetooth devices.

2. It has component video in, which is good. I have an older model Xbox 360 that doesn't have the HDMI port. Connecting directly to the TV I can get 1080p and it looks great. This Onkyo, however, requires that the component video source (read: analog HD) be set to output at 480i only (read: standard definition). Why does it force an HD input to standard defintion? Therefore my Xbox will remain connected to the TV directly. This is worse than other AV receivers that don't even have component video in, because this got my hopes up only to smash them down. Component in was one of the main reason I chose this over the competing Sony device.

product_title: JBL E50BT Black Premium Wireless Over-Ear Bluetooth Stereo Headphone, Black
review_headline: Great in all regards except proprietary charging/audio port and cables
review_body: I recently purchased the JBL E50BT headphones.  I was disappointed in the lack of specific technical documentation both on the product packaging and on the JBL website.  I wanted to see if the the product used a common micro-USB charging port.  I was specifically disappointed to see that these headphones require a proprietary charging cable and proprietary headphone audio cable for non-Bluetooth use.  There is one dual purpose charging and audio port on the device.  So, you cannot charge them while you are using them.  This port is a NON-STANDARD size being smaller than the global standard of 3.5mm.  Also, the proprietary tiny plug uses 4 inline connections.  I looked on the net to see if I could find a replacement proprietary JBL charging cable in case the one supplied became damaged.  I was unable to locate any.  I was disappointed that JBL decided to use a proprietary port instead of the common standard.  In fact, I have so many micro-USB charging cords and devices, that I decided not to keep this product based on this one product limitation.  I want to be able to charge with my existing plethora of charging devices.  In all other regards, I liked the product.  The audio was AMAZING with great rich sound and surprisingly deep bass extending to the low sonic range.  The volume capability of the headphones was more than enough.  The battery life was also quite long.  Bluetooth pairing and use was simple and effective.  Cell phone integration and call use also worked well.  They were comfortable and fit around the ear nicely.  They are somewhat large in size, but that is typical for high-quality around-the-ear headphones.  The headphones included controls on the left ear that work well also.  I honestly wanted to keep these headphones, but I was just too concerned that if the charging cable developed a flaw, that I would then have a useless $150 Bluetooth device.  Also, it would be a pain to keep the charging cord with me whenever I wanted to recharge them.

product_title: Terk Leapfrog Remote Control Extender Kit LFIRX
review_headline: Terk Lacks an important feedback feature.
review_body:
I've own nearly every brand ofd RC extender over the years. I have good luck and bad luck with the Terk as with most other brands.
What makes Terk more frustrating to use than the other brands is the absence of an LED feedback. In real life situations, these devices require a lot of experimentation (location, angle, avoidance of bright light such as morning sun) to work reliably.. With other brands, there is a LED on the transmitter unit which would blink whenever a signal is detected from the remote controller. With Terk, there is no feedback to indicate that the transmitter has detected the remote controller signal. Terk saved a few pennies by eliminating the LED at the transmitter end, but added an unnecessary layer of ambiguity during setup. As an aside, on my Terk receiver, there are random voltage spikes at the extender LED output--as seen on my oscilloscope. This interference may be reason why it may take repeated pressing of a key to successfully relay the RC signal.
IMHO the omission of an LED feedback is a significant omission of a needed feature.

product_title: Comply Foam Premium Earphone Tips - Isolation T-100 (Black, 3 Pairs, Large)
review_headline: Do Not Fit My Bluebuds BBX1 Earbuds.
review_body:
Purchased the Comply T-500 Tips for use with Bluebuds BBX1 Earbuds. Comply web site specified they would fit. They do not. Not even close. The diameter of the rigid plastic sound tube of the Comply's is the same diameter as the Bluebuds housing. Email correspondence with Comply customer service said they would fit if I attempted to install them properly, namely place the tip onto the BBX1 at an angle to start the stretch fit onto the BBX1 housing, then straighten tip and push onto BBX1 housing. Sounds like a plan, but the Comply sound tube is rigid and does not stretch easily, or at all. After struggling several minutes to force one on, the Comply tip looked like an 18-wheeler ran over it in the process. Then asked CS to send me a pair with a larger diameter tube to fit over the BBX1 housing. Not possible. All tubes are the same diameter. In-house engineering determines which ear buds are compatible with their tips. Unfortunately engineering was overly optimistic with judgment as to adequate fit with the BBX1. Gave up and returned them.

Fortunately, Bluebuds came to my rescue and after discussing the issue with them, Bluebuds sent me some complementary sets of their tips. I'll stick with Bluebuds tips.

product_title: Bluedio HT Turbine Wireless Bluetooth 4.1 Stereo Headphones with Mic (White)
review_body:
They are nice in appearance, but I was disappointed to discover that they were all white rather than the white and chrome-like appearance in the photo. The headband and ear pieces are both strong, but look cheap. The fabric that touches your ears and on the headband is a soft brushed material that feels comfortable to wear. The metallic elements appear to be real metal.

They fit snuggly... almost too snuggly. I am a female with an average size head, so I was surprised by how much they squeezed my head. The trade-off is that I had good, clear, uninterrupted sound.

The sound quality is decent. I had to make a lot of adjustments to my equalizer settings to tone down the heavy bass. The volume tales some fine-tuning... it seems like one click is too low and the next can be too loud. It greatly depends on if you are listening to music or spoken word.

The set can be a bit disturbing to people around you. What you're listening to can be clearly heard at higher volumes. There is also a blue light that blinks incessantly when connected to Bluetooth. In a darker room, it is disruptive. I have yet to find a way to turn it off.

Connecting to Bluetooth has been hit or miss. I have to re-pair every time I switch to a different device. I'm not a Bluetooth expert, so I am not sure if this is common... but this has not been a problem for me with other devices.

Overall, it's a decent headset for the price.

product_title: SONOS Compact Wireless Speaker for Streaming Music
review_headline: Speaker great, software not so much
review_body:
I really like the Sonos PLAY:1. Its compact, loud, and has a good bass response. It was easy to setup and quick to start playing music. It has really brought music into our otherwise quiet house due to the fact that my kids love Kids Bop on Pandora, or selecting Taylor Swift on Pandora, or whatever they want to play.

Thats kinda my main gripe about the Sonos software. Its not locked down in any way, or I haven't been able to find a way that is perfect. ANYONE who can connect to the same wireless SSID that your sonos is on can control your sonos. They even have access to change your Pandora or other playlists. I've got 2 kids, a MIL, and wife all trying to play music on my sonos. kids favorite thing: "hey dad, i heard you like one direction" blasts crap music at full volume. Listening to your favorite song? Wife changes it. Just found the right volume? Kids mess with it. I hope you like the same music as your technically inclined mother in law.

I thought about buying another PLAY:1 for the bedroom as an alarm, or just to listen to music, but since I cant control who does what with the speakers, I don't want to open myself up for my kids accidentally blasting alvin and the chipmunks at 6 in the morning.

Until the software gets better, I wont be investing anymore into their products.

product_title: Klipsch Image S4i-II
review_headline: 3rd pair of Klipsch earbuds failed and stopped working within 14-18 months. Their customer service sucks after warranty.
review_body:
My 3rd pair that stopped working. All three klipsch earbuds failed on me within a year or two. I take VERY good care of my earbuds, and I always keep them in their protective case. I don't even use them that often because I got some nice wireless bluetooth earbuds from Jaybird.

On my first pair of S4i earbuds, the left earbud stopped working, followed by the microphone and volume control buttons. They replaced the first pair under warranty after I provided my proof of purchase and receipt, but even the replacement they sent failed after 8 months or so.

My current pair were a gift for which I don't have the receipt, and they won't do anything to replace them.
The speakers on these still work (for now) but the microphone and control buttons stopped working after a few months.
After contacting Klipsch, they offered me 30% off a replacement pair based on their FULL MSRP on their website, which means 0% discount.
For example, They said I could get 30% off their R6m earbuds at their MSRP of $100 even though Amazon sells them for $70. So their 30% discount basically just matches Amazon's price. So lame.

I'm never buying anything from Klipsch again. The sound quality is great, but the product quality is crap, and absolutely not worth the money since you have to replace it every year.

The AK is definitely the better player but significantly more money of course(3.5 times). I just picked up a Chord Hugo earlier this week. Running optical into the Hugo the AK sounds incredible through my Hifiman 560's. And I'm not deaf(have lost some upper frequencies (like most do with aging),  just won't drive lower impedance headphones.The Pono is even less volume into the 560's than the standalone AK. product_title: TechPlay ODC21MKI-SL Fully Automatic Turntable, Aluminum tray,+/-10% PITCH CONTROL & PC LINK
review_body: I found the instructions to be confusing and lacking in detail. For instance, it says how to set the counterweight with the included cartridge but never specifically how much weight the cartridge requires. The instructed setting might be appropriate for the included cartridge but you do not arrive there by finding the even balance point yourself. Anti-skate is not explained very well either, just that the numbers on the anti-skate equal 1.0 gram of force while the numbers on the counterweight equal 0.4 grams of force. I would like to test the anti-skate with a blank record at some point. It can switch between phono and line out, yet I have tried both with no difference in sound quality (I plugged it straight into powered studio monitors but thought I would still need a phono preamp in between if using the phono out [but I'm no pro]). Stuff like that just leaves me wondering what's going on. With all that being said, once I balanced the tone arm according to the instructions (0 at the horizontal line, plus 3 clicks) everything sounded great. It fits my needs quite perfectly. It has a counterweight and anti-skate, auto-return and start/stop, and I was able to plug it straight in to my Fostex studio monitors. I just need a cheap mixer to act as an EQ and master volume. In the realm of sound quality, and maybe its the speakers, it beats out the other turntables I have been using. I was worried with all the features at that price, but so far I'm more than happy and it is great to hear my records at this quality. Maybe I'll post an update if I can more accurately gauge the recommended tone arm weight and anti-skate force.  UPDATE:  1) Strobe, like other reviewers mentioned, is useless. Does nothing as reading speed goes. Just a blue light. 2) The anti-skate is not fully effective. I turn it all the way to 4 and put on a blank record; it still slid towards the inside of the record, just at a slightly slower rate of speed. 3) I would be happier if I had gotten this at the current price of $95 rather than the original $180. 4) This turntable still sounds far better than what I had previously, but a couple features appear to do nothing (anti-skate, strobe, line/pre switch) which leaves me worried.  5) I will probably at the very least, buy a new needle for this at the suggestion of a few other reviewers. 6) Even with this update, I imagine there are far worse turntables you could unleash on your records. Even if the counterweight is inaccurate, at least it has one. I've seen tables with all these features (granted, better functioning features) go for $300... so, it's up to your wallet maybe.

So it was trial and error getting it set up and, frankly, I gave up on a couple of things until I have more time to play.  The battery life is abysmal.  I only got four hours of continuous play (player was fully charged) with my Bluetooth speaker.  Now I just plug it into a USB port and I can play my own music as long as I want (I have decent speakers attached to my computer).  Had I known about the battery life, I wouldn't have spent so much time researching models with Bluetooth.  It was a waste of time.  Even in my car I can connect via USB.  Would I purchase this if I were an audiophile?  Definitely not.  Although I'm happy with the quality of sound through my connections, a music purist wouldn't be.  Will I send it back?  No.  As the review title states, it's adequate for my needs.  Would I purchase it again?  I try to never say never but I would look at other options first.

review_headline: I wanted to like this, and probably would if price were lower
review_body:
I want to give this a review that's fair, because I really wanted to like this.

THE GOOD
For its size, the sound is amazing.
Nice look and feel to it.
Buttons are responsive, easy to navigate.
Suction cup keeps it where it's at,
Bluetooth finds right away, connects no issue.

THE BAD
FM tuner is horrid. I bought this primarily to use as an FM radio in the shower in the mornings, and use it for BT for weekend showers. I can understand the tuning issue without an antenna, but I do live in Phoenix Metro which should have dozens of stations. This one picks up on about three. It's impossible to see which one (which I know) but I kept a $6 kids fish radio right next to it and it can pick up on over a dozen stations. I wasn't trying to tune into one small one, it's a station that does have a high output and easy to tune without other bleed over (98KUPD for Arizona residents wondering)

The battery life is awful. Now keeping it on in the shower with bluetooth (can't speak for FM only, since, see above) it doesn't last more than an hour or two. I'd expect maybe for 30 minutes in the morning for my wife and I to get through morning routines shouldn't require a charge every day. I know this is just a matter of inconvenience and may not be an issue for you if you plug it in each time, but for me it is. I would imagine once a week would've been my tolerance.

THE UGLY

review_headline: I got it as a replacement for my 'old' Denon1900 that shamefully started to have problem with one surround channel occasionally
review_body:
Its OK. If you are OK with OK. And with paying more than for just OK. I got it as a replacement for my 'old' Denon1900 that shamefully started to have problem with one surround channel occasionally going off and with problems passing BD video signals (works fine with DVD player upscaling to 1080p but choking on the same when signal comes from BD). Looked around and found out that these days seems all the brands are pretty much produce the same junk - my Denon is less than 4 years old and already malfunctioning, and users complain about problems and quality issues all over with Sony, Denon, Pioneer, all of them. I wonder, is that whats happening when Sony Japan becomes Sony USA? And pride in 'made', engineering and simple conscientiousness are replaced as a leading motivation by 'marketing' for which all these words are just silly vibrations of the air. My previous Kenwood worked for 18 years without single problem and Im sure still works for somebody (gave it away as wanted to upgrade to modern technology-hence Denon). Anyway, I decided to go for replacement with VSX-80 Elite brand as I was told by repair facility that for whatever reason they see less Elite brands than pretty much anything else. Also, Qdeo video processor and SABRE DAC appealed to me as high end components used in top of the line models (including Pioneer own, OPPO BD, etc.). And I had good luck with Pioneer TV, DVD player, headphones. So now on to results:
Got it at excellent price $530 (MSRP-$700). Look is nothing outstanding but still somehow pleasing, liked it. Feels sturdy. Setup and menus are much better than Denon's. Same goes for manual. So far so good. Now, there is a whole plethora of various applications like pandora-shmandora, roku-shmoku, some teenagers wonders (like controls from you iPhone) which I could not care less about. All this stuff is very unimportant for me personally - to get something from Internet I would use BD player or TV itself, which are better at it, anyway. Managing receiver from phone is a curiosity, I'd rather use its own controls and streaming some content from the phone is simply idiotic. For me the receiver/amplifier function is to amplify and control my home theater, not to double as a player or TV reception box. Still, to find that connection to Internet requires buying additional attachment is rather a put off at this price level.
So the most important - performance. Thats where surprise lied. It sounds fine - accurate and clear. Power is perfectly sufficient for average room (at least with my 8ohm speakers). Strangely the crossover for sub/speakers is a single for all the system, no way to adjust different crossover points for small surround speakers and larger and more capable front speakers (thats what cheaper Denon allows you to do). Still, subjectively I did not find it to be a problem (and maybe its not for perfectly automated EQ). But... the overall sound is just not as good as I have from Denon. Which is at least $200 cheaper and 4 years older. In comparison vsx-80 sounded, well, kind of 'metallic', simpler. Like loosing some overtones or frequencies along the way. Maybe if I did not compare I would be perfectly happy with it but switching from Denon just gave me that feeling that from full, rich, 'warm' sound Im switching to leaner, cooler, 'simpler' one. Tried different options but it was just that - its not a setup, its vsx-80 nature. So whats this SABRE DAC is doing? I guess jamming in best components does not necessarily produce outstanding results.
I did not send it immediately back, I went to the store (should have done before ordering) and started comparing there. So SC-81 sounded definitely better than vsx-80 (and cost $300 more). Similarly priced Yamaha and Denon (1200 model was it?) sounded very definitely better, giving out very natural, pleasant, rich sound. Even Marantz 1432 ($300 less) sounded not worse (though different). So got back home, packed the unit and sent it back. Withsorrow - liked the feel and look (Elite badge looks pretty). But in the end I want the best sound I can get for the money spent. Sadly it did not look to me the vsx-80 would provide it, even at $530. Since Im not up to paying $1000 for receiver (and thats where seemingly Pioneer starts to put some care into their receivers line) the Pioneer is off for me. Dismayed by my Denon quality of built I dont go for new Denon, either. And I hate to spend more time playing test engineer with more units. So in the end Im staying with my 'old' Denon circumventing video problems by connecting hdmi directly to TV and a separate digital coax to Denon for sound and thinking of the way dealing with one surr channel (maybe repair is an option). If it becomes a real necessity I'll have to try Sony. But unless I start feeling that $1000 is not that much money seems I will not enjoy a view of 'Elite' badge in my AV stand.

Design: They fit just as well as any other in-ear buds I've owned. The problem, however, comes with the little addition to the wire that includes a button that can stop and start your song at will. I don't like it, it's poor design. I regularly roll up my earbuds around my itouch and put it in my pocket. Any slight bump and the button gets pressed, blasting music out of my pocket. Having to disconnect your earbuds at the end of each session is very tedious.

Durability: I used these an average of 2 hours a day over the course of one month. After one month, one of the earbuds has decreased in volume by 50% or more. It makes it very hard and very annoying to listen to music. For earbuds that you're paying 100 dollars for, which are supposed to last many months, this is absolutely ridiculous. review_body:

Where to Use: THIS is the reason I'm no longer using these bluetooth headphones. They would not stay in my ear while running, even after trying all three ear settings. DO get these if you want a cheap, portable bluetooth headphone system for travel/walking.
DO NOT get these for exercise, unless you're doing yoga or some other slow-moving sport. These are advertised as "Sport", but I don't know of any sports that these could actually be used while participating. Maybe riflery. Or Chess. Not running.

I'm keeping them for travel, as a pair of bluetooth headphones I won't feel bad about beating the crap out of (mostly because if I return them, I have to pay $6 return fee, which is 33% of the whole price). product_title: HiFiMan In-Ear Headphones
review_headline: Can't recommend due to reliability, durability
review_body: These headphones have a lot going for them. I bought them due to a glowing review on InnerFidelity and the sound quality certainly lives up to the review's praise. The tonal balance is flat (similar to my studio monitors) and the transient response is excellent--everything sounds crystal-clear and extremely crisp and detailed. There are a lot of other nice things about these headphones, e.g., they are extremely small and lightweight and they basically fit inside your ears, making them easy to wear comfortably for hours on end. They also provide excellent noise isolation: when I listen to them on an airplane, I only have to turn them up a little bit vs. when I listen to them in a quiet room. The tips are made of very compliant rubber and the dual-flange design means you can just pop them in your ears and get an excellent seal with almost zero effort. And finally, the nylon-wrapped section of cord is very tangle-resistant.  If they're so great, why am I giving them 2 stars instead of 5? Notice the plethora of negative reviews of these headphones, complaining that they break in a matter of hours/days/weeks. "Won't happen to me," I thought. "I'm super careful and gentle with all my electronics, especially headphones," I thought. "I don't even wear my headphones to do sports, I always store them in hard cases, and I'm never in situations where I might tug or pull on them," I thought.  Well, it turns out that after ~10 months of extremely careful and gentle use, they still break anyway. The right and left channels are now cutting in and out intermittently with mine, depending on the angle of my head as I walk around and the angle of my phone in my pocket. Some connection inside of the headphones is falling apart somewhere. This is in addition to the annoying, intermittent "clicking" sound I heard since day one of owning the headphones, which I have attributed to static discharge, and which I've never heard with any of my other pairs of headphones. I did send these headphones back to the factory once to address the clicking (didn't work) but at this point I don't think I'm going to bother with the time, trouble, and cost of sending the headphones back to get the internal connections sorted out. Better to just switch to a different brand that will last longer, even if they don't sound as good and won't be as comfortable.

product_title: ART USB Phono Plus
review_headline: You need to be comfortable with a soldering iron and removing the circuitboard, But it will work great in under an hour
review_body:
There is an awful lot of hum. Have read in other reviews. If it gets worse or doesn't go away I will return it.
SOLUTION:
Take it apart! (remove the screws and it will slide out of the chassis) You'll see if it supposed to be grounded via a spring-loaded metal tab. Metallic paint is dabbed onto the bottom corner. This is your only connection to the circuitboard. (shoddy engineering or just a shot in the dark?) Weld a 2-3 inch insulated wire to the underside of the circuitboard (the bent piece of metal is the best place without melting the bottom circuitboard) Unscrew the short screw that is marked for "ground" on the outside. It's probably already be loose from shoddy workmanship. Be sure to use a couple of locking washers on the inside. Wrap a half or so of the ground wire (already soldered to the underside) between the locking washers and tighten as tight as you can without stripping screws from the inside. This will also correct the problem if you have a loose grounding pin on the outside.
This sounds like a lot of work. If you are not comfortable with this stop here and chose another product. If you are already primed in electronic assembly give it a go. (Intermediate: about 30 to 60 minute job.
If the ART USB Phono Plus was built this way from the factory I would give it 5 stars. Since I had to completely design my own ground wire and internal connection I would give it no stars ZIP/ZERO/NADA. It is described as plug-n-play.
If it were sold as a kit from an electronics hobby store it would be a nearly deluxe gadget, but it is not.

product_title: Bose Acoustimass 5 Series III Speaker System
review_headline: You can get better with less money down on this set.
review_body:
These's something in regards th these speakers and all I can say is it's performance is just... fubar when compared to Klipsch, JBL, KEF, Logitech, Mirage, or whoever it may be. There are several things that are wrong with these speakers.

Sound Quality

I've mentioned it already, but I want to elaborate upon it. The sound that it reproduces is just too thin, sounds too boomy, and most of the content is either localized to the bass module or it's completely lost in the system's poorly designed crossover. Simple, nothing too crazy, just want to make it simple for you guys.

The bass module is in a 7th Order Bandpass enclosure, which serves only to output more SPL at the expense of bass accuracy. True subwoofers start at 8 inches and taper off at 15 inches. Size depends on application and what type of music you listen to. Smaller subwoofers tend to have a tighter, limited, more punchy bass, while larger subwoofers can hit lower and louder.

Build Quality

The build quality of this set is just a joke. For you folks who like to take apart things, I once pulled off the grilles on the satellites carefully and I observed what drivers it uses. The drivers are just simply manila hemp cones. Quality is besides the point, as any paper has perhaps horrendous resonant properties in the high, mid, and low frequencies. The wood used for the bass module is also the lowest grade of fiberboard negotiable. Almost ALL manufacturers will turn to MDF (Medium-density Fiberboard). Also a rule of thumb is that the wood be at least 0.75 inches thick and be well braced. Also I found out that it's drivers are of the same species as I have pointed out earlier.

Performance

This system actually lacks performance in terms of playback. It's crossover is also designed poorly as well.

Playback wise, you can actually hear gunshots and explosions in the bass module and not the imaging screen. Music is a little different,you can hear the voices and any bass in the bass module and not the converging point of the front speakers. this is known as very poor 'sound imaging'.

Conclusion

I can guarantee you at least a few better speakers than this fubar speaker set for less money down. Go for the Panasonic SC-HTB20 2.1 240-watt speaker set and you will feel better knowing that you got something better for significantly less. I can't explain that part any better.

review_headline: Stylish design, and light, but lacks functional controls (not ergonomic at all), and very poor battery life
review_body:
There are some things to like about this headset, and many things I don't. Lets start with the Pro's list since it's shorter.

Pro's:
Very light, very small, relatively comfortable, voice prompts for power on/off, sync status, etc., easy to pair, and stylish.

Con's:
I tried to like this headset but it has too many negatives for me at least. These are not conducive to removing one from a single ear while leaving the other side in. Something I often do at the gym when speaking with my gym partner or wanting to hear something over the loudspeaker. The right ear stem/bud also digs into my ear in a painful manner regardless of which ear bud size I use. This design assumes that everyone's ear canal would have the exact same angle and that doesn't appear to be the case in my case. The flaps to hold them securely in the ear work pretty well, but take a little getting used to in order to seat them correctly.

The controls are also not very ergonomic. They are tiny, and by tiny I mean impossible to find with any consistency, so I often end up taking it out of my ear just to find something as simple as the power button or the volume button. They also provide no feedback other than the power button if you manage to find it while in the ear. The control buttons are also made of the same material as the rest of the headset plastic. They should have made them with some kind of different surface material or touch pattern so you at least knew you were in the right place. This adds to the issue I noted above about taking one out of your ear. It causes the other side to yank out of our head.

The last gripe is with the battery for these. I've owned both Motorola S9's and LG Tone's. Both easily lasted a week. This one lasts 2 days on a charge, which I don't consider acceptable.

Disappointing.

review_headline: Overall good headphones BUT too TIGHT. Hurt my head/ears (I wear glasses)!
review_body:
I enjoyed the headphones, but had to return them because they hurt.

Pros:
1) I am not an audiophile, but for my purposes, the sound quality of the headphones was relatively good. E.g. I could discern more instruments during a song than with generic headphones.
2) The sound isolation on the headphones was adequate. These headphones would be nice for studying in a library.
3) There was little to no sound leakage. Again, these headphones would be nice for studying in a library.
4) The headphones look stylish, in my opinion, which was a factor for me when purchasing headphones.
5) Also, the build of the headphone felt sturdy.

Cons:
1) These headphones HURT after wearing them for more than 15 minutes. I felt a lot of pressure on my head, and my ears especially feel sore. I am not certain if this is due to the size of my head (slightly above average?) or the fact that I wear glasses. It is possible that the headphones pressed my ears onto the arms of my glasses, causing pain after extended wear time. I tried stretching out the headphones, but it did not help.

2) Only comes with one proprietary cable so if it tears or snags, it will be difficult to replace.

3) Comes with a cloth bag carrying case that doesn't offer any real protection. The On-Ear Sennheiser Momentum which is priced similarly or less comes with 2 cables and 2 cases if I'm not mistaken.

product_title: OmniMount Fixed TV Mount for 13-Inch to 37-Inch TVs
review_headline: One major flaw and two minor flaws
review_body:
First, the major flaw... (See photo #1)

I am very surprised that no one has mentioned the major and fatal flaw of this mount - OC40FMX. I am even more surprised that OmniMount engineered/manufactured this mount in this way. I have other Omnimounts, but none have the significant engineering or manufacturing flaw of this model. The flaw with the model became glaringly obvious to me because I move this mount several times every day. If you plan to move the arm on this mount and leave it, this product will probably work for you. If you plan to move the arm of the mount repeatedly, you are bound to run into the issue described here.

This model has a plate with a hook that attaches to the TV/monitor, which then attaches to a plate on the articulating arm. The problem is that the hook on the TV/monitor plate is 1-2 mm smaller than the cradle on the arm that holds the hook. There is a screw which holds the bottom plates together and secures the unit. However, the 1-2 mm difference in hook and cradle sizes causes the top of the TV/monitor to rock back and forth in the hook's cradle. No amount of tightening the bottom screw eliminates this because of the gap at the top of the plates. I tried putting some different items in the small gap left in the rear of the hook after the plates are secured together to see if that would make a difference. I tried a washer and foam tape separately. They help, but don't completely eliminate the rocking of the unit in the hook's cradle. It's a an engineering flaw or a manufacturing tolerance issue.

First minor flaw... (See photo #2)

There is no way to tighten the screw holding the plate together with a normal screwdriver. They placed a large nut in the way of getting a normal screwdriver in there to tighten down the plates. You'll end up stripping the screw a little to tighten down the plates. This seems like a no-brainer issue that could have been resolved if someone from Omnimount tried to actually install one of these units. All they would need to do is flip the bolt around so that the nut is on top.

Second minor flaw... (See photo #3)

The plastic used for the cord management is so flexible that cords just fall out of the bottom. This again was poor engineering/manufacturing. There is no included mechanical way of completely closing the cord management. It is supposed to stay closed by design, but my power cord and ethernet cord just slip right through and fall out when moving the unit. The only fix I've found is to use a plastic zip tie to hold the cord management closed so that I am not constantly stuffing the cords back in several times each day.

I called Omnimount at 4 PM on a Friday to get help with the unit. The call was answered by their parent company and the rep. was absolutely no help. She told me to call back earlier in the day for an Omnimount tech, but I think I will just end up returning the unit. I can't live the major flaw of the unit rocking back and forth whenever it's moved and I need a mount that can be adjusted multiple times each day. I thought spending a little extra for a reputable brand would result in a superior design, but FAIL!

ETA: I contacted Omnimount technical support by email. They offered to send a replacement head, but the pictures they provided to me showed that the replacement would be identical to the unit I have. This leads me to believe that the major flaw is an engineering oversight or a manufacturing problem, probably the former. In 2012, Omnimount was consolidated in with its sister company. Draw your own conclusions.

I told the rep. by email that I thought the pictures showed an identical product to the unit I had. I never heard back again. I even sent photos, which are in this review, and never heard another word - no thank you or acknowledgement of receipt. Either they are completely careless in their business (as they are in engineering mounts) or they don't take constructive feedback well - which is maybe why they are producing an inferior product like the OC40FMX with big problems.

I found the [[ASIN:B00HYSG0CS QualGear QG-TM-005-WHT 23-Inch to 42-Inch Premium Quality Contemporary Style Ultra Low Profile Full Motion Wall Mount LED TVs, White]] and installed it. It is leagues ahead of the OC40FMX in terms of engineering and thoughtfulness in design. If you are ok with the white color, it has a longer arm reach and smarter cable management. It also has smoother operation and lays flatter against the wall with retracted. It is also a few bucks cheaper. I only wish that I had found it first before going through two inferior mounts. (P.S. I don't work or have any relationship with QualGear.)is maybe why they are producing an inferior product like the OC40FMX with big problems. product_title: RTL-SDR, FM+DAB, DVB-T USB Stick Set with RTL2832U & R820T. Great SDR for SDR#, HDSDR
review_headline: Great Device - NOT FOR NEWBIES! Read Review
review_body:
I ordered this after seeing an article on the internet about 'Software Defined Radio'. I placed the order in early September, it arrived mid-October, so plan on a 6-week shipping time-span (though it did come within the projected time). My 3-star rating of the product has to do with the product, itself, however.

When I got this, it came in a bubblepack envelope, about the size of a cigarette pack. Ok, opened it up, and there is EXACTLY what you see in the product image. Great, so far (except for that bubblepack envelope from China. I'm AMAZED it didn't look like ground up plastic confetti by the time it got to me, but hey, it got here in one piece and in working condition, so OK).

I pull it all out, find the little mini-CD disk (assuming it is the driver disk, as there are no other drivers or documentation with it), so I put the disk in first. OH, WOW, says disk 'needs to be formatted' first. Tells me that it is a blank disk. Looking at the bottom of the disk, I see it HAS been written to, so my assumption is that it is formatted for APPLE, not WINDOWS. Ok, would have been nice for them to mention this small detail first. Whatever. I go online and search for 'RTL-SDR USB2832, and find the drivers - again, generic and from dubious sites.

Fine, forget this, I just plug the dongle into my Win7 64-bit computer and it finds it. Great. NOW, I go and search for SDR# (the Software Defined Radio software) and download it from SDR# itself, a free open-source program). It comes with a custom program called ZADIG that is used to properly configure your drivers for the dongle first, then you run the SDR software to 'control the radio' functions.

There's a lot of data out there on custom things you can do with this device, but in its current format and support level, it is NOT FOR LAYPERSONS! Don't buy this if you barely know how to turn on a computer, YOU WILL NOT GET IT TO WORK. If you understand driver files, hunting for software and manuals, and have the patience of a saint to figure out the radio technical nomenclature used in the configuration settings (without the help of an owner's manual), then this is the GADGET FOR YOU! I had it scanning police frequencies within an hour of installing it, and have already started putting together a full 'favorites listing' within the software (nice feature). It is also capable of (believe it, or not) of taking radio telescope data and by way of four different software packages (not included), able to take the radio signal, decode it, configure it into a graphic image, and display this image on your PC (it also works with the Russian Meteor2 Weather satellite system, to see global weather images). It has a LOT of great tech applications, none of which at this time, are really suitable for noobs.

If you want a GREAT frequency range scanner (talking down to 24Mhz up to around 2-Ghz, haven't checked top side yet), this thing has it. FORGET IT if you want to see TV with it in America, this is NOT for U.S. TV (but being DVB, will work in Europe as a straight-up TV dongle). It works on both Apple and Mac, but forget the disc that comes with it, if you are harboring intentions of using it on a PC - you are ON YOUR OWN (I HIGHLY recommend starting with SDR# software and Zadig drivers, and going from there). Oh, and my 3-stars? They have decent sound quality, so as a temporary solution they're decent. I have slightly larger than normal ears, so I don't know if it is just me or not but I can only wear them for so long because they will cause cartilage pinching.

Also, after only a few months of moderate usage, I have discovered the connections for the left speaker and the inline control/microphone are both loose right underneath where the microphone and control button are on the cable.

Overall, if the intent is to use these every now and then, then I would have to say they're alright, but that's all they are good for. I'm rather disappointed in the fact that I have to go headphone hunting again.

TL;DR: Not what I expected, cartilage pinching, breaks pretty soon. Would not recommend.

product_title: Symphonized Nrg Premium Wood Noise-Isolating Headphones with Mic, White
review_headline: Those had more bass and although they only sounded average at first they cooperated really well with the ipod equalizer to end u
review_body:
These are decent-but-not-great earbuds. They generally meet the expectations of the price range. I picked these up after my previous two sets from different manufacturers fell apart.

I started with JBuds J2 a few years ago. Those had more bass and although they only sounded average at first they cooperated really well with the ipod equalizer to end up sounding pretty nice. We ended up with like 4 pairs of these due to some sales. I really liked them but each of them failed after a few months when inevitably the left (or was it right?) channel would stop working.

Next option was the MEElectronics Sport-Fi M6. These didn't sound quite as good and didn't really benefit from the equalizer. They still sounded good but they couldn't quite reach the level of the J2. What they could do was stay in my ear. The wrap-around thing worked well and the fact that they could keep a good seal meant that they actually sounded pretty nice without having to mess with them. After a while the bendy wrap-around part for your ear developed a split in it and this exposed the metal wire to hold the shape and also the signal wires. It worked like this for quite a while but eventually that ear stopped playing. It also came with a little case that was pretty useful for protecting them on the way to work and back.

Finally I got these. They look good and sound decent. Not quite as good as the equalizer-friendly J2 but generally comparable to anything in this price range. They also seem to be holding up better than my previous earbuds. Unfortunately they aren't without drawbacks. They comes with a nice little bag to store them in which is nice but they also like to stay twisted and coiled and won't ever really lay flat or straight. On my desk this generally means that the cord likes to spiral up a few inches off of the desk right in front of my keyboard which always gets in my way. I still can't find a way to prevent this and it's very annoying. The mind-of-it's-own cable also probably isn't helping with the other problem which is that they don't like to stay sealed in my ears. When I first put them in they sound pretty nice but inevitably after a few minutes they will shift around just enough to break the seal and drastically reduce the sound quality. I've tried all the sizes and even all the parts from my previous earbuds and it just doesn't seem to give me a solid fit nomatter what I do. It's unfortunate because when they are seated correctly they sound nice and the look and construction seem above average to me.

If these fit you well and stay in you'll probably be satisfied. If you like the look you'll also probably be satisfied. For me the frustrating cord and inability to maintain a good seal prevents me from liking them as much as I otherwise would. They are good enough to keep using but once these break I will probably get another pair of the M6 again.

product_title: Pro-Ject Debut Carbon Premium WITH Ortofon 2M RED Turntable
review_headline: The Grumpy Guys are kind of right...but there's hope
review_body: This turntable seemed to be the consensus "high-end starter" turntable as I looked around the web. I checked out the amazon reviews, which were quite usual...mostly positive, and a few grumpy ones. You know, there always seem to be a few grumpy guys, so I ordered the turntable. Well, it turns out that the grumpy guys were right, but there's a twist...  The good news first...it looks slick and comes with a good cartridge that is pre-mounted, and it can be made to work well...but the turntable I got didn't work well out of the box.  Here's the story...my copy of the turntable had A LOT of 240 Hz mechanical rumble. It was also mechanically noisy just standing next to the turntable. It was all quite obvious in quiet portions of the record, or in a quiet groove. So I went looking around the web, and found some folks had tackled this problem by adding a fender washer and two neoprene washers to two of the mounting screws. You then have to tune the tension of the mounting screws for minimum rumble. The good news: it drops the rumble by 17 dB. The bad news...that you'd have to bother with such shenanigans in the first place.  I contacted the manufacturer to ask if I should consider my turntable as defective, and to return it. Their response was that it was not defective, that you had to expect to tune up a high end turntable. Really?  I documented the measurements and the improvement technique at a web site called "the objective turntable". You may find it interesting and useful if you buy the turntable.  Other impressions...the cables didn't make good ground connections...a little plier work helped, but I substituted cables that have a reliable low resistance ground connection out of the box. The cueing lever is a bit floaty...when you let the arm descend, it drops so slowly that the arm will often skitter across the record, especially on the opening groove.  In spite of all of this, I'm keeping it...After the tune up the rumble is acceptable...and the floaty cueing is one of those things you live with. Vinyl still has its charms with respect to CD's, and I've had some enjoyment listening to old, rarely played records in my collection.

review_body:

Securing the tv onto this mount is fairly easy. The mount is solid when attached to the wall, as well as the back braces when it is connected to the TV. The install is definitely a two person job. Everything that was needed for the install was included, as well as some extra parts for different scenarios. The whole unit looks clean and not overly complicated. The braces and everything don't block any of the ports on the back of my TV.

I have three main complaints about the mount:
The first is that the actual mount is tilting from the wall brace to the plate that is attached to the braces on the TV. It's not drastic, but concerning considering my TV is less than half the rated weight limit on this thing at 60lbs. It seems to be from the joints in the arms on the mount.

The second is that the four bolts that hold the TV in the desired tilt position, don't function properly and slide along the grooves making the TV tilt more than I would like. I will have to go buy four new bolts to secure the thing in place like someone else stated.

The Third, and not majorly concerning, is the four bolts that attach the wall mount to the plate that the TV brackets go onto. They seem somewhat small for linking up between the heavy TV and heavy wall mount.

I'm not concerned about the safety of my TV being up on the wall, just somewhat annoyed at the fact that everything isn't as solid as it should be and is tilting from the mount to the TV and tilting from the bolts sliding in the tilt adjustment piece. I bought it because it has dual arms for strength and is able to fit my 60lb 52" Samsung TV with the large vesa standard. I don't see how this could hold up 135lbs, I'm not sure that I would trust that much weight being on there. It's been holding up fine,but I will be going out and buying some new bolts for the tilt mechanism.

When my folks purchased one, this was one of the least expensive Blu-Ray home theatre systems available. I strongly suggested picking up a standalone home theatre system, or a slightly higher end unit- a $350 Samsung vs this $290 Philips.

Initial issues with the unit were the lack of optical input, the single coax SPDIF being functional, but incompatible with a growing amount of equipment. Startup time and input toggling time is atrocious. The unit returns to its "Home" mode upon power on instead of recalling the last used input. There aren't any ways to directly select the desired input either. You must repeatedly use the input command to cycle through all of the inputs. There is a ten second delay where the unit doesn't respond to the remote after changing inputs, in addition to a twenty second power on time before you can select an input. If you want to watch cable and use the system, it will be at least 50 seconds before you hear audio from the coax input. To remedy this, my folks left the unit on all the time... That was until it stopped playing discs. I investigated and discovered the rear fan runs constantly when the unit is powered and pulls air from inside the case- or rather dust through the disc tray. After serious cleaning, I picked up a Harmony remote to make power on easier... This unit takes so long to power on and switch inputs that the Harmony software required as much delay tweaking as it allows and even then it's tenuous.

If you put a Blu-Ray movie in, expect to wait 45 seconds to six minutes to see the menu.

The lack of Netflix support is also disappointing, but HD component output was useful.

review_headline: Okay, but not a really strong value...
review_body:
This is a Bluetooth receiver. Not a transmitter. Not an extended range device. Just a receiver useful for connecting your Iphone or Ipad or tablet or whatever to a common output device that has no Bluetooth capability. I started to think about it and realized that there are fewer and fewer devices on the market these days that do not have Bluetooth built in. Wireless capability is everywhere. However, if you have an older home stereo system or A/V receiver that does NOT have BT...well then this receiver might be for you.

I initially hooked up my Iphone to an A/V receiver that I have setup and connected to a pair of JBL 112s. These are a pair of prized speakers and continue to function at a very high level after many years of solid use. The A/V receiver obviously does not have BT, so this was an excellent way to test this receiver. The phone paired up with the receiver almost immediately and proceeded to function as expected. The sound was well received although it left a little to be desired as far as full frequency response was concerned. I have come to expect my Iphone to handle sound better than that, and my JBLs are virtually flat across the spectrum... so I was a little disappointed to hear what I perceived to be something less than optimal sound from the pairing.

The receiver seemed to function okay although the received distance seemed a little shorter than expected. Since I know my Iphone BT is solid based on previous use, the difference had to be in this receiver.

Anyway, I found the receiver to function pretty much as expected in a manner equivalent to its perceived value. I can find no real defects with the device other than my perceptions and expectations. It continues to function like it did when I first connected it. I really dislike the annoying habit of having to re-pair every time the unit powers down. That bothers me, although I realize a lot of receivers react in this way. So, no real fails here---but nothing exceptional either. It's just okay.

product_title: ButtKicker Simulation Kit
review_headline: I am a little disappointed, but glad I have it.
review_body:
I bought this to attach to a PlaySeat that I also purchased as part of a larger system for an Oculus Rift based racing simulator platform running Assetto Corsa. It does add a little bit of realism to games by providing some vibration feedback when you go over bumps and such. Overall, I am glad I bought it, but I am also disappointed. Below are some bullet points of both the good and the bad:

Positives:

+ Added realism and immersion by vibrating your chair. (This one positive does outweigh all the negatives I list below.)
+ It comes with a nice remote control

Negatives:

- Vibrations are not that realistic, sometimes inappropriate. Since the Buttkicker works off of the low frequency zone of the game sound, it will sometimes do weird stuff. Likewise, while my force-feedback wheel may pick up on the rumble strip I just drove over, the butt kicker may be mostly unaware, or when some stray sound in the game occurs, the Buttkicker may provide feedback not related to how a car would really vibrate.
- Sometimes it just clacks (makes clacking noises), for no apparent reason (mostly when I'm starting the car, or coming to a complete stop). I just pretend it's something wrong with my car :)
- In general, the vibrations are not strong enough. I cranked up the bass on my system, bolted the Buttkicker directly tot he frame of my sim seat, and put my rig up on the included rubber mounts, but it's still a pretty weak effect.
- The supplied mounting options were incomplete. It should have included some bolts, and secondary hardware to secure it to stuff.
- It came with no clear instruction on how best to mount it.
- It should have come with some wire nuts, which are required to attach the pigtail from the vibrator to the cable that goes to the amp.
- The controls on the amp are a bit confusing.
- The amp is difficult to turn on. Clicking the "on" button apparently does not do anything, but then sometimes the power light turns yellow, and sometimes it turns green, and sometimes it flickers to one color and then back to off. Eventually, it does turn on, perhaps by some particular method of turning it on that I am not aware of.
- I *think* the unit will overheat and turn itself off. I say this because sometimes it just seems to not work, then magically start working again.

Perhaps some of the minuses above are my own fault for how I mounted it, I don't know, since there were no tips on how to mount it in the relatively poor included instructions. The way I mounted it was to drill two holes through the frame of my Playseat, roughly below where my butt would be, such that it did not rub on the seat or the floor, and then I bolted it securely in. I then I lifted the entire Playseat frame off the floor by attaching the big rubber shock mounts provided in the Buttkicker package.)

Perhaps the experience might be better with other games. I am using this for Assetto Corsa. I have not tried in rFactor, iRacing, etc.

Although my review may seem a bit negative, all in all it does add to the experience, so I would still recommend it as "better than nothing". I am still glad I bought it. The problem is that it is not everything that it could be. I would recommend to shop around, then come back and buy this if you don't find anything better.

product_title: Senbowe SBW Bluetooth 4.1 Sweatproof Wireless Headset with Microphone
review_headline: Fit is terrible - I've tested many and this is the worst so far. Sound quality decent.
review_body: Edit on Feb. 1 '15: Senbowe read my review and reached out to me offering an exchange (which would not resolve the problem I have with this headset) or refund. This shows that they care enough about their consumers which is definitely a positive.    Original review:    Note: I am giving this product 1 star solely based on in-ear fit as I need a headset for running and moving around in general. This does not take into account sound quality as sound quality doesn't matter if the headset doesn't stay in your ears.    Background: I am an earphone / headset junkie and collect these things, changing approximately every 3 months. In the past I've mostly owned corded headsets for listening to Music while on the go, mostly for running.    Decision: As I got myself a brand new iPhone 6 and did not want to risk getting it wet on my runs, I decided to go for a set of bluetooth earphone, allowing me to safely store away my phone in a waterproof pocket. I was considering buying some of the very small high-end earphones but based on reviews, the failure rate of bluetooth earphones is relatively high, especially when used for sports and that across all price ranges. So I decided that instead of spending $ 200.- and getting into a warranty exchange frenzy, I'd go for 2 different type of low-end headsets, price-wise, not worrying about fit and warranty if problematic.    Purchase: I purchased the Cootree 220 headset as well as the Senbowe heaset (this review), each for $ 30.- and recently received them. I will update my review in case my opinion changes over time.    Fit: This is the most important criterion for me as I use them for doing sports outdoors, where the quality of sound are secondary compared to FIT. I typically do not like in-ear headphones for sports for various reasons though I've tried many models (SAFETY as these block out all noise which is not desired when running, FIT as they tend to fall out sooner or later when running, COMFORT - I yet have to find one that doesnot feel uncomfortable after 90 minutes of wearing). The best in-ear headphones I've had on all 3 dimensions were Yurbuds which are made for runners and perform very well (though I still prefer headphones with a behind the hear security design).    When it comes to this headphone, the fit is catastrophic:  1) The small rubber band is useless and a design flaw. As you can see in all commercial photos from the company, none of the wearers has the rubber band in the ear-crease where it's designed to go. I believe this is because they simply photo-shopped them over, but that tells a lot about a company - they likely never did any consumer research and testing on the fit. So you can safely take these little rubber bands off, and you end up with a good old pair of in-ear headphones.  2) They seal pretty tight - but will come out quickly (for me within 2 minutes, no matter what size and how quiet I am, how deep I push them etc.). While these things depend on the shape of your ears, humidity, ear wax production (gross I know) and sweat levels, I am comparing to the Yurbuds, which are made out of an anti-slip silicone, whereas these earphones use the standard soft and slippery tips. I could imagine that replacing them with foam tips would keep them in the ears longer. What makes the Senbowe worse than other in-ear headsets, especially corded ones is that they are bulky on the outside, as mentioned by other reviewers. Bulk = weight and coupled with a poor fit means they come out quicker.  3) Related to the fit are the commands. They are not intuitive (very difficult to feel) and fiddly. It is hardly possible to use the commands (volume, play, pause etc.) while on the go without displacing them once they're in your ear. You literally are quicker pulling out your phone and using commands there.    Net: Unless you know that silicone tip in-ear tips work well for your ears, give these a pass as they'll perform worse than standard corded in-ear headphones. This is the case for meboth in a situation where I move / run as well as sit still at my desk (that's how bad they are).    Sound quality: I am not rating sound quality here as it doesn't matter if the earphones don't stay in your ear. But I agree with most reviewers that sound quality is decent for such a low-end headphone. That being said, the Cootree sound quality is better, crisper, louder, less mellow and doesn't suffer from white noise like these do sometimes.    Recommendation: So, if you read this and tend to have problems with in-ear silicone tips, my recommendation would be that you either go with an over the ear design like the Cootree (can feel a little warm on the ears), a behind-the ear design (there are many models that have a holder behind the ears) or with the Yurbuds if you want in-ear for sports.    Hope this helped future purchasers

review_headline: Decent but quality control could improve.
review_body:
Sewell seems to be savvy at filling a niche market with cabling products for discerning "cine-mediaphiles" and audiophiles. The wires sound good however, you'll want to do an inspection of connection points, like the jacket and composite connector to ensure they are not separating, exposing the shielding underneath.

Try a gentle test bend at each end. In this case, the wire remains functional and electrically sound however the jacket separated from the connector plug. The 12 gauge speaker wires are sound transparent, claiming high strand counts and upscale connectors. Unfortunately troubleshooting intermittent signaling to one channel was required leading to a discovery that the set screws located under the milled barrel covers, which hold the actual wire in place were all loose to varying degrees. The barrels themselves were also an issue because of loose thread tolerances. Loctite resolved this issue. Tightening these screws resolved the continuity issue and now the sound output is great.

Good - the performance claims seem valid
Bad - Quality Control is spotty requiring inspection to avoid electrical issues.

Troubleshoot the product to resolve issues. Or, find some other cabling product.
Yep.
