HOW TO PROVE TO YOURSELF HARMAN / AKG TRUMPS BOWERS P5 AND BOWERS P7
- Go to the store
- Play "The Four Seasons by Antonio Vivaldi" on Harmon Kardon CL / AKG K550 and Bowers P7
- Listen for the swells of the music
- Listen to the lead violin
- Listen to the soft plucking of the harpsichord
The Harmon CL / AKG K550 will blow you away, the music will sing!
The Bowers P7, in comparison, will sound muddy and uninspiring.

review_headline: Latency limits the uses for which this device is appropriate.
review_body: The unit sounds OK and the range is fine.  However, anyone who buys this has to be clearer than I was about where this unit will be useful and where it won't.  If you are using this for audio from your phone or MP3 player, this unit will be fine.  I thought I might use this unit with bluetooth headphones to watch TV and as an in-ear monitor system for live music performance.  My intended uses were the wrong uses for this unit because of the latency in sound delivery.  If you're watching TV, the sound reaches your ears after you've seen the lips of the actors move.  If you're using the unit as the transmitter for in-ear monitoring of miked stage performances, the sound reaches your ear too long after you've sung into the microphone.  Bluetooth might not be the right technology for my intended uses, but I didn't try anything super high-end.  Maybe that's what it takes.

review_headline: Jolting delay between tracks - obviously missed by ALL that have reviewed this player...
review_body:
Why do people refuse to mention this players MOST fatal flaw? Has nobody noticed that it IMPOSES A 2-3 SECOND DELAY BETWEEN SACD TRACKS?! How can this obvious and super annoying attribute be overlooked by anyone using the machine? I'm in constant amazement at how little accurate and relevant information is shared or realized in 2014. Or the fact that a product as flawed as this would make it to market in these times. The delay between tracks completely ruins the listening experience of nearly all my SACD's. Pink Floyd, The Moody Blues, The Who's Tommy, classical, etc., etc., etc.

And yes, the drawer not opening 100% is ridiculous. Obnoxiously unnecessarily so. Makes me think that a cheap computer transport bought at a closeout bargain price was used here. I *hate* the fact the drawer does not open 100% Oh - and the remote, despite purchasing a silver model, is BLACK! I purchase silver audio equipment not just for its looks - they're much easier to see and read. Seems like common sense, but would be nice if silver faced products included silver remotes.

No firmware update from TEAC to correct the unnecessary delay between tracks either. Wow.

Machine sounds great otherwise. Somewhere between my Oppo 105 and Schiit BiFrost with upgraded Uber DAC. Ended up returning my unit as the SACD \\"feature\\" was completely useless to me. Amazed people are putting up with this, especially on the 2000 and 3000 models! Distinct products indeed.

product_title: Sony HMZ-T3W  Head Mounted 3D Viewer (2014 Model)
review_body:
I do not like this product.
Sony made a sincere effort to advance the state of the art of video glasses. The picture is good, though it can be felt that the resolution is two generations back. Video quality and sound are good too; after all this is Sony. However, this is the end of my praise of this product.
First of all the viewing angle is too big for me. It feels like sitting in a front row of a cinema. I had to decrease the screen size to about 70%. After that the picture became bearable for me, but at the price of loosing 30% of the pixels, which where scarce to begin with.
The second problem is of course the comfort. Trying to wear the device with my glasses was a frustrating experience. When I dumped the glasses and put on my contacts, the experience became reasonable. However, no matter how hard I tried with the straps and forehead support adjustments, I could not find a setting with which I could feel comfortable even for an hour.
Another disappointment was video sharing. Once you connect the video source to the glasses, nobody else can watch it. Probably this problem can be overcome using an HDMI splitter (which needs to be purchased separately), but I did not have an opportunity to test this setup. Most probably it is not possible to connect wirelessly to HMZ's to the same video source.
This product goes to my drawer, and will wait for an opportunity to be passed over to somebody else.

review_headline: I was expecting more from Sony..
review_body:
Ordered the product, & it arrived sooner than expected.. (Thanks Amazon) - I spend at least 2 hours a day at the pool to get my daily workout laps in. So far, I have only used this device on 3 trips to the pool.

COST: I purchased the 4GB, that was double the cost of other brands I have purchased in the past, however those I purchased in the past were not wireless.

SOUND QUALITY: Negative 1 star..!!! I tried all the supplied swimming earbud sizes, & none of them helped at all.. I hear more of the water sloshing & rushing by my ears than my music files, even though the volume is maxed out. The bass or low end could not be heard at all, sounds very similar to those very old AM radios from back in the day.

BATTERY LIFE: Unknown, I have not had my device long enough to provide any information. However, I am concerned reading some of the other reviews "Battery Will Not Take A Charge Anymore After 3 Months Of Use"

At this point, its fair to say I am disappointed with this product, I will most likely return the product, & go back to my swimming MP3 players with the wires, & with good sound quality..

product_title: JBL Charge 2+ Splashproof Portable Bluetooth Speaker
review_headline: Not as loud as original JBL Charge
review_body:
I bought this product as an upgrade to the original JBL Charge, and am disappointed to say the sound volume is noticeably not the same. Pros: beautiful color, added options for social interaction and speakerphone usage while on a call, and water resistance. Cons: slightly larger than the original JBL Charge, side speakers aren't "mesh" looking, but instead have a round plastic cover that vibrates/booms with the music, and lastly the volume is synced with your phone volume (meaning, volume only goes as loud as your phone volume - not the case with the original). I literally did a side-by-side comparison of both speakers, and the original Charge was MUCH louder and clearer, so I will be keeping it over the Charge 2+. Gave product 3 stars for its pros and because even thought it's not as loud, sound is still decent, as you'd expect from JBL. Just wish they hadn't compromised sound over new features!

Tip: Original JBL Charge can be found nowadays for $100 or less (I paid $150 when it first came out).

They have very vague and sloppy positions so if you think you have turned off the alarm you probably haven't.  Same for turning on the alarm.  The switch for setting the time or the alarm is the same, poorly designed.  Who would put the Run setting BETWEEN the Time and Alarm especially with switches that are so loose?  There is so little room for error but the switch slides up and down quite a bit before engaging the actual switch moves to the set time or alarm position.  And if it isn't set to run, and mind you have less than an 1/8 of switch travel in either direction with about the same amount of slop, the alarm will not go off.  This is a poorly designed hunk of junk that is wasn't even worth taking it back for a refund because it would cost more in fuel than it actually cost.  After about a year of use it ceased functioning.  Why?  Because after the alarm failed again because of the above mentioned crappy switches I threw it at the wall.

review_headline: Very Nice Design, My Pair Was Defective
review_body:
I purchased these as a backup to my normal gym/running headphones. Out of the box, they fit very well and are comfortable to wear. They are so light as to be practically unnoticeable. The cord isn't excessively long, so no swinging around when you run. There is also a volume control on the cord. The parts that touch your skin are rubberized, so it should hold up well to sweat. All in all, these are nicely designed headphones.

Unfortunately, the pair I received had a defective right headphone. Five minutes out of the box I noticed intermittent static (suggesting a loose connection) which got progressively worse. The sound out of the left speaker is pretty good, not mindblowing, but these are $5 headphones.

I'm going to return them to Amazon and order another set. If the next pair works, I'll up my review to four stars.

product_title: 66 AUDIO - BTS+ SPORT - Bluetooth Wireless Headphones - 25+ Hour Battery, Voice Call Noise Cancellation, Stereo Sound
review_body: I was excited to receive these, as the reviews are glowing. However, after wearing them and listening to various types of music (dance, downtempo, jazz, chorale) I cannot see what everyone is so excited about.    In my opinion, the sound quality is average, at best. I have owned much less expensive, open-air headphones (Sennheiser)  that would outperform these by a mile. I have also owned slightly more expensive, BT cans (Plantronics) that would similarly embarrass these. So, I cannot agree that the 66 Audio BTS+ are good even \\"for a $50 pair of headphones\\".  Most notable among its sound deficiencies is an overall lack of warmth, a sensation like the sound has been watered down or is coming from another room.  The weak bass response makes dance and electronic music sound like someone is thumping the bottom of Styrofoam cup with the eraser end of a pencil, right next to your ear.  Highs, furthermore, sound like they have been clipped. I'm not an audiophile, but I know nice sound when I hear it, and I just wasn't impressed by these at all. In fact, I was yearning to ditch them just so I could listen through my little $35 Boston Acoustics computer speakers - which also blow these 66 Audios away.  Their best feature in terms of sound is a decent midrange, fairly clear and well imaged; voices sound quite nice.  But, continuing with the negatives... these things have terrible BT range.  I have a premium smartphone (Galaxy Note 3), so I'm pretty sure it's not the phone's shortcoming.  Even holding the phone at arm's length, barely 3 feet away, these headphones could not stream my music continuously.  If the phone was in my right hand, things went better, but in my left hand, the intermittent skipping was just ridiculous.  Sometimes, just turning my head would be enough to interrupt the connection. How this set of headphones is marketed as a \\"sports\\" set is beyond me.  I also tried wearing these while I was cleaning, with the phone in my pocket - again, barely 3 feet away -and I spent as much time listening to nothing as I did to the music, as the interruptions were non-stop.   The lamest thing about these headphones becomes evident when you try to change the volume or skip a track with the on - ear buttons. Just moving your hand in place to tap one of the buttons is enough to interrupt the BT signal (all of the buttons are on the right earpiece, which, apparently is also where the cans pick up the BT signal).  If you are trying to adjust the volume, you will have a hard time because every time you raise your hand to your ear, the music will cut out, and if you tap the button it won't have any effect on the volume because no music is playing; which means you have to get your hand out of the way to let the signal reconnect, but then you are still needing to adjust the volume... the only way I found to circumvent this absurdity was to bring the phone up to my right ear with my left hand, and then change the volume on the headphones with my right hand. Needless to say, this just made me laugh and start planning how soon I can get my money back.  One saving grace: you might find these useful if you are just going to sit in a stationary position with your device also resting in a stationary position.  You will still have problems using the on-ear buttons, but at least the BT will work a little better.  But then again, I don't know why you would want to spend $50 for that.

review_body: I had these headphones for about 4-5 months before the headband snapped. I can say that they are fairly nice in terms of functionality, but the customer service is not what I would expect when paying this price.    First, the product: it seems to be limited almost only by the fact that it is bluetooth. I can't use headset mode and still have good quality sound - it needs to switch between the modes and this can cause all sorts of issues when pairing them with your computer or phone. Not Sennheiser's fault as far as I can tell. I think this is a bluetooth limitation - you can either use half bandwidth for both headphone and microphone or you can have full bandwidth used toward accurate sound reproduction.    In terms of customer service, I have been quite disappointed. This is my 4th Sennheiser product and I believe it will be my last. I've had HD497's, HD 595's, and currently own HD280's and HH380's. I kept sticking with them because I like what my ears hear. Neutral, natural sound.    However! One day recently I went to pull my MM 500-X's out of their case and as I was getting them out, the headband snapped near the center - not any sort of force that caused it. In fact, I couldn't figure out what was wrong until I put them on and notice the off center break and the fact that now they would fall off my head if I leaned over.    I contacted customer support in Asia (bought in WA state, but currently living in Korea) and was told that they have a policy of physical damage not being covered. Further the price to get them repaired (replaced in this case) was around $150. So now here I am with a product just a few months in and another high price tag attached to get them working again after they broke through no fault of my own. Not only that, but the headband seems to be quite simple - I don't know how they can justify that cost!    Sadly, I think it's time to find a new brand for me to buy.

product_title: Outdoor Technology Wired Chips Universal Snow Helmet Audio
review_body:
At first glance, this seems like a nifty little device perfect for outdoor enthusiasts who want to enjoy their tunes. Meant to slip cozily into a hat, this seems a great solution for dragging sound equipment out.

Except it's not that great of a solution. review_headline: READ BEFORE YOU BUY! This could save you and the lives of millions.
review_body:
Think carefully of the damage this can do to those around you and be very cautious! As soon as I got this electrical magic transmitting cable I opened the box and cried tears of joy. This was it, my television would be transmitting sound and images in such hi-def that production companies would have to pay me for shooting their films in my living room. This was my plan for early retirement.

But then it happened... As I was getting ready to plug this into the TV I sat this down on my couch. No big deal, It plugged into my television with no problems at all so I moved onto my BluRay player. Picking the cord up, trekking across my living room to my BluRay player I came to a sudden stop. I had my pool boy measure the distance from my TV to the player, 52.51 feet!!! This cord was 0.02 feet off!!! In a rage I slammed this cord down on the ground... This was the mistake. This cable in motion actively looks for the smoothest path for its (yes it has its own) waves to travel. A black hole is created when an object with any mass (in this case MY NEIGHBORHOOD) is shrunk continuously and infinitely somehow creating infinite gravitational pull. I was lucky being the first pulled in when the cable plugged itself into my dogs skull, poor little guy. As I'm getting pulled through and shot into another end of the galaxy, I'm watching mansion after mansion, neighbors, pets, children, swimming pools, Lamborghini's and of course light getting sucked through. The last ones to come through are getting stretched, deboned and crushed all at the same time. My pool boy of course came through dead which is alright since he got me into this mess. Those of us still alive were entangled in the Unicorn hairs that make up this cable, it kept us alive. It provided enough oxygen, magic and radiated enough rainbows that we were able to swim forward in time and eventually back to earth.

I think it's unnecessary to say that I sent the cord back right away. Even though this incident was operator error I firmly believe that not just anyone should be handed power of this level. I wouldn't say that I would give this a product a zero star rating simply because it saved my life during my unwanted journey into space. Just be aware, that when you hold this cable you also hold the lives of possibly millions of people. Imagine if I lived ground level in the heart of Tokyo!

product_title: Winegard Outdoor HDTV Antenna
review_headline: Careful when purchasing, be certain this will meet YOUR specific needs.
review_body:
I knew better.
I live in a rural area. Approximately, according to antennaweb, 45-50 miles from the station's tower. Nothing.
Okay, it was GB Packer season and I'm in Michigan and I didn't want to get DTV. So, antenna. Fox, specifically. I knew I needed a quality antenna, and probably an amplifier. At one time I sold this type of antenna, and knew it really was only useful in a metro area. BUT, the reviews overall were good, and I know the Winegard line up is usually pretty good equipment, though I prefer Channel Master as a rule. BUT, it's winter, and I don't want to install a tripod and mount an antenna. I want a quick fix so my wife can watch the Packers. Well, I'll be doing it right this summer. I did get the closer stations fairly well, but 50 miles is pushing it in the UHF band.
The antenna is well designed, good structure and fairly simple installation. I am not sure if the amplifier is in the antenna itself so the signal is amplified at the earliest point possible, or if the power inserter is also the amplifier. Either way, it does make a difference and is a vast improvement over an amplified indoor antenna, on which I received nothing.

product_title: Kidz Gear Volume-Limiting Headphones for Kids
review_headline: Ok headphones for kids but watch the volume
review_body:
Starting with the good: My 2 yr old loved these. They were comfortable for him to wear and they fit him well. His tablet no longer provided the background noise on family road trips which was nice for me.

Now for the not so great: I am not sure how they were considered "volume reducing" (unless they were counting the volume being reduced for me). There is a volume control on the cord for the headphones that my 2 yr old could turn all the way up with out any trouble. There were a couple of times that I put his headphones on myself to check how loud he had them and found them deafening, since he would have the volume on his tablet all the way up as well. I found myself concerned for his little ears, but luckily, whenever I asked him to turn it down (or did it myself on his tablet when he wasn't looking), he usually kept it down to a reasonable volume.

You may have noticed that I am referring to these in the past tense. I ordered them in late November, and they lasted less than two months. The main reason I had ordered them was for a trip from FL to ME we took for Christmas. We flew on JetBlue and I wanted him to be able to use the in-flight entertainment system which I knew would require headphones. They worked great on our flight up, and for the first leg on our flight home. However, on the last leg of our flight, they stopped working before we even took off. I thought it might have just been the jack on JetBlue's end, as it was off center, but the headphones don't work in the tablet anymore either. The plug looks ever so slightly bent which is making it so that devices no longer recognize when it's plugged in. I suspect it may have been damaged when we plugged it in to the jack on the aircraft which is obviously not the manufacturer of the headphones fault, but it is still a little disappointing since we didn't force it into the jack on the plane or anything.

product_title: Symphonized Wraith Headphones
review_body:
Good, not great. I had my eye on these for weeks after reading multiple reviews praising them so much. Theyre not bad at all, but theyre also not amazing. The fit and finish first of all was disappointing. The wood on mine came scratched on BOTH sides. The silver surrounding the wood is cheap silver painted plastic, and it looks it. The wood is very thin, I doubt very much youre getting any real benefit of wood, I thik its more for appearance to be honest. But there is a lot to like here too. The noise isolation is quite good. Aside from the fit and finish issues I mentioned, the rest of this set is gorgeous. The wood looks really sharp from a few feet away. The rest of the frame is real metal and looks it. The adjustments for size have a nice, solid click that is very satisfying. Theyre not heavy at all for what they are. I do wish they were a bit louder than they are.

I got these for $39 so Im pretty happy, but I really wish they at least didnt show up scratched up. Otherwise, pretty nice but probably not crazy better than some of my other headsets. BTW, the cables with the mic DO work with Android which is nice. Im using them with my Galaxy Note 4 and I have decent track control with the button. IF you can get them for $39, I do highly recommend them.

product_title: Sharp CDDH950P Mini System
review_headline: Terminally ugly piece of trash that quit working in less than a year.
review_body:
I bought it at a big-box retailer. I thought it was ugly even then, but bought it anyway because there aren't very many choices if you want to use a bookcase system to load multiple CDs and also play cassette tapes. The cords for the speakers were too short to actually separate them, but I figured I could make my own speaker wire extensions. But then I never did. The sound quality wasn't all that great for classical music and opera, although it did give satisfyingly loud booms when my little nephew, who has an unhealthy fascination for "sub-woofers" (he fondles the speaker grilles) played pop music on it.

Then the trouble started: I was annoyed with the bizarre, flashing LED display that tells you, day and night, what a wonderful machine it is, even when it is turned off. Have these people never heard of energy conservation, or of people who put a bookcase system in the room they sleep in? I got so annoyed that I finally googled and found (in addition to vast hordes of annoyed purchasers) that there was a "demo" button on the remote that would turn it off. Silly me, I PRESSED THE BUTTON, and from that very moment, the CD drive stopped reading CDs, giving a "menu not found" message.

Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me. I PRESSED THE BUTTON AGAIN. The CD drive started working intermittently, but never again worked reliably. It is now loaded into my car to go out and serve its highest function: generating a few dollars for the local thrift store as electronic waste recycling.

product_title: Cable Matters Micro USB to HDMI Adapter with integrated USB Charging Port and 6 Feet Charging Cable for Samsung Galaxy S3/S4/S5/Note 2/Note 3/Note 8.0/Note 10.1 - Black
review_headline: Using the device is a little more cumbersome than I would have liked. Here's how it works
review_body:
I'm using this adapter to play YouTube videos from my Samsung Galaxy S5 on TVs that don't have wireless connections or "Smart" features. Using the device is a little more cumbersome than I would have liked. Here's how it works: You plug the adapter into the microUSB charging port on your phone, then plug a power connector into the adapter, and then plug an HDMI cable into the adapter that will run to the TV you want to show the video on. That's a lot of stuff to have to manage. On top of it being a little bit of a wiring nightmare, your phone will drain at a pretty fast rate despite the adapter being plugged into a charger, and both your phone and the adapter get very warm. Finally, the signal is a little iffy and drops out every once in a while, requiring you to move things around to get the picture back. I can't figure out if it is the connection to the phone, the power, or the HDMI cable that is loose enough to cause the connection to stop.
When the adapter works, it works fine and the picture quality is good. Its just sort of a hassle so I don't use it that often.

product_title: Yamaha RX-V677 7.2-channel Wi-Fi Network AV Receiver with AirPlay
review_headline: Quality is great, if the inputs work
review_body: I decided to get this as an upgrade to my current RX-V371, which has been working great for years.  In particular, I wanted to be able to upconvert the analog inputs to HDMI output.  My setup is pretty simple: 5 speakers; fronts, center, surrounds; and a subwoofer.  Inputs are Blu-ray, Chromecast, a PC (HDMI), and a Wii.  On the RX-V371, this configuration works fine (aside from the inability to upconvert the Wii).    When the RX-V677 arrived, I connected it up in the same configuration that the RX-V371 was in, ran through the setup process, and started testing it.  First thing I tested was the Chromecast.  It seemed fine at first, but about every 5 minutes, the audio would drop out for about a second, accompanied by the speaker indicators on the front panel flashing off and on.  I thought this was a problem with the Chromecast at first, but when moving it back to the RX-V371, the problem went away.  Switching back to the RX-V677, I decided to see if the problem would go away over time; instead, it became more frequent.  I tried different audio programs and played around with the settings, but nothing made a difference.  At this point I was fairly sure it was a problem with the receiver, but decided to test another input source in case the Chromecast was at fault.    The second thing I tested was the PC.  I switched to HDMI3 and ... nothing.  The TV was not receiving a signal (not even the receiver's default background image that normally shows if an input is not connected), and the orange HDMI indicator on the receiver's front panel was flashing on and off rapidly.  To try to diagnose the problem further, I connected the PC to some of the other inputs.  It worked perfectly and consistently when connected to HDMI4, but not when connected to HDMI3 or HDMI2.    Assuming that this was a defect in that particular item, I returned it for a replacement of the same model.  When the replacement arrived, I connected it up exactly as before, but had identical issues (except that the audio dropouts with the Chromecast were significantly more frequent, every few seconds as opposed to minutes).    I've returned the second RX-V677 for a refund, and am going to try ordering a RX-V675.  I didn't actually need any of the additional features of the RX-V677 over the RX-V675, but at the time, they were the same price, so I decided to go with the slightly more recent model.  The audio quality is great, user interface is easy-to-use, and composite video upconversion works fine, which is why this gets 2 stars instead of 1, and also why I'm sticking with Yamaha.  I hope that the RX-V675 and RX-V677 are different enough that these issues will not affect the RX-V675 as well.    Update: The RX-V675 does not have the same issues and seems to work perfectly.

review_headline: In my opinion, based on my experiences, this charger is not quite ready for prime time.
review_body:

The first charger arrived and I happily proceeded to insert AA & AAA batteries of several brands(Energizer, Tenergy, Maha, etc. I had about 30 or so batteries handy to utilize.) into the charger. After I noted loading problems with the charger, I proceeded more methodically, first checking each cell in a quality LaCrosse smart charger to ensure readability and that they tested A-ok.
1)Batteries were often sensed, and started charging, but then either the charger lost contact/sensing the battery, or registered an error code, and ignored the batteries.
2)Some batteries were either not sensed, or needed to be jiggled extensively and repeatedly for it to maintain contact/sensing.
3)On at least one occasion it appears to have "killed" a battery that had just been charged by a top rated LaCrosse charger just fine.

All batteries it had the above problems with, (Except the one it killed) were then tested on the Lacrosse charger and registered/measured and charged fine.
These problems seemed to be very consistent and repeatable. Some "bays" seemed more problematic than others. (Needing batteries to be inserted, removed, re-inserted several times, before they would continue to charge without the above problems. Sometimes disappearing right away, other times after extended periods.)

Their tech department, reported that they could not repeat any of my results.... They were very courteous, professional, and helpful in facilitating the return of the first charger.

When the second charger arrived, it works better than the first, but still requires far too much effort to use...exhibiting some of the same problems as the first, although not to such a large extent. Cells would often still require a bunch of jiggling or re-inserting several times to get the charger to continue charging without losing contact or whatever was causing them to disappear on the display. Bay 5 on the left most bank was by far the most problematic.

product_title: VideoSecu TV Wall Mount Articulating Arm Monitor Bracket for most 12"-24", some up to 27" LCD LED Plasma Flat Panel Screen TV with VESA 100/75mm ML10B 1E9
review_body:
The Good: Its weight implies that it's made of some pretty solid feeling materials. The price is a big upside. It has three different pivot points for a pretty customized viewing angle. Mounting hardware that was included was of good quality.

The Bad: This thing is off level! It's loosely fitting internal hardware makes this thing very wobbly, and permanently off level, even if you are very careful in perfectly mounting the bracket at the correct level, the monitor itself will sag and become off level. Mind you, I am not mounting a very heavy monitor, it's a small 24-inch LCD monitor that weighs approx. 9lbs, and it was mounted securely into the center of a wood beam in the wall (as recommended) Coupled with that, these instructions are terrible. There are tons of spelling errors, and I'm not being just grammar-picky, it makes it hard to understand how to mount it right out of the box. Eventually through re-reading directions multiple times, and using previous DIY experience, I was able to figure it out, and get a nice strong mount to the wall.

The Verdict: Don't buy it. It feels quality, but it is not. Even the experienced Do-It-Yourselfer cannot make this product a viable mounting option. You'd be better off leaving it off on a desk or table, because at least on a desk it would be level. Unless you're desperate to wall-mount your monitor for less than $20 at any cost, save yourself the time and invest in a more quality product.

product_title: Creative Labs Sound Blaster AXX 200 Intelligent Wireless Sound System - A portable wireless speaker with Bluetooth, NFC and microphone
review_body:
This is definitely a "jack of all trades, master of none" type of speaker. I've seen reviews that call it a swiss army knife speaker which it is in many ways. Not the best sounding speaker, but far from the worst. The fact that it does so much is what sets it apart from any other bluetooth speaker.

First, the sound. Bass is lacking and the treble is quite harsh. The bass is all punch and little-to-no boom. The bass port does help a bit though if you put the speaker up against a wall to reflect. You can EQ it to boost the bass some, but at the cost of some high end clarity. I find it best to turn off all the SBX features aside from EQ. I appreciate the multi-band EQ adjustment that this thing has (about twice as many as the 5-band on the UE Boom). The EQ is absolutely necessary to produce a good sound and i found that boosting around the 150hz area by a few db and lowering 8k area a few db, makes the speaker sound fuller and smooths out the brightness. The volume itself is merely-sufficient for a 12x12 room, but not recommended anything bigger. If you go anywhere past 85% volume, you'll likely run into some distortion, so I always keep it at least one bar/notch below maximum. I would say this is strictly an indoor unit. I imagine it would sound comparatively tiny out doors. It's fine for personal use or for small gathering, but probably not in a party setting.

Second, the microphone. It works, but vocals do not sound very clear, and there is a delay in the vocals (roughly 100ms delay) which is quite annoying if you're going to be using it for karaoke. Also, the mic is in dire need of a pop filter. It is very sensitive at picking up pop sounds when you're using it as a mic which I also found equally annoying. It's probably much better suited for a megaphone than a vocal microphone. There's also no EQ of any kind for the microphone.The only thing you can get are some gimmicky effects to change your voice.

Third, the ease of use. The NFC works exactly as it should. Paired my Nexus 5 and Nexus 7 with no setup required. It says you can pair up and connect two devices at a time. I've done this, but looks like you can only stream audio one at a time. I'm not sure how you're supposed to switch back and forth between the two devices though while they're both connected by bluetooth. I can play music on one device and then when i stop and play music on the other device, it doesn't always work and it seems to confuse the speaker.

These are the only things i've tested so far after about an hour of use. I can't really speak about all the other things it can do since I'm not sure I will be using those other features. I was tempted on giving this product 4 stars because it can do so much, but decided to give it 3 stars based on only the things I'm going to use it for which is mainly music. I'm getting in a UE Boom soon to compare and I'll probably end up returning the one that sounds worse.

review_headline: I expected much, much more from a genuine Walkman.
review_body: Sony provides two types of ear buds. One type for swimming and one for normal use. The swimming buds block water from entering a sound chamber in front of the driver and drowning out the sound altogether. Until you shake or blow any water out of that chamber, you're not hearing anything. Unfortunately, the same "membrane" (it's really just a thin rubber gate) that keeps the water out, also keeps much of the sound in. Consequently you're hearing about half the volume you would if you had the regular buds on. This lower volume combined with splashing and the augmented sound of underwater breathing while swimming, makes these a poor solution for swimming. I want to love them, so, much, but the extra cost, slightly cumbersome fit, and poor swimming performance makes no sense. I would have thought Sony, the inventor of personal music devices, would have got this one right. Bottom line: they need a more powerful driver to push through the water in the sound chamber. I don't need music for 8 hours in a pool. I need a sick beat for 90 minutes to get me through my workout, swim, and sauna.

product_title: Kicker 40CWD124 CompD Series 12 inch Subwoofer Dual 4 Ohm
review_body:
Let's start off by saying this isn't some fake review, though I did not purchase this sub brand new I bought a single 12 with no box in like new shape for 40 bucks off a friend of mine. I ended up building a custom built 2.1 cubic ft (after displacement) ported box tuned to 33 hz, which is right in kicker specs.

Over all build quality is not too bad, it's what you would expect from lower end kicker. For some reason the magnet is screwed into the basket from the back, if you unscrew the screws the magnet will come loose... lol weird design. The cone seems a bit lighter in design from the older comp models, and the surround isn't stitched to the cone anymore. The terminals absolutely REQUIRE the female spade terminal connectors in order to wire up the speaker, which in my opinion is stupid... a simple cheap spring terminal would've sufficed but they make it so you NEED the female spade terminal.

Now onto the sound quality, for the most part the still sound like the same old loud, boomy, muddy kicker sound.. it's improved just a tad, but over all its still not all that great. I have the kicker spec'd ported box, and the correct amount of power going to it, so it's not like I threw it in an atrend box and called it a day. Bc the cone is a bit lighter and the suspension of the sub is not as stiff it did improve a bit in sound quality, but it's no game changer. For the most part it's the same old kicker just a newer look, the only thing I will give it is that it does get pretty loud, for one 12 in a custom box it does get decently loud, but like anything kicker, they need a huge box to get there... two 12's requires right around 4 cubes all together, which is a huge box just for 12's. But if you're on a budget and looking for something that's cheap and sounds half decent I would stay away from anything kicker, though they do get loud they just pump out loud muddy bass and wouldn't recommend them for any SQ design. Their is plenty other brands out there with lower end model subs that cost the same as this, and would blow this sub out of the water, look at brands like sundown, soundqubed, RE audio, Dayton audio, Skar audio, alpine and phoenix gold just to name a few. Hope this review helped!

review_headline: Probably will have to toss out the TV....
review_body:
Not a happy camper... I have a Vizio TV in a small RV. The remote quit working. After going through all the troubleshooting and doing a "test" (viewing the remote through a camera to see if it is sending the infrared signal) It appeared that the original remote had gone bad. Unfortunately the new remote was not the solution. I had contacted Vizio and they gave me instructions to "reset" the TV and Remote (see their web site FAQ). Yet doing this did not restore functionality. (Yes, I repeated the process several times.) It's beginning to look like I need to toss this TV out and get another brand that works.

Note: The remote is especially important when a TV is in an RV, since you need to "initialize" the TV for each cable system you attach it to. This can be done my manipulating the various control buttons on the side of the TV, but it is much more intuitive using the function specific (e.g. Menu/OK, direction) buttons on the remote.

With the price of 19" TVs so relatively low, it's looks like it will be easier to just replace it rather than fix it. What a waste.

product_title: Teac CD-2000 Super Audio CD Player with USB Input
review_body:
Prospective purchasers should be aware that this unit, along with its brand mates CD-1000 and the $2,000 CD-3000, mutes playback and inserts a three-second pause as one SACD track ends and the next begins, even when the music is supposed to play uninterrupted. This situation is most common in classical music, but it is not exclusive to that genre.

As one reviewer of the CD-1000 wrote, "How can this obvious and super annoying attribute be overlooked by anyone using the machine? I'm in constant amazement at how little accurate and relevant information is shared or realized in 2014." My only quibble about the quoted sentences is that the second hasn't been updated to include the first quarter of 2015!

I wish that I had read one of the few critical reviews of this product line before I bought the CD-3000 (my review of that model is [[ASIN:B0085TX3MK here]]). The SACD track glitch is beyond belief in a machine retailing for $2,000 and still inexcusable in units half or a third of that price. I feel that I have been ripped off by Teac and by everyone else involved in the sale. (Worst of all, I bought my unit on the Bay of E, and so I have no warranty and no other course of action to pursue.)

Please note, too, that Teac customer service has been 100 percent unresponsive to my queries and complaints about the CD-3000. Having first designed and engineered a SACD player line that won't properly play SACDs, the company now refuses to remedy or even acknowledge the problem it created. For shame!

review_headline: My expectations were too high, now I know what to expect in this level of shower speaker unit for my personal enjoyment.
review_body:
The bass is simply not there, distorts at sound levels needed to mask shower noise, suction cup weak (unit fell off of cleaned glazed tile in a few minutes but unit took the hit, a positive!). Granted this is a tiny sound source, not likely to generate any sort of bass heft. I'd suggest a larger unit with better bass and no sound distortion at higher sound output levels. Maybe a suction cup AND a lanyard. Nice for bass shy low volume listening but it can't be challenged much beyond that. I can't tolerate the slightest distortion in my music. The best that I can compare this sound experience to is a static free FM signal on an average grade clock radio. The kind of listening you do for a minute when you get up in the morning.

Outside of a shower, I'd just as soon grab either around or on the ear headphones or a set of cheap earphones.

Sorry folks, if you are OK with this performance then you've got yourself a bargain. To each his own. Please do not tell me what I should like or tolerate. My source material was Halestorm (steampunk cover), Starset -Transmissions, The Pretty Reckless - live, Rickie Lee Jones - Pop-Pop, U2 Boy, Mickey Hart - Planet Drum.

I will either find a shower unit that meets my listening expectations or switch to a more traditional wireless speaker system and place it out of range of the shower spray.

product_title: Klipsch In-ear Headphone
review_headline: Good for talking, not for music. Falls out of ears.
review_body:
I was trying to replace a similar pair of stereo headphones with microphone. In comparison, I really dislike the Klipsh S3M headphones.

PROS
+ other voices are easy to hear and understand
+ your voice is understood by others
+ background noise doesn't seem to be a problem
+ stereo

CONS
- music is tinny and shallow, so stereo is a waste on music
- microphone is right at the collar line for me, it needs to be higher or lower
- buds pop out of the ears at the slightest provocation

Details:

I bought these during a flash sale so I didn't have much to lose. The price was right for a flash sale, and even then it might have been high.

The audio quality is engineered for human voice. This means talking to people is great, but listening to music is totally worthless; there's almost zero bass. The previous headphones I replaced (also a cheap set) were much better. In fact, I bought these headphones more to listen to music and less to talk to people.

A neat trick I've found when talking while walking or riding a bike is to tuck the cord, including the microphone, under my shirt. It stops the wind from interfering with my voice. With this pair, the microphone is right at the collar, so it rubs uncomfortably and it constantly pops out from under the shirt anyway.

The worst problem with these is that the buds fall out of my ears. It's usually the bud with the microphone on it. I don't know if the cord is too stiff or what, but a little bit of tension or bumping will loosen the bud; that makes it harder to hear. If I don't fix it immediately, it'll usually retreat out my ear hole and dangle under my chin. I have no ear holes down there :(

product_title: iMBAPrice feet 2RCA Male to 2RCA Male Python Home Theater Audio Cable
review_body: The outer rings of these connectors are very weak.  I installed this 3 ft cable between my phono preamp and my amplifier.  The cables seemed to slide on very easily and when I turned on the units I had a loud hum. I was not really surprised because of the lack of friction when making the connection.  I squeezed the outer ring with my fingers and they bent in very easily.  After reconnecting them, I turn the units on again and there was no hum, so I started to move them back into place and the hum started again.  I checked the connections and they were loose again, so I replaced this cable with a standard quality RCA cable that I had on hand and everything worked fine.  I was adding a turntable and an Emotiva phono preamp to my Marantz amplifier and wanted to use high quality cables to be sure I had the best possible sound from my records.  I have used dozens of RCA cables over the years and these were by far the weakest connectors I have ever experienced so I returned the cable to Amazon.

product_title: RioRand® DC/DC BUCK Stepdown Converter Regulator 4.5-40V 12V To 5V/2A USB Charger Voltmeter Display
review_body:
Using a bench power supply I am able to test this device on input voltages between 0-30 volts. At first everything seemed great, when input voltage was above 6 volts the output was always rock stable at 5v. But that's where the good news stops. After about 4 minutes with no load the TO-92 package device (probably a transistor) next to the input header started getting hot. The higher the input voltage, the hotter it got. The output voltage did stay at 5v. After 10 minutes of sweeping around between 6 volts and 30 volts the TO-92 was way too hot for my liking, and I stopped the testing. I suspect if you stay under 12-14 input voltage you'd be ok, but at this point I'm not risking my downstream USB devices on it.

If your input voltage is below 5volts, it will gladly pass that onto the output voltage (- about 0.7v), which can be bad. Some devices, if they are expecting 5V, and you give them say 3V, they won't be happy, and may damage the downstream device.

[USABILITY]: It's a little hard to actually use. It's got two buttons, Top button is main power, bottom button is output power switch. They are both "soft switches", meaning they are controlled by some form of logic, IE a microprocessor. I suspect the microprocessor is underneath the LED display. In order to get it to start outputting power, first you have to press the top button to turn on the main unit, then it starts displaying input voltage only on the LED, I wasn't able to get it to show anything other then the input voltage. After it's displaying voltage then you press the bottom button and it turns on the output voltage. Not sure why/what they intended that usage for.

Later I'll do a actual destructive test on it and see if it'll fail on me, and if it does fail, what output voltage it'll put out when it does fail.

Pros:

Small Size

Cons:

* Gets way too hot to handle/touch.
* Output voltage can dip below 5V ifinput voltage dips below 6ish volts.
* Have to manipulate buttons to get it to output any voltage.
* LED display only displays incoming voltage, no amperage, no wattage.
* No way to turn off the display, and provide output voltage.

product_title: Bose QuietComfort 25 Headphones (wired, 3.5mm)
review_headline: DON't get for BUS rides. the vibrations travel through the headphones and ruin the music
review_body:
I have a few very important things to review about this headphone. 1st this headphone does an amazing job at noise cancelling ( especially low constant frequencies) however, the higher frequencies still come through, but slightly muffled. If you have NC on and someone is talking to you, you will here the top upper half of their vocal tone (although muted somewhat) but the lower frequencies of there speech will be gone. If you're trying to block out loud speaking and its a dude, you're going to kill most of the sound, however, children screaming or annoying high-pitched women still come through.

the sound is a little sloppy, the base is too loose, the treble is a little to shrill and a HUGE HUGE annoyance is that the speakers tend to distort and crackle at louder parts of your music. this is really bad right out of the box. However, after about a hundred hours of music at reasonable volume, these headphones clean up nicely, the base gets a little tighter, the shrill treble cuts down and the crackling is greatly reduced to a much more tolerable amount. overall, the best sound one can expect is about a B to B+.

i got these for studying (I am a collage student) and for my daily bus rides to and from school. for studying alone i would have payed 200 dollar because these headphones are sooooooooooooooo comfortable and the NC is priceless. however, i can not use these on the BUS at all. the bus bouncing causes vibrations that transfer through the seat, up your body and into your headphones. this causes repeated air compressions that make your music very inconsistent and very irritating to listen to so if your getting these for your bus ride (the bumps are the only problem) then don't. but for plain rides i wouldn't get anything else.

product_title: VideoSecu ML531BE TV Wall Mount for most 22"-55" LED LCD Plasma Flat Screen Monitor up to 88 lb VESA 400x400 with Full Motion Swivel Articulating 20 in Extension Arm, HDMI Cable & Bubble Level WP5
review_headline: Received a USED and damaged product when I paid for NEW
review_body:
When I took the VideoSecu television wall mount out of the box, it was covered in scratches and a couple of the screw packages had been opened. It was obvious that the bolts (which were stripped) and mount had been installed onto the wall and just put back into the box when the previous owner had decided not to keep the product. Very disconcerting - someone had returned the mount I almost wondered if the mount was safe or not to use. There's no doubt I had paid for NEW not USED. It took almost a week for my payment to go through and then at least another week for the product to arrive so all I wanted was to put my television up. I had read so many good reviews about this product, I was so surprised to see that someone would return one. After thoroughly inspecting the mount, I decided it looked safe enough to install. There was no installation manual book in the box, just the mount and a dozen packets of screws (only a third of them you end up using and I had to buy new lag bolts). I was so anxious as to whether this mount would hold my 55" television that I left four 25lb weights to hang on it overnight and the next day. It's been almost a week now and the television is still up. So other than the terrible delay for payment to go through and receiving a product that was anything but NEW - it seems I be a sturdy product.

So I take off two stars because I was deceived when I paid for NEW. If I wanted USED, I would have paid less and expected it. If USED constituted as NEW whenever you purchased something online, there would be no need for a section for USED products.

review_headline: Great Looking, Uber Comfortable... sound falls short.
review_body:
I ordered these in anticipation of using them with my Pono Player. As they are a brand new release as of this writing, they weren't available to demo in any store, but I thought I would give them a shot as they looked they might be a good all-arounder.

It should be noted that many headphones at this range and up are going to require break-in periods of varying lengths (40-100 hrs, apprx.) to really fall into their best sound. That said, I hope to at least be slightly pleased by the sound I'm hearing within the first few hours of listening. I found them to be lacking, with an overall muddiness, suffocated soundstage, and not enough separation of musical elements.

However, some people seem to really be liking them. Just try to audition them at a store before you buy, or be prepared to do a return (props to Amazon for the ease of returns).

That said, the comfort of these are off the charts, and they look awesome, especially the silver/brown model. But I ended up returning them and opting for the slightly more expensive Bowers & Wilkins P7's, which I love.

product_title: Zeo Personal Sleep Manager
review_headline: An okay clock with nice perks
review_body:
Zeo was a good idea with an okay implementation. Unfortunately, they failed to develop a sustainable revenue model before sleep tracking became a free add-on feature for other fitness devices and even cell phones. The company itself suspended normal operations over a year ago.

This clock has several good ringers and the sleep analysis feels accurate. The screen can be dimmed enough to not wake you during the night. When it does wake me, I don't feel magically refreshed and ready to spring out of bed, but I suspect that's more my fault then the clock.

The clock has several shortcomings which keep it from being truly great:

1) The pads on the headband have a finite lifespan and replacements may be hard to come by now that Zeo is out of business.
2) The device lacks any sort of wireless connectivity, so you have to drag the SD card back and forth between your night stand and computer to get at the data.
3) There is no nap function. I'd love to be able to press a button and have it automatically wake me after a proper power nap, but that's just not an option.
4) With Zeo all but dead, don't expect any updates to the firmware or support from the manufacturer.

Pros:
Price, Design, Convenience
Satechi iTour starts crackling when you increase the sound too high. This DKnight does not do that.

Cons:
Satechi iTour has better bass, even though it is 2.5 times smaller. I wish the DKnight has more bass and longer battery life. The battery lasts only a day's worth of use. The bluetooth connection periodically gets disconnected as well, and I would have to disconnect and reconnect the device. Sometimes, it would lose connection for a brief second and then continue playing the song. Sound quality-wise, it's nowhere as good as Logitech X-140 that my friend got for me for $25 "back in the day" (but the Logitech is also 10x bigger and the wires drive me crazy).

Overall impression, meh. I use it over my laptop and cell speakers, and I use it regularly. Sound's passable for price.

After we finally got it connected we had to keep readjusting the position. I thought it could just sit on top of the TV or hang on the back but it had to be attached to a wall with the command tape. I've tried everything imaginable to keep them from causing Mac OS 10.10 audio layer from crashing. They work great after a clean reboot but as soon as you shut them off or plug them in to charge and then turn back on all audio apps that use the microphone stop functioning and hang indefinitely (Skype, Lync, FaceTime, etc). Restarting the apps doesn't work nor does restarting bluetooth itself. Other Bluetooth headphones work fine in similar use cases on OS X which leads me to believe it's this device.  Testing these headphones on iPhone and iPad they work pretty good. The audio is decent, though not as vibrant as I'd hoped. It didn't cause any crashes like on OS X which was better (only reason for the 2 star review here). The range I was able to obtain from my iPad was under 5 feet at which point audio cut out intermittently which I found weird. Other headphones had much further ranges but this wasn't a requirement as much as a convenience being able to walk around the room and talk / listen to a conference call.  The pain points aren't worth the cost so I'll be returning these tomorrow.

review_headline: Works great -- but not if your iPod/iPhone is in a case
review_body:
I bought this for my husband for his birthday, so he could use it with his new iPod Touch (his old speaker dock works only with the older iPod Classic). This speaker dock is very small, easy to use, and will be great for listening to music out on the deck (or on vacation -- the size makes it very portable). The sound is very good -- my husband really likes it.

But -- and it's a BIG but -- the only way to get the iPod (or iPhone) to attach properly to the speaker is to remove its case. And that's just ridiculous. The case my husband uses on his iPod is very thin -- just a protective bit of rubber to keep the iPod safe in case he drops it. But the iPod will not seat properly on the speaker connection unless the case is removed. And those cases are annoying to remove -- no one wants to have to do it on a regular basis.

product_title: Philips Sports Headphones
review_headline: comfortable, but didn't fit my ears well with very poor bass & sound isolation
review_body:
I was first introduced to Philips earphones with their [[ASIN:B00V4X6R2C Philips NC1/27 Fidelio Noise Cancelling Premium Headphones with Ergonomic Memory Foam Cushions, Black]], which I absolutely love. I do listen to music and watch movies on my iPad while riding an exercise bike, so I thought these ActionFit Earbuds would be worth a try.

The earbuds arrive in a nicely packaged box that is easy to open and reseal. The earbuds are fully assembled and come with three different sizes of ear tips for a more custom fit. The band is designed to be worn behind your head, and hooks go over each ear to keep the earbuds secured in your ears. The cord is sturdy, seems tangle-free, and has a handy clip to secure it to your clothing if desired. A lightweight mesh bag is included to store the earphones when not in use.

I found the earbuds very comfortable to wear, and the design of the band keeps them in my ear no matter how much I move my head. There is no adjustment to the positioning of the ear tips, though, and I found I could not get a good seal in my ear no matter which size tip I tried. The end result was no sound isolation and very little bass response, although midrange and treble were good. The cord is very well-insulated, and there was no noise artifact when it brushed against my clothing with movement.

Pros:

solid construction
band keeps them secured in your ears well
cord is well-insulated with no artifact
multiple sizes of ear tips provided
waterproof and sweatproof design

Cons:

lack of adjustment in earbud tip may prevent sound isolation for some people
poor bass reproduction (could be due to lack of good seal in my ear)
somewhat bulky (can't be folded up for compact storage)

In summary, these are comfortable earbuds that are clearly designed for wear while exercising. They are well-constructed and fit very securely no matter how much you might move around. While they do have different sizes of ear tips included to help customize their fit these earbuds have no swivel at the tip which may prevent a good seal in your ear and, as a result, may compromise sound isolation and bass response for some people. If you want sturdy earphones that will stay in place during running or other exercise these may be a good choice if they fit your ears well. review_headline: Craig Bluetooth 2.0 - An Honest Review for a Non-Mobile Bluetooth Speaker
review_body:
INTRODUCTION :
I purchased this bluetooth speaker from Rite Aid in hopes of having a decent speaker with a lot of bass. This is my honest review of this product.

BUILD :
The build on this product isn't very good. The cloth that covers the grill looks like it would tear easily if caught on something. The light is in a random spot on the front of the speaker, and the speaker is very round and kind of ugly looking. All of the buttons and switch are on the left side of the device...which is fine. The plastic is very cheap and looks like it would chip really easily if dropped.

SOUND QUALITY :
I will be honest here. I expected this speaker to have superior bass because of the holes on the back, which allow the power from the bass sound to pour out in an air form. This speaker has almost no bass unless you configure the audio with an equalizer. This speaker can go pretty loud, but I expected louder. A smaller speaker I own that is almost half the size can pour out the same amount of bass and go even louder than this one; and was $10 cheaper.

OTHER INFORMATION / THE MAIN PROBLEM :
Honestly, I would have given this product 4 1/2 stars if it weren't for this key aspect that is missing from this item: There is no battery. This is NOT a mobile device, meaning it does not include a battery. I mean yes, you can buy a 4000mA battery for like $10 and then just plug the AC cable into that, but that is a true pain to do. I had bought this product mainly to use for a mobile, quality build, and I recieved a cheap product that did not fulfill my expectations.

However, the reason I am giving this product 3 stars is because of the price. Most quality speakers are around $100+, and this is only around $35. Still though, I expected much more from this product than what I received.

So, that was my honest review on the Craig Bluetooth 2.0 speaker.

review_headline: Soft plastic PG16 cable gland has limited usefulness
review_body: These PG16 plastic cable glands are made of too soft a plastic, so that they really can't be properly tightened down into threaded receptacles such as junction boxes (and yes, the threads of the junction Appleton junction box were the same PG16 specification). I suppose when used as through-hull cabinet fittings using the supplied backing nuts, they will probably work OK, but that is not why I had purchased them. Used as cable glands for junction-box entries, where a degree of water-tightness is expected, you cannot tighten them enough before the threaded part going into the junction box strips out (plastic junction box threads remained OK, it is just the soft threads of the cable gland that deform and strip). I should have known this from the low cost. The gland part that grips the cable is OK, though, so in future I'll only use them as entries into non-threaded thin-wall cabinets.

product_title: J-Tech Digital JTDBTAR Premium NFC-Enabled Bluetooth Audio Receiver for Sound System
review_body:
[[VIDEOID:d6959152eeaa9a1e6b81f82b07e7f197]] As opposed to a Keedox device that I had recently tested, J-tech goes for a more simplistic approach with its Bluetooth Audio receiver.

Included with the desktop Bluetooth audio receiver is a male to male audio jack cable (approximately 3 feet 3 inches in length), an USB to micro USB cable (approximately 2 feet 5 inches in length) and the user manual. The device itself is relatively small at roughly 2.5 inches by 2.5 inches and about an inch high. This only has a Bluetooth connect button with an Aux audio port and a micro USB port for powering the device in a wall charger. There are 2 LED indicators on the front that is used for pairing status.
Pairing is relatively easy, just press the connect button on the device for 5 seconds or so and the blue LEDS will flash. This paired pretty simply to my S4. This can be paired with the Bluetooth way or via the NFC.

I tested this first with playing music from my phone (but can be done from any Bluetooth capable device) into a pair of regular computer speakers that have a 3.5mm audio jack and the music played with no issues. The one thing missing from this device that another receiver I recently tested was the ability to plug a pair of RCA cables into it and the home stereo (which tend to give better sound than the Aux cable). I would have preferred to have that option for plugging in RCA cables as well. The range for this device was ok but not nearly as strong as the Keedox brand that I recently reviewed. I could maybe go 15 feet before the device's ability to play started cutting out. I did not get any occasion popping sounds when idle like I experienced with the Keedox (although I haven't at this point confirmed it was caused by the Keedox device) and the sound through the audio cable matched the audio cable sound of the Keedox. Unlike the Keedox, the J-tech does not have the ability to be used for phone calls. This is not a big factor in the rating for me as I would not use this for phone calls usually anyways.

The biggest problem here is the J-tech (16 bucks) is currently only 3 dollars less than the Keedox (19 bucks). Even though the Keedox is not perfect either (especially with its poor instruction manual), it has a lot more features and capabilities than this device and the Bluetooth range is way better.

Simple is fine in most cases as it works well for what it is capable of but the price versus features kept this from being higher rated.

product_title: Sennheiser CX 400-II Precision Ear-Canal Phones with Bass-Driven Stereo Sound (Black)
review_headline: A waste of money due to uncontrolled microphonic interference
review_body: A waste of money. I have admired and owned many models of Sennheiser cans and my last earbuds before this were the CX-300s, which had flaws but fell into the "get what you paid for" category. For this pair I decided to step up and pay extra for a pair of CX-400IIs.  The results were extremely disappointing. While the sound quality is just fine, you have to sit perfectly still and not let ANYTHING touch the cables.  The microphic noise (that "stethoscope" sound you hear when you jostle the cable of a pair of cheap ear buds) is just completely out of control on these... way worse than on my CX-300s. Microphonic interference is caused by the quality of material used to cover the cables. Thickness and material selection are both factors that impact the degree to which mechanical vibrations can be transmitted up the cable and amplified by the ear bud speakers.  But for the CX-400II Sennheiser has apparently opted for the worst of all possible combinations in designing and making these cables. The consequence is just horrendous. Yes I know that if I loop the cable over my earlobes, my earlobe can have the effect of dampening the vibrations slightly. But if I have a small ear lobe and wear glasses, so it is not like I have a lot of room to be wrapping headphone cables around by earlobe every time I listen to music (people with well endowed ears may experience different results).  I do notice that the microphic effect gets progressively worse as vibrations occur further up the cable. Vibrations occurring on the cable between the plug and the volume control get dampened by the volume control itself and only a mild nuisance.Between the volume control and the left-ear/right-ear Y splitter the effect becomes much worse. But it only becomes absolutely unacceptable and intolerable on the individual cables from the Y-split to the ear bud itself. In any event, I intend to continue my search for a better pair of ear buds to replace my CX-300s. I will not be settlingfor the CX-400II.

[[VIDEOID:eb77e6fdd003868fffa9f1c8711fbe21]]I have mixed feelings about this MP3 player. I have a Sylvania 4GB MP3 player that I bought for 13 bucks, and here is a 16GIG for 7 dollars more. I don't want to sit there and put all my songs into a single directory, renaming all those Track 1s and Track 2s. I just may have to, though, in the end.

Still, battery meter and shuffle (both of which I sorely missed on my Sylvania MP3 player), and a crunking volume output. The Recording function works surprisingly well, too. I am guessing what I though was a lanyard hook is actually the MIC.

All in all, I do rather like this player, and will just switch between the two depending on which still has juice (this one seems to have a far better battery stand-by than the Sylvania), but have some mixed "Phhhtb" about it too. Mainly the always defaulting to the lowest sub-directory. :p

Good clarity.
Not very loud.

the speaker does "warm up" after some listening time.

I think most would appreciate a more common charging cord because the one supplied is very short.

I'm happy with the quality of the speaker especially for the price and would recommend it to anyone who is looking for a inexpensive portable speaker.

product_title: Koss Bluetooth Speaker
review_body: When I first bought this little speaker, it was awesome. Now here I am, 7 and a half months in, and it's falling apart. The battery is lasting about a third of the time it used to, and the speaker cone is starting to rattle. I do use the speaker daily for about 20-30 minutes as I get ready in the morning, plus hanging out poolside this summer. But still, it shouldn't be crapping out like this. ----------------------------- For the price and the size it's pretty solid. It has great mid-range, decent bass, but lacks treble. I was honestly worried that the sound would be too "tinney," but it's the exact opposite - there isn't enough treble for me.  Unlike some reviewers, I have had no problem syncing this to my iPhone 6 or my tablet. The battery doesn't last quite 5 hours, but that's also probably because I play it loud. I mean, this thing packs some volume!  Another plus - minimal distortion when it's played loud. I have noticed very little distortion, no matter how loud it goes. It's a very consistent product.  I would certainly recommend it... just don't be expecting really, really high quality sound from a $50 bluetooth speaker.

However, these headphones were not worth the price and I would gladly pay a few dollars extra in order to get a decent pair.

-Good color
-Don't look cheap

Now onto some of the more negative aspects:

product_title: JENSEN JCR-232 AM/FM Dual Alarm Clock with Digital Retro Flip Display
review_body:
The LOOK of this clock radio is nice, but that's the best I can say of it.

I returned mine because the radio didn't work, despite an hour of trying to get it to using the instruction manual. And I'm glad it was defective, because at least I could return the thing without having to pay shipping. The controls are, to put it mildly, counter-intuitive. By trying to make all the clock and radio controls operable with the six buttons on top (probably because it was cheaper), the manufacturer has made something as simple as turning up the sound volume as complicated as trying to program a 1980s VCR. I'd have happily spent more money to get some separate controls, and some better build quality. This thing is made of such lightweight plastic it would blow away in a light wind.

And that's the problem with this clock radio: it's flimsily made, without regard to either ease of use or durability. Very disappointing.

product_title: Addicore 10 Pack LM317T Adjustable 2.2-37V LM317 Voltage Regulator in Antistatic Foam
review_body: All ten of the ST Micro LM317s in the package I received were defective. Not one of them would pass a basic function test and I suspect them to be counterfeit. I cannot imagine ST letting ten in a row slip through their quality control. The test I used was connecting the ADJ pin to ground and applying from 0-30V to IN while measuring the voltage across OUT over a 100 Ohm resistor. The expected result is that from roughly 3V upward, 1.25V appears across the resistor. That behavior is exhibited on the National Semiconductor and Texas Instruments versions I have at hand and is described in the datasheet. These would regulate up to about 12V input, then break down and pass roughly the input voltage to the output. As @Rini noted in his review, this can be very frustrating as you try to understand why your circuit is not working as expected. On the plus side, I learned a lot more about the details of the LM317 and about the problem of IC counterfeiting. However I recommend you seek a more reliable source or minimally test these before entrusting your circuit to it.

product_title: Smart battery charger, iGrace NITECORE NEW i4 (2016 New Version) Universal Smart battery Charger for Li-ion/IMR/LiFeP04/Ni-MH/Ni-Cd with 12V Car Adapter and iGrace Battery Box
review_body:
I'll go ahead and get the bad stuff out of the way first, since I feel like it's pretty important.

I had issues charging four batteries. I know the batteries I attempted to charge were a little under halfway discharged. Usually, when charging, there is a blue light in the top-right of the charger that stays lit up. There are also yellow blinking lights that indicate the charge progress. The blue light would be lit up, and the yellow lights would be blinking. Then, all of the lights would go off, and stay off for 10-15 seconds. Then it would come back on for another minute or two, then shut off again. After about four hours of that, I picked the charger up to take the batteries out. The unit was hot. Like, almost painful to touch. It smelled like hot electronics. I tested the voltage on the batteries, and it hadn't changed at all from the time I put them on the charger. It should be noted that so far, I've only used the charger to charge 18650s.

Now the good stuff:

I put two batteries in and left the other two out. I figured maybe trying to charge four batteries was just too taxing on the unit, or something. After a number of hours, the two batteries I'd put back in the charger were at full capacity, as indicated by the charger. I tested the voltage on them and they were reading at what a freshly charged battery should read. Also, after charging just the two batteries, the unit was warm, but definitely not hot like before. I put the other two batteries on and went to bed. Got up the next day and the charger had finished charging them. Didn't overcharge or anything, so at least that feature works properly.

Bottom line is, I suppose I can't really recommend this product over any comparable chargers, because I have no experience with other chargers. I can say this, though: when using half of the battery slots, the batteries charge fine. When the batteries are at full capacity, the charger stops charging them. It mostly works like it's supposed to, with the exception of a few things. For the price, I guess I really couldn't expect it to be a perfect charger.

I can play my ipod, but it only works plugging it into the auxilary port. It will not play when plugged into the USB port, which kind of sucks. It won't charge it, either, but I didn't really expect it to. Luckily ipods have good battery life. I have tried the SD card slot, and it will play music from there, but you can't shuffle songs and the controls are kind of limited. If you turn off the radio and then turn it back on, it won't remember the last song you left off at and instead will start the playlist all over again. I don't use it much anymore.

Overall, for what I wanted - a work radio with decent speakers and the ability to play my ipod - it works out fine. If you're looking for something fancier, such as the ability to charge an ipod while playing it, or the ability to tune into more than one local radio station while inside a building, I suggest looking elsewhere, as you're probably going to be disappointed.

review_headline: A Good Second Attempt, but the AN-MR600 is Better
review_body:
Aesthetics: 5 out of 5 stars - Looks great, and feels great in the hand. It is very smooth, sleek, organic-looking, and ergonomic.
Material: 4/5 stars - High-quality plastic. Most of the remote is made of shiny/glossy plastic, while the button panel/area is a matte plastic.
Craftsmanship: 5/5 - Built well, no creaks with the creases and button areas while handling/pressing the buttons. The buttons have a nice firm "click" and tactile response.
Size/Weight: 5/5 - It is right at 6 inches long, and weighs 4.25 ounces with the 2 AA batteries installed.
Functionality: 3 out of 5 stars - While the remote itself is high-quality, beautiful, lightweight, and easy to function, the functionality is lacking. First, it takes a while to get use to the "air mouse/Wii controller" functionality and to wave it around and properly place it over the areas where you want to click. Second, when you perform a button press, the controller naturally is lowered because of your button-pressing movement, so you have to be very still and precise when you press the button. Finally, there is no dedicated "OK/Enter" button - rather, you press down on the scroll wheel like on some mouses. But because you have to click down on a scroll wheel, it is very easy to slip off the scroll wheel and miss the press, or have the pointer move out of place and miss the area where you are supposed to click on.
The other negative is - although there are few buttons on the controller so you don't get caught in "button-hunting" - there are not many dedicated buttons to function what you want. So to bring up the settings menu, you have to click on the "home" button, then move the point or directional button to the settings on-screen button, then lick the scroll wheel. There is also no button to quickly change the video/visual modes, so if you're watching a news program, and switch over to a movie, you can't switch from standard to cinema mode easily, and have to go through that whole procedure to get into the settings menu again. There is also no dedicated Netflix button, no channel number buttons, and so on and so on.

So in the end, although this is a good remote control, there is still a lot of room for improvement. I recommend the 2015 edition - model number AN-MR600 - but on the LG website it lists that it can work only with certain 2015 TVs, and are not backward-compatible. Let's hope LG comes up with a firmware update so you can use the 600 version with older TVs.

The dongle works fine - you connect it to a USB port on the back of LG TVs that have a ethernet port to turn it wireless.d have to go through that whole procedure to get into the settings menu again. There is also no dedicated Netflix button, no channel number buttons, and so on and so on.

product_title: Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 Carry-bag (Grey)
review_body:
The ROAR 2 is certainly a good speaker. The ROAR 2 Carry-bag, however, is much more mediocre.

Pros:

1.) No zippers etc that could damage the finish of the device itself.

2.) Fully reversible (dark grey on one side, and light grey on the other).

3). Comes with a carry-strap.

4.) Offers reasonable scratch protection in a bag.

4.) It's cute (it really is).

Cons:

1.) A little fiddly to get the unit into the case. Once you've done it a few times it gets slightly easier, but it still is a bit awkward, and doing it in a rush might result in an accident, so don't be in a hurry!

2.) While the case itself looks like it fully protects the unit before you put the speaker in it, once in, there are clear gaps on both sides between the top flap and the rest of the case - where the speaker could suffer scratch damage etc. If you don't use the carry strap, there are further gaps in the case, too.

3.) When the speaker is somewhat in there, it's only natural to want to push down on the middle of the speaker to fully insert it into the case. DO NOT DO THIS! (note the caps). The sides of the speaker are small subwoofers, and if you press on them too hard they WILL break.

4.) The speaker itself weighs 2.2 lbs, and I'd imagine if you dropped the speaker from even a few feet in this case, your speaker is going to get dented/damaged.

5.) It's very expensive for what it is.

Overall, it feels like the design team of the ROAR 2 itself had very little communication with the design team of the case, and as such, the case is a passable solution. At this time of review there probably isn't much in the way of other options, sadly..

3 stars out of 5. It's... OK...

*Sample received for objective review*
